items.text: Presheaves and sheaves on a space
Session of 4 April 1973
Tape 1, side A
The open sets $\mathcal{O}(X)$ of a space $X$, ordered by inclusion, form a category: $\mathrm{Hom}(U,V)$ is a singleton if $U\subset V$, empty otherwise.
A presheaf of sets on $X$ is a functor $F\colon\mathcal{O}(X)^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Set}$; the maps $F(V)\to F(U)$, $U\subset V$, are the restrictions.
A morphism of presheaves $F\to G$ is a natural transformation: maps $F(U)\to G(U)$ compatible with the restrictions.
$F$ is separated if, for every open covering $U=\bigcup U_i$, the map $F(U)\to\prod_i F(U_i)$ is injective.
$F$ is a sheaf if, for every covering $U=\bigcup U_i$, the sequence $F(U)\to\prod_i F(U_i)\rightrightarrows\prod_{i,j}F(U_i\cap U_j)$ is exact (equalizer).
The sheaves on $X$ form a full subcategory $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ (denoted here “Top(X)”) of the category of presheaves.
Examples of sheaves
For a set $E$, the presheaf $U\mapsto E^U$ of maps from $U$ to $E$ is a sheaf.
A subpresheaf $G\subset F$ is a family of subsets $G(U)\subset F(U)$ stable under the restrictions.
A subpresheaf of a separated presheaf is separated.
A subpresheaf $G$ of a sheaf $F$ is a sheaf if and only if membership of a section in $G$ is a local property on $U$.
If $E$ is a topological space, the continuous maps from open sets of $X$ to $E$ form a subsheaf of $U\mapsto E^U$.
For differentiable (or analytic) manifolds $X$ and $E$, the differentiable (resp. analytic) maps form a sheaf.
For $p\colon E\to X$ continuous, the continuous sections $\Gamma(U,E)$ over the open sets $U$ form a sheaf.
The sheaf of continuous maps from $X$ to $E$ is isomorphic to the sheaf of sections of the second projection $E\times X\to X$.
On a locally compact space $X$, the Radon measures on the open sets of $X$ form a sheaf.
On a differentiable manifold, the distributions on the open sets form a sheaf.
$U\mapsto\{\text{subsets of }U\}$, with restriction by intersection, is a sheaf; the closed subsets of $U$ form a subsheaf.
On an analytic space, the analytic subsets of the open sets form a sheaf.
Sheaves of sections and the case of a point
The sheaf of sections $\widetilde{E}$ of a space $E$ over $X$ defines a functor $\mathrm{Fib}(X)\to\mathrm{Sh}(X)$, $f\mapsto(s\mapsto f\circ s)$.
This functor is not fully faithful: for $X$ a point, it is identified with the forgetful functor from topological spaces to $\mathbf{Set}$.
On a point, the functor $\Gamma\colon F\mapsto F(\mathrm{pt})$ is an equivalence of categories $\mathrm{Sh}(\mathrm{pt})\simeq\mathbf{Set}$.
For $U$ open, $\Gamma_U\colon F\mapsto F(U)$ is a functor $\mathrm{Sh}(X)\to\mathbf{Set}$; we write $\Gamma(F)=\Gamma(X,F)=F(X)$.
Tape 1, side B
Limits and colimits
Tape 2, side A
On the word « étalé »: it comes from domaines étalés in complex analysis, has no English equivalent, and 'local homeomorphism' is judged misleading and unfit for differentiable or analytic settings.
Asked whether the oldest étale maps are Riemann surfaces, the lecturer agrees, once ramification points are removed, though sheaves were not then in view.
The notions dual to products, equalizers, fibre products and the terminal object are coproducts, coequalizers, pushouts and the initial object.
In $\mathbf{Set}$, coproducts are disjoint unions and the initial object is $\varnothing$.
In $\mathbf{Set}$, the coequalizer of $E\rightrightarrows F$ is the quotient of $F$ by the equivalence relation generated by the image of $E$ in $F\times F$.
In groups, the coproduct is the free product; the coproduct of $n$ copies of $\mathbb{Z}$ is the free group on $n$ generators.
For the usual algebraic structures, limits are computed on the underlying sets, but colimits are not.
If $S$ admits limits (resp. colimits) of a given type, $\mathrm{Hom}(C^{\mathrm{op}},S)$ admits them too, computed argumentwise.
The category opposite to $\mathrm{Hom}(C^{\mathrm{op}},S)$ is $\mathrm{Hom}(C,S^{\mathrm{op}})$.
Presheaves on $X$ admit all colimits, computed open set by open set.
The subcategory $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ is not stable in presheaves under any of the usual types of colimit.
The coproduct, taken in presheaves, of the terminal object with itself (the constant presheaf with two elements) is not a sheaf.
For every sheaf $F$, $F(\varnothing)$ is a singleton ($\varnothing$ being covered by the empty family).
The initial presheaf $U\mapsto\varnothing$ is not a sheaf.
A colimit of sheaves exists if and only if the functor $G\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(P,G)$ on $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ is representable, $P$ being the colimit taken in presheaves.
The associated sheaf
The sheaf associated to a presheaf $P$ is a sheaf $\widetilde{P}$ equipped with $P\to\widetilde{P}$, universal among morphisms from $P$ to sheaves.
Every presheaf admits an associated sheaf, unique up to unique isomorphism.
$\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ admits all colimits, the sheaf associated to the colimit computed in presheaves.
A presheaf and its associated sheaf have the same stalks.
In terms of étalé spaces, the coproduct of a family of sheaves is the disjoint topological sum, which is étalé over $X$.
The coequalizer of $F\rightrightarrows G$ (étalé spaces over $X$) is $G/R$, with the quotient topology, $R$ the generated relation; $G/R$ is étalé over $X$.
Coproducts and coequalizers of double arrows suffice to construct all colimits.
Exactness properties of sheaves
Principle: $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ has the exactness properties of $\mathbf{Set}$ that involve arbitrary colimits and finite limits.
In $\mathbf{Set}$, an arbitrary product of epimorphisms is an epimorphism; this is false in $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ in general.

Infinite products of epimorphisms are epimorphisms in sets, because surjections split there, but not for sheaves; the lecturer warns that infinite inverse limits behave differently and promises to return to it.
Categories of presheaves (of functors to $\mathbf{Set}$) have all the exactness properties of $\mathbf{Set}$, limits and colimits being computed argumentwise.
The functor $a\colon P\mapsto\widetilde{P}$ is left adjoint to the inclusion $i$: $\mathrm{Hom}(P,iF)\simeq\mathrm{Hom}(aP,F)$; it commutes with colimits.
The associated-sheaf functor is left exact (it commutes with finite products and equalizers).
In $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$, coequalizers are stable under base change: $\mathrm{Coker}(F\rightrightarrows G)\times_H H'$ is the coequalizer of the inverse images over $H'$.
In $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$, coproducts are stable under base change: $(\coprod_i F_i)\times_F F'\simeq\coprod_i(F_i\times_F F')$.
Quotients and equivalence relations
A quotient object of $F$ is a class of epimorphisms $F\to G$ up to isomorphism under $F$.
Tape 2, side B
For every morphism $F\to G$, the fibre product $F\times_G F\subset F\times F$ is an equivalence relation on $F$.
To an equivalence relation $R\subset F\times F$ is associated the coequalizer of $R\rightrightarrows F$, a quotient of $F$ (an epimorphism).
A quotient is effective if it is the quotient by its relation $F\times_G F$; a relation $R$ is effective if $R=F\times_{F/R}F$.
In $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$, as in $\mathbf{Set}$, equivalence relations and quotients are effective and correspond bijectively.
Torsors and stalkwise checks
Session of 11 May 1973
Tape 1, side A
In $\mathbf{Set}$, $G$ acts simply transitively on $E$ if $G\times E\to E\times E$, $(g,x)\mapsto(gx,x)$, is bijective; $E$ is a torsor if moreover $E\to\mathrm{pt}$ is surjective.
$E\to F$ is a monomorphism if and only if $E\to E\times_F E$ is an isomorphism; dually, an epimorphism if $F\sqcup_E F\to F$ is an isomorphism.
A torsor under a sheaf of groups $G$ is a $G$-sheaf $E$ with $G\times E\simeq E\times E$ and $E\to 1$ an epimorphism (and not $E(U)$ a torsor for every $U$).
A morphism of sheaves is an epimorphism if and only if it is one on stalks; $E$ is a $G$-torsor if and only if each $E_x$ is a $G_x$-torsor.
A torsor is trivial (isomorphic to $G$ acting by translations) if and only if it admits a global section; nontrivial ones exist.
Principle: statements about structures defined by finite limits and colimits can be checked stalkwise, the fibre functors forming an exact conservative family.

The principle that statements proved for sets transfer to sheaves by checking on fibres is recalled with a historical remark: Chevalley devoted a year of his IHÉS seminar around 1958 to formalising it.
The structures of field and of integral domain cannot be expressed by finite limits alone.
A sheaf of rings $K$ is called integral if $K'\sqcup 1\to K$ (inclusion and zero section) is an epimorphism, $K'$ being defined below.
For two sheaves $K$, $L$, the presheaf $\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(K,L)\colon U\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(K|_U,L|_U)$ is a sheaf.
The sections $f$ of $K$ whose left and right multiplications are monomorphisms of $K|_U$ form a subsheaf $K'$ (a local property).
Generating families and images
$(Z_i)$ is a generating family of $C$ if every monomorphism $E\to F$ such that $\mathrm{Hom}(Z_i,E)\to\mathrm{Hom}(Z_i,F)$ is bijective for all $i$ is an isomorphism.
In $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$, $(Z_i)$ is generating if and only if the family of functors $\mathrm{Hom}(Z_i,-)$ is conservative.
In $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$, every morphism factors, essentially uniquely, as an epimorphism followed by a monomorphism (image).
In $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$, a morphism that is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism is an isomorphism.
An open set $U$ of $X$ defines a sheaf: $U(V)$ is a singleton if $V\subset U$, empty otherwise.
For every sheaf $E$, $\mathrm{Hom}(U,E)=E(U)$; the open sets of $X$ therefore form a small generating family of $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$.
Abelian sheaves and injectives
The abelian sheaves on $X$ (abelian group objects of $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$) form an abelian category $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$.
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ admits limits and colimits; filtered colimits there commute with the forgetful functor and are exact.
An abelian sheaf $I$ is injective if every morphism $F\to I$ extends along every monomorphism $F\to G$.
An abelian category with exact filtered colimits and a small generating family has enough injectives; this is the case of $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ (free abelian sheaves on the $Z_i$).
For a sheaf of rings $A$, $\mathrm{Mod}(A)$ is abelian, with exact filtered colimits and generators, hence has enough injectives ($\mathrm{Ext}$, cohomology).
In general $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ does not have enough projectives; filtered limits there are not exact.
Direct and inverse images
Tape 1, side B
For $f\colon X\to Y$, an $f$-morphism $G\to F$ is a family $G(V)\to F(U)$, for $f(U)\subset V$, compatible with the restrictions.
An $f$-morphism is equivalent to a family $G(V)\to F(f^{-1}(V))$ compatible with the restrictions.
$V\mapsto f^{-1}(V)$ is an increasing functor $\mathcal{O}_Y\to\mathcal{O}_X$ that commutes with arbitrary unions.
Direct image of a presheaf $F$ on $X$, $f_*F(V)=F(f^{-1}(V))$, a presheaf on $Y$.
The $f$-morphisms $G\to F$ correspond bijectively to the morphisms $G\to f_*F$ of presheaves on $Y$.
On presheaves, $f_*$ commutes with arbitrary limits and colimits.
The direct image of a sheaf is a sheaf.
$f_*\colon\mathrm{Sh}(X)\to\mathrm{Sh}(Y)$ commutes with arbitrary limits.
In general $f_*$ commutes neither with coproducts nor with epimorphisms: for $Y$ a point, $f_*$ is $\Gamma(X,-)$.
The inverse image $f^*G$ is equipped with a universal $f$-morphism $G\to f^*G$; $f^*$ is the left adjoint of $f_*$.
For every functor $\varphi\colon C\to D$, the restriction $\widehat{D}\to\widehat{C}$, $P\mapsto P\circ\varphi$, has a left adjoint and a right adjoint.
$f^*G$ is the sheaf associated to the presheaf inverse image $f^*_{\mathrm{pr}}G$.
$f^*$ commutes with arbitrary colimits (left adjoint).
$f^*$ is left exact (it commutes with finite limits).
The inverse image of a space $G\to Y$ under $f$ is $X\times_Y G\subset X\times G$, with the induced topology; it is a fibre product in topological spaces.
The property of being étalé is stable under base change.
For sheaves viewed as étalé spaces, $f^*G$ corresponds to the fibre product $X\times_Y G$.
Étalé spaces over $Y$ are stable under finite limits in spaces over $Y$.
The fibre of $X\times_Y G$ at $x$ is homeomorphic to the fibre of $G$ at $f(x)$.
$(f^*G)_x\simeq G_{f(x)}$; hence again the left exactness of $f^*$.
Tape 2, side A
Stalks and epimorphisms
Tape 2, side B
Two morphisms $u,v\colon F\to G$ of sheaves are equal if and only if $u_x=v_x$ for all $x$: the fibre functors form a faithful family.
The fibre functors commute with colimits and finite limits and form a conservative family.
$F\to G$ is an epimorphism of sheaves if and only if every section of $G$ lifts locally to a section of $F$.
An epimorphism of sheaves is not in general an epimorphism of presheaves: $\Gamma(F)\to\Gamma(G)$ is not always surjective.
For $X$ compact, $\Gamma(X,-)$ sends epimorphisms of sheaves to surjections if and only if $X$ is totally disconnected.
Algebraic structures on objects of a category
A composition law on an object $E$ of $C$ is an arrow $E\times E\to E$; commutativity and associativity are expressed by diagrams.
A left unit is an arrow $1\to E$ ($1$ terminal) such that $E\simeq 1\times E\to E\times E\to E$ is the identity.
Via the Yoneda embedding, a law $E\times E\to E$ is equivalent to laws on the $E(Z)=\mathrm{Hom}(Z,E)$, functorial in $Z$.
An algebraic structure (group, ring, module, etc.) on $E$ is such a structure on each $E(Z)$, functorial in $Z$.
The structure of a category ($D_1\rightrightarrows D_0$, composition $D_1\times_{D_0}D_1\to D_1$, units) is described by fibre products.
A category internal to $C$ is a pair $(D_0,D_1)$ with a category structure on $(D_0(Z),D_1(Z))$, functorial in $Z$.
The embedding $C\to\widehat{C}$ commutes with arbitrary limits, but not with colimits in general.
A structure defined by limits on a sheaf $F$ is equivalent to the same structure on each $F(U)$, functorial in $U$.
A sheaf of groups is a functor $\mathcal{O}(X)^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Grp}$ whose composite with the forgetful functor is a sheaf.
The axioms of a structure defined by finite limits can be checked stalkwise.
A functor that commutes with finite products sends group objects (ring objects, etc.) to objects of the same type.
The stalks of a sheaf of groups (of rings, etc.) are groups (rings, etc.).
For a $k$-coalgebra $A$, an $A$-comodule is a $k$-module $M$ equipped with $M\to M\otimes_k A$ satisfying coassociativity and counit.
The tensor product of modules is constructed by colimits (sums, quotients), not by limits alone.
For sheaves of modules, $M(U)\otimes_{k(U)}A(U)\to(M\otimes_k A)(U)$ is in general neither injective nor surjective.
$E$ is a torsor under a group $G$ if $E\neq\varnothing$ and $G$ acts simply transitively on $E$.
Étale morphisms and slice categories
Session of 18 May 1973
Tape 1, side A
For a point $y$ of $Y$ and the inclusion $i_y:\{y\}\to Y$, we have $i_y^*F\simeq F_y$: the stalk is the inverse image under a point.
If $f:X\to Y$ is étale, $X$ is an object of $\mathrm{Sh}(Y)$ and $\mathrm{Sh}(X)\simeq\mathrm{Sh}(Y)/X$; a composite of étale morphisms is étale.
For an object $X$ of a category $C$, the category $C/X$ has as objects the arrows $X'\to X$ and as morphisms the commutative triangles.
If $f:X\to Y$ is étale, $f^*G$ is the product $G\times X$ in $\mathrm{Sh}(Y)$, viewed as an object of $\mathrm{Sh}(Y)/X$.
For $g:X'\to X$ in $\mathrm{Sh}(Y)$, the functor $g^*:\mathrm{Sh}(Y)/X\to\mathrm{Sh}(Y)/X'$ is the base change $F\mapsto F\times_X X'$.
$f_*$ sends every structure defined by limits (group, ring, etc.) to a structure of the same kind, but not torsors.
$f^*$ respects structures defined by finite limits and colimits: the inverse image of a $G$-torsor is an $f^*G$-torsor.
Ring and field objects
A ring object $A$ of $C$ is an object equipped with a ring structure on each $A(Z)=\mathrm{Hom}_C(Z,A)$, functorial in $Z$.
The units $A^*(Z)\subset A(Z)$ form a group-valued functor, represented by the fibre product of $m:A\times A\to A$ and $1:e\to A$.
A ring object $A$ is a field object if the morphism $A^*\sqcup e\to A$ (inclusion and zero section) is an isomorphism.
Integrality, first condition: for $C=m^{-1}(0)\subset A\times A$, the morphism $A\sqcup A\to C$, $x\mapsto(x,0)$, $x\mapsto(0,x)$, is an epimorphism.
A morphism $S\to C$ is an epimorphism iff the canonical arrow $C\sqcup_S C\to C$ is an isomorphism.
Integrality, second condition ($0\neq1$): the kernel $e'\subset e$ of $0,1:e\rightrightarrows A$ is initial; in $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$, $e'$ is the largest open set where $A=0$.
Every kind of structure defined by finite limits and arbitrary colimits admits a “classifying topos”, equipped with a universal model.
Normal rings, reduced rings, rings with connected spectrum can also be defined by such diagrammatic axioms.
A sheaf of rings is never a presheaf of fields: its value on $\varnothing$ is the zero ring.
A question shows that a sheaf of fields in the usual sense can never be a field object: sections over disjoint opens form a product of fields, and the empty open gives the zero ring.
On a space, such an axiom is checked stalkwise: a sheaf of rings $A$ is a field object iff each stalk $A_x$ is a field.
Constant sheaves and sheaves of fields
The constant sheaf $I_X=p^*I$ ($p:X\to\mathrm{pt}$) has étalé space $I\times X$; it is the coproduct of $I$ copies of the terminal object.
If $I$ is a group, a ring or a field, $I_X$ is a sheaf of groups, of rings or of fields; for example $K_X$ for a field $K$.
On a reduced and locally irreducible complex analytic space, the sheaf $\mathcal{M}_X$ of meromorphic functions is a sheaf of fields.
The stalk $\mathcal{M}_{X,x}$ is the total ring of fractions of $\mathcal{O}_{X,x}$; it is a field as soon as $\mathcal{O}_{X,x}$ is a domain.
On an integral scheme, the sheaf of rational functions is a constant sheaf of fields; the analytic sheaf $\mathcal{M}_X$ is not.
Internal Hom and the subobject sheaf
$\mathcal{H}om(F,G)(U)=\mathrm{Hom}(F|_U,G|_U)$ defines a sheaf on $X$, to be distinguished from the set $\mathrm{Hom}(F,G)$.
Tape 1, side B
For $X'$ étale over $X$: $\mathrm{Hom}(X',\mathcal{H}om(F,G))\simeq\mathrm{Hom}_{X'}(F\times X',G\times X')\simeq\mathrm{Hom}(F\times X',G)$.
In a category with products, $\mathcal{H}om(F,G)$ is, if it exists, the object representing $X'\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(F\times X',G)$; it exists in $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$.
For group objects $F,G$, $\mathcal{H}om_{\mathrm{gr}}(F,G)$ represents $X'\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{gr}}(F_{X'},G_{X'})$, homomorphisms of group objects of $C/X'$.
The sheaf $\mathcal{P}(F)$: $\mathcal{P}(F)(U)$ is the set of subsheaves of $F|_U$; for $X$ a point, it is the set of subsets of $F$.
$\mathcal{P}(F)$ represents $X'\mapsto\mathrm{Sub}(F\times X')$; the subobjects of an object of $C/X'$ are the same in $C$ and in $C/X'$.
For the terminal object $e$, $\mathcal{P}(e)$ is the sheaf that associates to $U$ the set of its open subsets; it represents $X'\mapsto\mathrm{Sub}(X')$.
If $\mathcal{P}(e)$ exists, $\mathcal{P}(F)$ exists iff $\mathcal{H}om(F,\mathcal{P}(e))$ exists, and they are isomorphic; in $\mathbf{Set}$, $\mathcal{P}(e)$ has two elements.
A subsheaf of $\mathcal{P}(F)$ is a family of sets of subsheaves of the $F|_U$, stable under restriction and local in $U$.
A topology on a sheaf $F$ is defined as a subsheaf of $\mathcal{P}(F)$ satisfying the usual axioms, read in $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$.
For $f:X\to Y$, there are canonical arrows $f^*\mathcal{H}om(F,G)\to\mathcal{H}om(f^*F,f^*G)$ and $f^*\mathcal{P}(F)\to\mathcal{P}(f^*F)$.
These arrows are not isomorphisms in general, for example for a fibre functor; they are if $f$ is étale.
Stalks and infinite products
$f^*$ does not commute with infinite products in general; there is a canonical arrow $(\prod_i F_i)_x\to\prod_i(F_i)_x$.
Its injectivity means: if $f_i,g_i$ have the same germ at $x$ for every $i$, they coincide on a common neighbourhood of $x$.
$U_i$ open neighbourhoods of $x$ whose intersection is not a neighbourhood, $F$ the sheaf of maps to $\{a,b\}$, $f_i=a$, $g_i=a$ on $U_i$ and $b$ elsewhere.
The stalk functor at $x$ commutes with products iff $x$ has a smallest open neighbourhood; if points are closed, iff $x$ is isolated.
In $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$, an infinite product of epimorphisms is not always an epimorphism; one reduces to the case of the $F_i\to e$.
$X$ locally connected, $x$ closed, $U_i$ open neighbourhoods of $x$ whose intersection is not a neighbourhood, $F_i=U_i\sqcup(X\setminus\{x\})$; $\prod_i F_i\to e$ is not an epimorphism.
Looking for a counterexample to products of epimorphisms of sheaves being epimorphisms, the lecturer finds none on locally connected spaces such as a line, nor on totally disconnected compact ones.
If $X$ is compact and totally disconnected, $F\to G$ is an epimorphism iff $F(U)\to G(U)$ is surjective for every clopen set $U$; every product of epimorphisms is an epimorphism.
Connectedness and cohomology
$X$ is connected iff the terminal object of $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ is not a sum of two non-initial subobjects.
Tape 2, side A
$X$ is nonempty iff $\varnothing\to e$ is not an isomorphism in $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$; $X$ is empty iff $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ is equivalent to the point category.
The abelian group objects of $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ form a category with enough injectives; $H^i(X,F)=R^i\Gamma(F)$, with $\Gamma(F)=\mathrm{Hom}(e,F)$.
For an abelian group $M$, we set $H^i(X,M)=H^i(X,M_X)$; these groups depend only on the category $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$.
$X$ is connected iff $\mathbb{Z}\to H^0(X,\mathbb{Z})$ is surjective; connected and nonempty iff it is bijective.
The sections of $I_X$ over $U$ are the locally constant maps $U\to I$.
The lattice of open sets of $X$ is that of the subobjects of the terminal object of $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$; the Čech constructions (Artin–Mazur) follow from it.
Covering spaces and torsors
If $X$ is connected, locally connected and locally simply connected, the covering spaces of $X$ correspond to $\pi_1(X,x)$-sets.
The covering spaces of $X$ are the locally constant objects $X'$ of $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$: $X'\times U_i\simeq\coprod_{S_i}U_i$ for a covering $e=\sup_i U_i$.
For $X$ connected and locally connected but not locally simply connected, the covering spaces are classified by a pro-group.
For a sheaf of groups $G$ not necessarily commutative, $H^1(X,G)$ is the set of isomorphism classes of $G$-torsors.
A $G$-torsor is an object $P$ equipped with an action of $G$ such that $G\times P\to P\times P$ is an isomorphism and $P\to e$ an epimorphism.
$G\mapsto G_X=\coprod_G e$ is left exact; the $G_X$-torsors are the Galois covering spaces with group $G$.

For $X$ connected, locally connected and locally simply connected, $H^1(X,G)$ is identified with $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1(X,x),G)$ modulo conjugation; $X$ is simply connected iff all these $H^1$ are trivial.
Stacks and gerbes
A fibred category over $\mathcal{O}(X)$ associates to $U$ a category $F_U$, and to $V\subset U$ a restriction functor, transitive up to coherent isomorphism.
$U\mapsto\mathrm{Sh}(U)$, fibre spaces over $U$, sheaves of groups on $U$, $G|_U$-torsors.
items.name: which are stacks

items.text: A fibred category is a stack if the presheaves $\mathcal{H}om(F,G)$ are sheaves and if every gluing datum (cocycle on the $U_{ijk}$) is effective.
For $G$ noncommutative, $H^2(X,G)$ is defined as a set of classes of stacks (gerbes) attached to $G$ (Giraud); it depends only on $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$.
A stack over $\mathcal{E}$ is a fibred category over $\mathcal{E}$ with descent along epimorphic families, the intersections becoming fibre products.
Restriction and extension give an equivalence between stacks over $\mathcal{O}(X)$ and stacks over $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$.
Gluing and quotient topoi
$\mathrm{Sh}(\coprod_i X_i)\simeq\prod_i\mathrm{Sh}(X_i)$: the sum of spaces corresponds to the product of categories.
If $Z$ is closed in $X$ and in $Y$, $\mathrm{Sh}(X\cup_Z Y)$ is the 2-fibre product of $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ and $\mathrm{Sh}(Y)$ over $\mathrm{Sh}(Z)$.
For an equivalence relation $R$ on $X$, the sheaves on $X$ equipped with descent data relative to $R$ form a quotient topos, even if $X/R$ is pathological.
Irreducible closed sets and sober spaces
A space $Z$ is irreducible if it is nonempty and not a union of two distinct closed subsets of $Z$.
A separated space is irreducible iff it is a point; a variety is irreducible for the Zariski topology iff it is so in the algebraic sense.
The closure of an irreducible subset is irreducible.
We write $\tilde X$ for the set of irreducible closed subsets of $X$ and $i:X\to\tilde X$, $x\mapsto\overline{\{x\}}$; $i$ is bijective if $X$ is separated.
The subsets $\tilde U=\{Y\in\tilde X : Y\cap U\neq\varnothing\}$, $U$ open, form a topology: $U\mapsto\tilde U$ respects unions and finite intersections.
We have $i^{-1}(\tilde U)=U$; $i$ is continuous and induces a lattice isomorphism $\mathcal{O}(\tilde X)\simeq\mathcal{O}(X)$.
Consequently $i_*:\mathrm{Sh}(X)\to\mathrm{Sh}(\tilde X)$ is an isomorphism of categories, with inverse $i^*$.
Tape 2, side B
$i:X\to\tilde X$ is injective iff $X$ is $T_0$; if $X$ is separated, $i$ is a homeomorphism.
A generic point of a closed set $Z$ is a point whose closure is $Z$; $i$ is surjective iff every irreducible closed set has a generic point.
A variety over $K$ reduced to its $K$-rational points has irreducible closed sets without a generic point.
$X$ is sober if every irreducible closed set has exactly one generic point, i.e. if $i:X\to\tilde X$ is bijective, hence a homeomorphism.
For $Y$ an irreducible closed set, the stalk $F_Y=\varinjlim_{U\cap Y\neq\varnothing}F(U)$ (filtered colimit) is left exact and commutes with colimits.
$F_{\overline{\{x\}}}=F_x$; in general $F_Y$ is the stalk at the point $Y$ of $F$ viewed as a sheaf on $\tilde X$.
$Y\mapsto(F\mapsto F_Y)$ is a bijection from $\tilde X$ onto the classes of fibre functors $\mathrm{Sh}(X)\to\mathbf{Set}$ (left exact, commuting with $\varinjlim$).
A fibre functor on $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ has no nontrivial automorphism.
$\tilde X$ is sober, and $X\mapsto\tilde X$ is left adjoint to the inclusion of sober spaces: $\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)\simeq\mathrm{Hom}(\tilde X,Y)$ for $Y$ sober.
On the set $\Phi(\mathcal{E})$ of classes of fibre functors, the sets $\tilde U=\{\varepsilon : \varepsilon(U)\neq\varnothing\}$, $U\subset e$, form a topology.
$X\to\Phi(\mathrm{Sh}(X))$ is a homeomorphism iff $X$ is sober: a sober space can be reconstructed from $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$.
If $X$ is $T_1$ (for example the closed points of a Jacobson scheme), $X$ is identified with the subspace of closed points of $\tilde X$.
Points and morphisms of sober spaces
Session of 25 May 1973
Tape 1, side A
For $f:X\to Y$ continuous, the point $f(x)$ corresponds to the fibre functor $\varepsilon_x\circ f^*$, since $(f^*F)_x\simeq F_{f(x)}$.
If $X$ and $Y$ are sober, every functor $\mathrm{Sh}(Y)\to\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ that is left exact and commutes with $\varinjlim$ is isomorphic to $f^*$ for a unique continuous $f$.
Two functors on $\mathrm{Sh}(Y)$ that commute with colimits and are isomorphic on the generating subcategory $\mathcal{O}(Y)$ are isomorphic.
For $f,g:X\to Y$, a morphism from $f$ to $g$ is a morphism between $f^*$ and $g^*$; if $Y$ is separated, there is one only if $f=g$, and it is the identity.
Definitions of a topos

A topos is a category having the exactness properties of $\mathbf{Set}$ (arbitrary $\varinjlim$, finite $\varprojlim$) and a small generating set. This first form is provisional: it is made precise by the axioms given a few minutes later.
items.name: first form

items.text: $C\subset\mathrm{Ob}\,\mathcal{E}$ is generating if $\mathcal{E}\to\widehat{C}$, $X\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(-,X)|_C$, is faithful.
In a topos, it amounts to the same whether this functor is faithful, fully faithful, conservative, or conservative on monomorphisms.
A topos is a category with (a) finite $\varprojlim$, (b) universal disjoint coproducts, (c) universal effective equivalence relations, (d) a small generator.
items.name: Giraud

items.text: A coproduct $X=\coprod X_i$ is universal if for every $X'\to X$, the arrow $\coprod_i(X_i\times_X X')\to X'$ is an isomorphism.
It is disjoint if the $X_i\to X$ are monomorphisms and $X_i\times_X X_j$ is initial for $i\neq j$.
An equivalence relation $R\subset X\times X$ (each $R(Z)$ being one on $X(Z)$) is effective if $R\simeq X\times_{X/R}X$.
It is universal if $X\to X/R$ is a universal epimorphism and if passage to the quotient commutes with base changes $Y'\to X/R$.
In a topos, the subobjects and the quotient objects of an object form small sets.
Cohomology in a topos
$\mathcal{E}_{ab}$ is abelian, with exact filtered colimits and a generator; it therefore has enough injectives.
An injective object of $\mathcal{E}_{ab}$ is injective in $\mathcal{E}$; in particular $\mathcal{E}$ has enough injectives.
In a topos, $\Gamma(X)=\mathrm{Hom}(e,X)$; its derived functors on $\mathcal{E}_{ab}$ are the $H^i(\mathcal{E},-)$.
The constant object $I_{\mathcal{E}}=\coprod_I e$: $I\mapsto I_{\mathcal{E}}$ commutes with $\varinjlim$ and finite $\varprojlim$; we set $H^i(\mathcal{E},M)=H^i(\mathcal{E},M_{\mathcal{E}})$.
A topos has homotopy invariants (pro-groups, the Čech method of Artin–Mazur), which recover the $\pi_i$ of a locally contractible space.
Basic examples of topoi
$\mathrm{Sh}(\varnothing)$ is equivalent to the point category: it is the “empty topos”.
A topos $\mathcal{E}$ is empty iff the arrow $\varnothing_{\mathcal{E}}\to e_{\mathcal{E}}$ is an isomorphism.
$\mathrm{Sh}(\mathrm{pt})\simeq\mathbf{Set}$ via $F\mapsto F(\mathrm{pt})$: it is the point topos, or “final topos”.
A topos $\mathcal{E}$ is a point iff the functor $\mathbf{Set}\to\mathcal{E}$, $I\mapsto I_{\mathcal{E}}$, is an equivalence.
For a discrete group $G$ acting on $X$, the category $\mathrm{Sh}(X,G)$ of étalé spaces over $X$ equipped with a compatible $G$-action is a topos.
$\mathrm{Sh}(X,\{1\})=\mathrm{Sh}(X)$; $\mathrm{Sh}(\mathrm{pt},G)=B_G$, the category of $G$-sets, is the “classifying topos” of $G$.
$(B_G)_{ab}$ is the category of $G$-modules, $\Gamma(M)=M^G$ and $H^i(B_G,M)=H^i(G,M)$, the cohomology of the classifying space of $G$.
The cohomology of $\mathrm{Sh}(X,G)$ is the equivariant cohomology $H^i(X;G,M)$ (Tôhoku).
Points of a topos
Tape 1, side B
If $G\neq1$, the topos $B_G$ is equivalent to no $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$.
The forgetful functor $B_G\to\mathbf{Set}$ is a fibre functor, with automorphism group $G$.
If $X$ is sober, every fibre functor on $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ is isomorphic to $F\mapsto F_x$ for a unique $x\in X$.
Specialization ($y\in\overline{\{x\}}$) is a preorder, which is an order if $X$ is sober; it induces $F_y\to F_x$, functorial in $F$.
There is a morphism $\varepsilon_y\to\varepsilon_x$ iff $y$ is a specialization of $x$, and it is unique: the points of $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ form an ordered set.
$B_G$ has a single point up to isomorphism without being the final topos: its points have nontrivial automorphisms.
In $\mathrm{Sh}(X,G)$, $\varepsilon^G_x:F\mapsto F_x$ is a point, with automorphism group the stabilizer $G_x$.
Giraud's theorem and elementary topoi
$\mathcal{E}$ is a topos iff there exist $C$ small and $i:\mathcal{E}\to\widehat{C}$ fully faithful with a left exact left adjoint.
items.name: Giraud

items.text: For every generating full subcategory $C$ of a topos, $\mathcal{E}\to\widehat{C}$ is fully faithful and has a left exact left adjoint.
Topoi in the sense of Giraud's axioms are exactly the categories of sheaves on a site.
In a topos, $\mathcal{H}om(X,Y)$ exists: it represents $Z\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(X\times Z,Y)$.
In a topos, the functor $Z\mapsto\mathrm{Sub}(Z)$ is representable by an object $P_{\mathcal{E}}$.
In a topos, $P:\mathcal{E}^{\circ}\to\mathbf{Set}$ is representable iff it sends colimits to limits.
Every topos is an elementary topos (Lawvere–Tierney: finite $\varprojlim$, $\mathcal{H}om$, $P_{\mathcal{E}}$); an elementary topos with small coproducts and a small generator is a topos.
Presheaf topoi and the classifying topos of a group
Lawvere's elementary topoi are compared with Giraud's: more general, with finitary axioms, though internal Hom is a very strong operation; adding generators and limits recovers sheaf topoi.
In $\mathrm{Sh}(X,G)$, limits, $\mathcal{H}om$ and $P$ are computed in $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$, with the induced action of $G$.
For $C$ small, $\widehat{C}$ is a topos (limits argumentwise, representables generating), with all the exactness properties of $\mathbf{Set}$.
$B_G=\widehat{C}$ for $C$ the category with one object whose endomorphisms are $G$.
For $X\in C$, $F\mapsto F(X)$ is a point of $\widehat{C}$; every point is a filtered colimit of these, and $\widehat{C}$ has enough points.
$\mathrm{Sh}(X,G)$ has enough points: the $\varepsilon^G_x$ form a conservative family.
For a group object $G$ of a topos $\mathcal{E}$, the objects of $\mathcal{E}$ equipped with an action of $G$ form a topos $B_G$; for $\mathcal{E}=\mathbf{Set}$, the $G$-sets.
$H^i(G,M)=H^i(B_G,M)$ for $M$ abelian with an action of $G$; $\Gamma(X)$ is the set of $G$-invariant sections of $X$.
$B_G$ classifies $G$-torsors: for $f:\mathcal{T}\to\mathcal{E}$, the morphisms $\mathcal{T}\to B_G$ over $\mathcal{E}$ correspond to the $f^*G$-torsors.
Induced topoi
For an object $X$ of a topos $\mathcal{E}$, $\mathcal{E}/X$ is a topos, the induced topos; $\mathrm{Sh}(Y)/X\simeq\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ for $X$ étale over $Y$.
Morphisms of topoi
Between topoi, every functor $f^*$ commuting with colimits has a right adjoint $f_*$ (representability lemma).
Tape 2, side A
A morphism of topoi $f:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{F}$ is a pair of adjoint functors $f^*\dashv f_*$, with $f^*:\mathcal{F}\to\mathcal{E}$ left exact.
The morphisms $\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{F}$ form a category $\mathbf{Homtop}(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$, whose arrows $f\to g$ are the morphisms $f_*\to g_*$ (or $g^*\to f^*$).
Composition: $(gf)_*=g_*f_*$ and $(gf)^*=f^*g^*$; it is associative.
Composition is a functor $\mathbf{Homtop}(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})\times\mathbf{Homtop}(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G})\to\mathbf{Homtop}(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{G})$: topoi form a 2-category.
A morphism $f$ is an equivalence of topoi iff $f^*$, or $f_*$, is an equivalence of categories.
For $Y$ sober, the category of points $\mathbf{Homtop}(\mathrm{pt},\mathrm{Sh}(Y))$ is equivalent to $Y$ ordered by specialization.
For $X,Y$ sober, $\mathbf{Homtop}(\mathrm{Sh}(X),\mathrm{Sh}(Y))$ is equivalent to the continuous maps $f$ ordered by $f\le g$ iff $g(x)\in\overline{\{f(x)\}}$ for all $x$.
If $Y$ is separated, this category is discrete.
Points of a topos and specialization
Session of 30 May 1973
Tape 1, side A

A morphism of topoi $f\colon E\to F$ is a pair $f^*\colon F\to E$, $f_*\colon E\to F$ with $f^*\dashv f_*$ and $f^*$ left exact; topoi, their morphisms and the natural transformations between morphisms form a 2-category, with hom-categories $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{top}}(E,F)$ (recalled).
For sober spaces $X$ and $Y$, the morphisms of topoi $\mathrm{Top}(X)\to\mathrm{Top}(Y)$ come, uniquely, from continuous maps $X\to Y$ (recalled).
A point of a topos $E$ is a morphism of topoi $\mathbf{Set}\to E$; the category of points is opposite to the category of fibre functors on $E$ (the inverse images of the points).

For $y$ in a space $Y$, the fibre functor $F\mapsto F_y=\varinjlim_{U\ni y}F(U)=\mathrm{Hom}(\text{“}\varprojlim\text{”}\,U,F)$ is represented by the pro-object of $\mathcal{O}_Y$ given by the open neighbourhoods of $y$.

Fibre functors on $\mathrm{Top}(Y)$ are represented by pro-objects of $\mathcal{O}_Y$ (by objects only for open points), and morphisms between fibre functors correspond to morphisms of the representing pro-objects in the opposite direction.

For $y,y'$ in a space $Y$, $\mathrm{Hom}(\varepsilon_y,\varepsilon_{y'})$ has at most one element, and is non-empty exactly when $y\in\overline{\{y'\}}$. So the category of fibre functors is the set $Y$ ordered by specialization, and the category of points is its opposite.

For continuous maps $f,g\colon X\to Y$, the set of 2-morphisms $f\Rightarrow g$ between the associated morphisms of topoi has at most one element, and is non-empty exactly when $g(x)\in\overline{\{f(x)\}}$ for every $x\in X$ (up to the convention on the direction of arrows).
For $X$ sober, every fibre functor on $\mathrm{Top}(X)$ is the stalk at a point of $X$ (an exercise, treated in Hakim's book).

Hence $X\mapsto\mathrm{Top}(X)$ is a 2-functor from spaces to topoi, the category $\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(X,Y)$ being the set of continuous maps $X\to Y$ ordered by pointwise specialization (taking sobrifications if needed).
Topoi of spaces with a group action

For a discrete group $G$ acting on a space $X$, $\mathrm{Top}(X,G)$ is the topos of $G$-equivariant sheaves on $X$ (étale spaces over $X$ with a compatible $G$-action); it is functorial in the pair $(X,G)$ for equivariant maps over group homomorphisms.

For an equivariant map $(X,G)\to(X',G')$, the inverse image of a $G'$-equivariant étale space $Y'\to X'$ is $Y'\times_{X'}X$ with its unique compatible $G$-action; this functor commutes with colimits and finite limits, hence defines a morphism of topoi $\mathrm{Top}(X,G)\to\mathrm{Top}(X',G')$.
The functor $(X,G)\mapsto\mathrm{Top}(X,G)$ is not fully faithful, and $(X,G)$ is not recovered from its topos in general.
If $H\lhd G$ is a normal subgroup acting freely and properly discontinuously on $X$, then $\mathrm{Top}(X/H,G/H)\simeq\mathrm{Top}(X,G)$.
Quotient topoi of this kind are the natural framework for moduli problems (abelian varieties, curves of genus $g$), where no space with the right properties exists.

For $G$ trivial, $\mathrm{Top}(X,1)=\mathrm{Top}(X)$; there is a morphism $\mathrm{Top}(X)\to\mathrm{Top}(X,G)$ whose inverse image forgets the $G$-action, but in general none in the other direction unless $G$ acts trivially.
Tape 1, side B
Points of the equivariant topos
For $x\in X$, the functor sending a $G$-equivariant sheaf to the stalk at $x$ of its underlying sheaf is a fibre functor on $\mathrm{Top}(X,G)$; these functors are jointly conservative.

For $X$ sober, the points $x,x'$ of $\mathrm{Top}(X,G)$ are isomorphic iff they lie in the same $G$-orbit, and $\mathrm{Isom}(x,x')=\{g\in G: gx=x'\}$; the set of isomorphism classes of points is $X/G$.
The topology on the set of isomorphism classes of points is the quotient topology of $X/G$; if $G$ acts freely and properly, $\mathrm{Top}(X,G)$ is the topos of $X/G$.
The classifying topos of a group
For a group $G$, the classifying topos $BG=\mathrm{Top}(\mathrm{pt},G)$ is the topos of $G$-sets; a homomorphism $G\to G'$ gives a morphism $BG\to BG'$.
Presheaf topoi and the functors $u^*$, $u_!$, $u_*$
For a small category $C$, $\widehat{C}$ is the topos of presheaves on $C$ (contravariant functors $C\to\mathbf{Set}$); $BG$ is the case of a one-object category.
In $\widehat{C}$, $\Gamma(F)=\mathrm{Hom}(1,F)=\varprojlim F$; for $F$ with values in abelian groups, $H^i(\widehat{C},F)=\varprojlim{}^i F$, the derived functors of the inverse limit.

A functor $u\colon C\to C'$ induces $u^*\colon\widehat{C'}\to\widehat{C}$, $F'\mapsto F'\circ u$, which commutes with all limits and colimits; it is the inverse image of a morphism of topoi $\widehat{C}\to\widehat{C'}$, whose direct image $u_*$ is the right adjoint of $u^*$.

For $u\colon C\to C'$, $u^*$ has both a left adjoint $u_!$ and a right adjoint $u_*$ (Kan extensions); more generally, the inverse image $f^*$ of a morphism of topoi has a left adjoint $f_!$ exactly when it commutes with arbitrary limits (granting a smallness condition left unstated in the lecture).
For $C'=\Delta$ and $C=\Delta_{\le n}$ (finite non-empty ordinals of cardinal $\le n+1$), $u^*$ is truncation of simplicial sets, $u_!$ is the skeleton and $u_*$ the coskeleton.
When they exist, $f_!$ denotes the left adjoint of $f^*$, and $f^!$ the right adjoint of $f_*$ (which exists when $f_*$ commutes with all colimits).
If $u^*$ has a left adjoint $u_!$ which is left exact, then $u_!$ is the inverse image of a morphism of topoi in the opposite direction, of which $u^*$ is the direct image.
If $C$ has finite limits and $u\colon C\to C'$ preserves them, then $u_!$ is left exact, hence the inverse image of a morphism of topoi $\widehat{C'}\to\widehat{C}$.

Without exactness hypotheses on $u$, a functor $C\to C'$ gives only a morphism $\widehat{C}\to\widehat{C'}$ in the same direction, and $C\mapsto\widehat{C}$ is a 2-functor (natural transformations give 2-morphisms).

The functor $\mathrm{Hom}(C,C')\to\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{top}}(\widehat{C},\widehat{C'})$ is fully faithful; when $C,C'$ are idempotent complete, the morphisms whose inverse image also commutes with all limits are exactly those coming from functors $C\to C'$.
Final and initial topoi

For every topos $E$ there is, up to unique isomorphism, exactly one morphism $E\to\mathbf{Set}$, with inverse image $I\mapsto I\cdot 1=\coprod_I 1$; the one-point topos $\mathbf{Set}$ is final among topoi.
The direct image of this unique morphism is the global-section functor $\Gamma=\mathrm{Hom}(1,-)$.

The inverse image $\mathbf{Set}\to E$ commutes with infinite products iff $E$ is locally connected (every object is a sum of connected objects); this expresses that products distribute over arbitrary sums in $E$.

Are the topoi of the form $\widehat{C}$ exactly those that are locally connected and, in a suitable sense, totally disconnected, i.e. those sharing all exactness properties of $\mathbf{Set}$, including those involving infinite limits?
The empty topos $\mathrm{Top}(\varnothing)$ (the one-point category) is initial among topoi: each topos receives a unique morphism from it.
The empty topos is strictly initial: a topos admitting a morphism to it is itself empty.
Strict initiality of the initial object fails in groups: the trivial group is initial and final, yet non-trivial groups map to it.
Classifying topoi in a topos, and sums

For a group object $G$ of a topos $E$, the classifying topos $B_EG$ is the topos of objects of $E$ with a $G$-action; a homomorphism $G\to G'$ gives a morphism $B_EG\to B_EG'$ (restriction of the action).
The sum $\coprod X_i$ of spaces is the disjoint union with each $X_i$ open; a map out of it is continuous iff its restrictions are, which is the universal property of the coproduct.
Tape 2, side A
Sums and quotients of topoi

The product category $\prod_i E_i$ of topoi is a topos, and $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{top}}(\prod_i E_i,F)\simeq\prod_i\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{top}}(E_i,F)$: it is the sum (coproduct) of the $E_i$ in the 2-category of topoi, the projections being the inverse images of the inclusions $E_i\to\prod E_i$.

Other limits and colimits of topoi (amalgamated sums, quotients) can be formed too; applied to spaces, a quotient taken in topoi may be well behaved where the quotient of spaces is wild (stated without proof).
Induced topoi

For an object $X'$ of a topos $E$, the induced topos $E/X'$ is the category of objects of $E$ over $X'$; it plays the part of the space $X'$ over the final object $X$ (for $E=\mathrm{Top}(X)$ and $X'$ étale over $X$, it is the topos of the space $X'$).

The restriction $j^*\colon E\to E/X'$, $Y\mapsto Y\times X'$ (viewed over $X'$ by the second projection), commutes with colimits and finite limits; it is the inverse image of a morphism of topoi $j\colon E/X'\to E$, the localization morphism.
$j^*$ has a left adjoint $j_!$, which forgets the structure map to $X'$, as well as the right adjoint $j_*$; the localization morphism is the analogue of an open immersion of spaces.
Sober spaces and generic points
Session of 4 June 1973
Tape 1, side A
A space is sober if every irreducible closed subset has exactly one generic point.
A question asks for a criterion characterising sober spaces, in the way sheaves of groups or rings might; the lecturer says he knows no such characterisation.

Spaces with the same sobrification have equivalent categories of sheaves. The sober space attached to a topos has the isomorphism classes of points as underlying set, with the topology given by the subobjects of the final object; for a space $X$ it is the set of irreducible closed subsets of $X$ with the evident topology.

For a finitely generated algebra $A$ over an algebraically closed field $K$, the set of maximal ideals with the Zariski topology (the spaces of Serre's FAC) is not sober: irreducible closed subsets of positive dimension have no generic point.
Hausdorff spaces and schemes are sober.

For a non-separated topological group $G$, the closure of a point is a translate of the closure of the unit; the associated sober space is the separated quotient of $G$ by $\overline{\{e\}}$, so passing to it identifies points but adds none.

On a set of ideals of a ring (maximal, prime, primary, …), the Zariski-type topology has as basic closed sets, for each subset $S$ of the ring, the ideals of the given type containing $S$; the closed sets are the arbitrary intersections of finite unions of these.
Such spaces are generally non-separated, and specialization ($x\in\overline{\{y\}}$) is then an order which need not be an equivalence relation.
Tensor product of sheaves of modules

For sheaves of modules $M$, $N$, the presheaf $U\mapsto M(U)\otimes N(U)$ is in general not a sheaf; the tensor product $M\otimes N$ is its associated sheaf, which solves the universal problem for bilinear pairings.

If $N$ is constant free of finite rank $n$, the presheaf tensor product is already a sheaf, equal to $M^n$; the same holds when $N$ is a direct factor of such a module, $M\otimes N$ being the image of the induced projector of $M^n$.
Algebras of finite presentation and passage to the limit
If $A$ is a reduced algebra of finite type over $\mathbb Z$, its normalization is of finite type over $\mathbb Z$.

If $K=\varinjlim K_i$ (filtering, $K_i$ of finite type over $\mathbb Z$) and $A$ is a $K$-algebra of finite presentation, then $A=A_i\otimes_{K_i}K$ for some $i$ and some $K_i$-algebra $A_i$ of finite presentation.

For most geometric properties of $\mathrm{Spec}A\to\mathrm{Spec}K$ (geometrically connected, irreducible or normal fibres, non-empty fibres, surjective, flat, smooth, étale, unramified), $A$ has the property iff $A_j$ has it over $K_j$ for all large $j$ (EGA IV, chapter on limits).
If $A$ is of finite presentation and flat over $K$, the descent datum can be chosen with $A_i$ flat over $K_i$.
Points of presheaf topoi
For $c\in C$, evaluation $F\mapsto F(c)$ is a fibre functor on $\widehat{C}$, and $C\to\{\text{points of }\widehat{C}\}$ is fully faithful.
Filtering inverse limits of points of $\widehat{C}$ exist, so $C\to\{\text{points}\}$ extends to an equivalence $\mathrm{Pro}(C)\simeq\{\text{points of }\widehat{C}\}$.

A point of $\widehat{C}$ is essential (its fibre functor commutes with all limits) iff it is a retract of a representable; if $C$ is idempotent complete, the essential points are exactly those coming from $C$.
If $\widehat{C}\simeq\mathrm{Top}(X)$ for a space $X$, then $C$ is an ordered category: there is at most one arrow between two objects.
A category is ordered if it has at most one arrow between any two objects; it is then equivalent to the category of a preordered set, $x\le y$ iff there is an arrow $x\to y$.
Conversely, if $C$ is an ordered category, $\widehat{C}$ is equivalent to the topos of a space with underlying set $\mathrm{Ob}\,C$.
The open sets of that space are the sieves $O\subset\mathrm{Ob}\,C$ ($x\in O$, $y\le x\Rightarrow y\in O$), which correspond to the subobjects of the final object of $\widehat{C}$.
In this topology, the smallest open set containing $x$ is $\{y: y\le x\}$.
Tape 1, side B
Topoi of ordered categories and of spaces
For an ordered category $C$ with the sieve topology on $\mathrm{Ob}\,C$, the sets $O_x$ form a basis of opens, $O_x\subset O_y$ iff $x\le y$, so presheaves on the basis are the presheaves on $C$.
For an ordered category $C$ and its associated space, every presheaf on the basis is a sheaf (a basic open covered by basic opens is equal to one of them), so $\mathrm{Top}(X_C)\simeq\widehat{C}$.

A point $x$ of a sober space $X$ is essential (its fibre functor commutes with arbitrary limits) iff $x$ has a smallest open neighbourhood; if $\mathrm{Top}(X)\simeq\widehat{C}$, the essential points must form a conservative family.

A subset $X'\subset X$ is very dense if every non-empty locally closed subset of $X$ meets $X'$; this is equivalent to the fibre functors at the points of $X'$ being conservative (two opens with the same trace on $X'$ are equal).
For a sober space $X$, $\mathrm{Top}(X)\simeq\widehat{C}$ for some category $C$ iff the set of essential points of $X$ is very dense; $C$ can then be taken to be that set ordered by specialization.
Localization of topoi

For $S'$ in a topos $E$, the morphism $E/S'\to E$ with inverse image $X\mapsto X\times S'$ is the localization morphism, and that inverse image the localization functor; a property of objects is said to hold locally if it holds after this base change.
For $E=\mathrm{Top}(S)$ and $S'$ an étale space over $S$, the localization morphism is the one induced by the map of spaces $S'\to S$.
Classifying topoi of subgroups as localizations

For a homomorphism $f\colon G\to G'$ of group objects of a topos $E$, the inverse image of $Bf\colon BG\to BG'$ restricts the action along $f$ and commutes with all limits and colimits (computed in $E$).

For a subgroup $H$ of a group object $G$ of a topos $E$, $BH\simeq BG/(G/H)$, and under this equivalence the morphism $BH\to BG$ is the localization morphism at the object $G/H$ of $BG$ (with $G$ acting by left translation).

The equivalence sends an object $A\to G/H$ of $BG/(G/H)$ to its fibre over the unit section, with the induced $H$-action, and an object $F$ of $BH$ to the contracted product $G\times^H F$ over $G/H$; these functors are quasi-inverse.
The morphism $BH\to BG$ behaves like a covering rather than an embedding: the localization object $G/H\to 1$ is not a monomorphism.
Galois theory of coverings and classifying topoi

For a connected, locally connected and locally simply connected space $Z$ with base point $z$, taking the fibre at $z$ with its monodromy action is an equivalence from coverings of $Z$ to $\pi_1(Z,z)$-sets; the inverse sends a $G$-set $E$ to $P\times^G E$, $P$ the universal covering based at $z$.
Thus the classifying topos $BG$ of a discrete group is the topos of coverings of a space $Z$ with $\pi_1(Z,z)=G$.
Subgroups $H\subset G$ correspond to pointed transitive $G$-sets $G/H$, hence to connected coverings $Z'\to Z$ with a point over $z$; and $BG/(G/H)$ is then the category of coverings of $Z'$.
Tape 2
Subgroups as coverings
For the connected covering $Z'\to Z$ corresponding to $H\subset G$, the map $\pi_1(Z',z')\to\pi_1(Z,z)=G$ is the inclusion of $H$; so, up to homotopy, $BH\to BG$ is a covering with fibre $G/H$.

For a group $G$ acting on a space $Z$ and a subgroup $H\subset G$, $\mathrm{Top}(Z,H)\simeq\mathrm{Top}(Z,G)/(Z\times G/H)$ ($G$ acting diagonally), the equivalence sending an object over $Z\times G/H$ to its part over $Z\times\{e\}$ with the induced $H$-action; $\mathrm{Top}(Z,H)\to\mathrm{Top}(Z,G)$ is the localization morphism.
Adjoints $f_!$ and $f^!$ in examples
Session of 6 June 1973
Tape 2 (from 3:43:44)
For a closed embedding $i\colon Y\to X$, $i_*$ is fully faithful on abelian sheaves (an equivalence onto the sheaves vanishing off $Y$), and commutes with all limits and colimits.
For a closed embedding $i$, on abelian sheaves $i_*$ has a right adjoint $i^!$: $i^!F$ is the subsheaf of $F$ of sections supported in $Y$, i.e. $\Gamma(U,i^!F)=\Gamma_{Y\cap U}(U,F)$.
The right derived functors of $i^!$ are the sheaves of local cohomology.
For an open embedding $j\colon Y\to X$, $j^*$ commutes with products, so $j_!$ exists on sheaves of sets: it views an étale space over $Y$ as an étale space over $X$, with empty stalks off $Y$.
For sheaves of abelian groups on an open $Y\subset X$, $j_!F$ is the extension by zero: $(j_!F)(U)\subset F(U\cap Y)$ consists of the sections whose support, closed in $U\cap Y$, is closed in $U$.
The $j_!$ for abelian sheaves is not the $j_!$ for sheaves of sets: the underlying sheaf of sets of the extension by zero has non-empty stalks off $Y$, whereas the set-theoretic $j_!$ has empty ones.
For a continuous map $f$ of spaces, $f_*$ preserves the initial (empty) sheaf iff the image of $f$ is dense; for topoi, iff the morphism is dominating, i.e. factors through no proper closed subtopos.
For a morphism of topoi, can the right adjoint $f^!$ of $f_*$ (on sets, not on abelian objects) exist unless $f$ is an equivalence?
On abelian sheaves $f^!$ is important (it underlies duality), and taking adjoints of the functors attached to a morphism of topoi often leads to further morphisms of topoi.
Local properties and the notion of site

A fibre space $E\to X$ is locally trivial if $X$ has an open covering $U_i$ with $E|_{U_i}\simeq U_i\times F_i$; being locally trivial is a property that is local on $X$, whereas being trivial is not.
For a group scheme $G$ over $K$, $X$ is a torsor under $G$ if, for every $K'$, $X(K')$ is empty or a principal homogeneous space under $G(K')$.

Such an $X$ is trivial over $K'$ iff $X_{K'}$ has a section (for a field $K'$, iff it is non-empty); it is called locally trivial for a chosen class of admissible base changes (arbitrary or Galois extensions) if it becomes trivial after one of them.
A site is a category equipped with a notion of localization, here called a topology by abuse of language (not a topology on the objects and arrows).
A topology on a category $C$ can be given, in a first form, by a set $\mathrm{Cov}(X)$ of covering families of morphisms $X_i\to X$ for each object $X$.
Tape 1
Coverings, pretopologies and local properties
On algebras over a ring $A$, the families $(B_i)$ for which some finite subfamily gives a faithfully flat map $A\to\prod B_i$ are the coverings of a (simplified) fpqc-type topology.
When $C$ has fibre products, covering families are required to be stable under base change: if $(X_i\to X)$ covers $X$ and $X'\to X$ is any morphism, then $(X_i\times_XX'\to X')$ covers $X'$.
Covering families are required to be transitive: if $(X_i\to X)$ covers $X$ and each $X_i$ is covered by $(X_{ij}\to X_i)_j$, then $(X_{ij}\to X)_{i,j}$ covers $X$.

A family consisting of a single isomorphism is covering; and covering families are saturated under refinement: if $(X_i)$ covers $X$ and each $X_i\to X$ factors over $X$ through a member of a family $(X'_{i'})$, then $(X'_{i'})$ covers $X$.
A class of families satisfying base change, transitivity and the trivial axiom is a pretopology; saturating it under refinement gives a topology.
Giraud later replaced covering families by covering sieves, which makes the formulas simpler and removes the assumption that fibre products exist.

Given a category $F_X$ attached contravariantly to each object $X$ (inverse images), a property of a situation over $X$ holds locally if it holds on the pulled-back situations over $X_i$ for some covering $(X_i\to X)$; for instance, an arrow is locally a monomorphism (resp. an isomorphism).
For a topology generated by a pretopology, a property is local iff it holds after pullback along a covering family of the pretopology.
Sheaves on a site

For a site $C$ with fibre products, a presheaf $F$ is separated if $F(X)\to\prod_iF(X_i)$ is injective for every covering, and a sheaf if $F(X)\to\prod_iF(X_i)\rightrightarrows\prod_{i,j}F(X_i\times_XX_j)$ is exact; $\widetilde C\subset\widehat C$ is the full subcategory of sheaves.
For a small site $C$, $\widetilde C$ is a topos (stated with technical provisos omitted).
Many different sites give the same topos, as a group has many presentations: the category $C$ plays the part of generators and the topology the part of relations.

$\widetilde C$ is the topos universal for functors out of $\widehat C$ commuting with colimits and finite limits that make covering families epimorphic; covering families are in general not epimorphic in $\widehat C$.
The associated sheaf on a site
The inclusion $i\colon\widetilde C\to\widehat C$ has a left exact left adjoint $a$, the associated sheaf functor.

For a presheaf $F$, $LF(X)$ is the filtering colimit, over the coverings $(X_i\to X)$, of the matching families $\ker\big(\prod F(X_i)\rightrightarrows\prod F(X_i\times_XX_j)\big)$; in terms of covering sieves $R\subset X$, $LF(X)=\varinjlim_R\mathrm{Hom}(R,F)$.

The functor $L\colon\widehat C\to\widehat C$ is left exact (a filtering colimit of finite limits), $LF$ is separated for every $F$, and $\mathrm{Hom}(F,G)\simeq\mathrm{Hom}(LF,G)$ for every sheaf $G$.
$F\to LF$ is a monomorphism iff $F$ is separated, and an isomorphism iff $F$ is a sheaf; if $F$ is separated, $LF$ is a sheaf. Hence $a=L\circ L$.

$\widetilde C$ is closed in $\widehat C$ under limits; a colimit of sheaves is the associated sheaf of the colimit taken in $\widehat C$; exactness properties of $\widetilde C$ involving colimits and finite limits follow from those of $\widehat C$ since $a$ is exact.

The representable presheaf $\mathrm{Hom}(-,X)$ is a sheaf iff a morphism $Y\to X$ amounts to a compatible family of morphisms $Y_i\to X$ on a covering of $Y$; when this holds for all $X$ (a subcanonical topology, a name not used in the lecture), $C\to\widehat C$ factors through $\widetilde C$.
Algebraic structures and exactness properties
Session of 20 June 1973
Tape 1, side A

Algebraic structures (groups, rings, modules, comodules, group actions, torsors) can be expressed by direct and inverse limits and arrows between them, so they make sense in any category with the appropriate limits, subject to exactness conditions.
A basic exactness property: filtering direct limits commute with finite inverse limits.
Topoi are, apart from infinite inverse limits, the categories with exactly the exactness properties of $\mathbf{Set}$.

Does every type of algebraic structure have a classifying topos containing a universal model, so that types of structure correspond to topoi, added axioms to subtopoi, and the homotopy type of the classifying topos gives a classifying space of the structure? (Programme stated as expected.)

For sets $D'$ and $D''$ of diagrams, $\mathrm{Cat}_D$ is the 2-category of categories having limits of type $D'$ and colimits of type $D''$, with functors commuting with them, and natural transformations as 2-morphisms.

An exactness property of type $(I,\Sigma)$, with $I\in\mathrm{Cat}_D$ and $\Sigma$ a set of arrows of $I$: a category $C\in\mathrm{Cat}_D$ satisfies it if every morphism $\varphi\colon I\to C$ of $\mathrm{Cat}_D$ sends the arrows of $\Sigma$ to isomorphisms.

A 2-sum of objects $I_\lambda$ of a 2-category is an object $I$ with morphisms $I_\lambda\to I$ such that $\mathrm{Hom}(I,C)\to\prod_\lambda\mathrm{Hom}(I_\lambda,C)$ is an equivalence of categories for every $C$; it is determined up to equivalence, itself unique up to unique isomorphism.

If 2-sums exist in $\mathrm{Cat}_D$, a conjunction of exactness properties $(I_\lambda,\Sigma_\lambda)$ is one exactness property $(I,\Sigma)$, with $I$ the 2-sum and $\Sigma$ the union of the images of the $\Sigma_\lambda$.

The $D$-envelope of a category $J$ is an object $\mathrm{Env}(J)$ of $\mathrm{Cat}_D$ with a functor $J\to\mathrm{Env}(J)$ such that, for every $C\in\mathrm{Cat}_D$, composition $\mathrm{Hom}_D(\mathrm{Env}(J),C)\to\mathrm{Hom}(J,C)$ is an equivalence of categories (a 2-universal problem).
Asserted without proof: if $D'$ or $D''$ is small, every category has a $D$-envelope; it is the category obtained by adjoining the limits of type $D'$ and the colimits of type $D''$.
A remark suggests 2-representability as a weaker substitute for representability when no genuine reflection exists; the reply is inconclusive.

The naive fibre product of categories (pairs of objects, resp. arrows, with equal images in $S$) is not invariant under equivalence: replacing $X$ and $Y$ by equivalent categories mapping into two isomorphic copies of $S$ makes it empty.

The 2-fibre product $X\times^2_SY$ of $f\colon X\to S$ and $g\colon Y\to S$ has as objects the triples $(x,y,\alpha)$ with $\alpha\colon f(x)\xrightarrow{\sim}g(y)$, and as arrows the pairs of arrows compatible with the $\alpha$'s.
If $X\to S$ is fibred, the naive fibre product is equivalent to the 2-fibre product.
The 2-fibre product is 2-universal: $\mathrm{Hom}(C,X\times^2_SY)\to\mathrm{Hom}(C,X)\times^2_{\mathrm{Hom}(C,S)}\mathrm{Hom}(C,Y)$ is an equivalence of categories, for every category $C$.

In any 2-category, a 2-fibre product of $X$, $Y$ over $S$ is an object $P$ with morphisms to $X$ and $Y$ and an isomorphism of the composites to $S$, such that this functor on Hom-categories is an equivalence for every object; it is determined up to equivalence, unique up to unique isomorphism.
2-limits of categories are taken of pseudo-functors $I\to\mathbf{Cat}$, for which composition holds only up to coherent isomorphism.

Envelopes, localization and a worked exactness property

All the universal problems considered are 2-universal, their solutions defined up to equivalence; 2-inverse limits are taken of pseudo-functors $I\to$ (a 2-category), and 2-direct limits by reversing arrows.
Asked whether the one-dimensional construction of coproducts would also be valid in the 2-categorical setting, the lecturer does not know and says the construction is ugly even at the lower level.
Size conventions: a universe $U$ is fixed; categories are required to have $U$-small Hom-sets, but may be large, such as the categories of all $U$-groups or $U$-rings.

Universality of sums as an exactness property: if $X$ is the sum of objects $x_\alpha$ and $X'\to X$ is any morphism, then with $X'_\alpha=x_\alpha\times_XX'$, the object $X'$ is the sum of the $X'_\alpha$.

This property is expressed by inverting arrows: realisations of the diagram type in $C$ are the functors from its envelope $\tilde J$ to $C$; those for which the squares are Cartesian and $X$ is the sum are the functors inverting a set $\Sigma$ of arrows of $\tilde J$; and the conclusion says that the canonical arrow $\coprod X'_\alpha\to X'$ is also inverted.

For $J\in\mathrm{Cat}_D$ and a set $\Sigma$ of arrows of $J$, $J[\Sigma^{-1}]\in\mathrm{Cat}_D$ is defined by the 2-universal property that $\mathrm{Hom}_D(J[\Sigma^{-1}],C)\to\mathrm{Hom}_D(J,C;\Sigma)$ is an equivalence onto the functors commuting with $D$-limits that invert $\Sigma$.
Existence of $\tilde J$ and $J[\Sigma^{-1}]$ is assumed; he expects it in all cases except possibly when neither $D'$ nor $D''$ is small.

An elementary exactness property is given by a diagram $\Delta$, diagrams $\Delta'_i$ (inverse limit type) and $\Delta''_j$ (direct limit type) with cones to vertices $x'_i$, $x''_j$ of $\Delta$, and further diagrams $\Lambda'_\alpha$, $\Lambda''_\beta$ with vertices $y'_\alpha$, $y''_\beta$: whenever a realisation of $\Delta$ in $C$ makes each $x'_i$ the limit and each $x''_j$ the colimit of the corresponding diagram, then each $y'_\alpha$ is a limit and each $y''_\beta$ a colimit of the corresponding diagram.

A doubt is raised about exactness properties holding vacuously because no suitable functors exist; the lecturer first dismisses it, then concedes the point, since constant diagrams need not satisfy the imposed conditions.

An elementary exactness property becomes a functor condition: with $\Sigma$ the arrows of $\tilde\Delta$ comparing the vertices with the limits and colimits, realisations are the functors $\tilde\Delta[\Sigma^{-1}]\to C$, and one requires that they invert the further comparison arrows for $y'_\alpha$ and $y''_\beta$.
For a set $\eta$ of exactness properties, $\mathrm{Cat}_{D,\eta}\subset\mathrm{Cat}_D$ is the full sub-2-category of categories satisfying them, with the same functors.

An algebraic structure $T$ realisable in the categories $C$ of a given class assigns to each $C$ the category $T(C)$ of realisations of $T$ in $C$, functorially in the functors $C\to C'$ commuting with the relevant limits.
The structure of group makes sense in any category with finite products; a product-preserving functor sends group objects to group objects.

An object $P$ with an action of a group $G$ is a torsor iff $G\times P\to P\times P$ is an isomorphism and $P\to 1$ is an epimorphism; so a functor preserves torsors only if it preserves epimorphisms.

A morphism $P\to Q$ is a monomorphism iff the square $P=P\times_QP$ is Cartesian, and an epimorphism iff the dual square is co-Cartesian; so preserving epimorphisms is an exactness property (commuting with certain pushouts).

Arbitrary inverse limits with limit-preserving functors, related to the embedding $C\to\widehat C$ and to viewing a structure on an object as a structure on the functor it represents.

Semi-additive categories (initial and final objects agree, sums agree with products) with additive functors; additive categories with an extra condition.

Categories with finite inverse and direct limits, with functors preserving them; with the exactness properties of topoi, the pretopoi (corresponding to coherent topoi).
Topoi: $D'$ the finite diagrams, $D''$ all small diagrams (so $D''$ is not a small set), with the existence of generators imposed separately; the corresponding 2-category of topoi is too large.

Are the essential topoi, i.e. topoi in which arbitrary products of epimorphisms are epimorphisms and arbitrary products commute with sums, exactly the presheaf topoi $\widehat C$ (when they have generators)?

Ordered sets with finite lower bounds and arbitrary upper bounds, with monotone maps preserving them; and those in which finite lower bounds distribute over arbitrary upper bounds (distributivity of products over sums).

An algebraic theory $T$ for a fixed $D$ is a pseudo-functor $C\mapsto T(C)$ from $\mathrm{Cat}_D$ to $\mathbf{Cat}$, $T(C)$ being the category of realisations of $T$ in $C$, with functors $\mathrm{Hom}_D(C,C')\to\mathrm{Hom}(T(C),T(C'))$ compatible with composition.

Representable theories and constructions

A theory $T$ is representable by $R\in\mathrm{Cat}_D$ if $T(C)\simeq\mathrm{Hom}_D(R,C)$, naturally in $C$; $R$ then carries a universal realisation of $T$, every realisation in $C$ being its image under an essentially unique $D$-functor $R\to C$.

Theories over $D$ (pseudo-functors $\mathrm{Cat}_D\to\mathbf{Cat}$), their morphisms (families of functors $T(C)\to T'(C)$ compatible with the transition functors) and the transformations between these form a 2-category, with hom-categories $\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(T,T')$.
(Yoneda) If $T$ is represented by $R$, then $\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(T,T')\simeq T'(R)$ for every theory $T'$.

A construction on $T$ is a morphism of theories $T\to\tau$, where $\tau(C)=C$ is the identity theory: a way of producing, functorially in $C$, an object of $C$ from a realisation of $T$ in $C$ (for groups: the centre, the abelianization, the $n$-th power).
If $T$ is represented by $R$, the category $\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(T,\tau)$ of constructions on $T$ is equivalent to $R$.
The category of constructions on any theory lies in $\mathrm{Cat}_D$: its limits of type $D'$ and $D''$, and its exactness properties, are computed objectwise.
Writing $R_T$ for the category of constructions on $T$, there is a canonical functor $T(C)\to\mathrm{Hom}_D(R_T,C)$, natural in $C$; thus $T_{R_T}$ plays the part of a representable envelope of $T$.
Base objects and the rules for algebraic theories

A theory $T$ has base objects indexed by a small set $I$ if there is a faithful morphism of theories $T\to\tau^I$, where $\tau^I(C)=C^I$; the realisations are then families of objects of $C$ with extra structure.

If $T$ is represented by $R$, morphisms $T\to\tau^I$ correspond to families $(R_i)_{i\in I}$ of objects of $R$ (equivalently to $D$-functors $\tilde I\to R$), and faithfulness means that $\mathrm{Hom}_D(R,C)\to C^I$ is faithful for all $C$; one then says that $I$ $D$-generates $R$.
Expected, not proved: if $I$ generates $R$, the objects of $R$ are obtained from the base objects by a bounded number of limit operations on the arrows already constructed.
Rule 1 (empty structure): for a small set $I$, $T(C)=C^I$ is an algebraic theory with $I$ as base objects, represented by $\tilde I$.

Rule 2 (adding axioms): if $T$ is algebraic and represented by $R$, and $\Sigma$ is a set of arrows of $R$ (arrows between constructions), the theory $T'(C)\subset T(C)$ of realisations whose $D$-functor $R\to C$ inverts $\Sigma$ is algebraic, and is represented by $R[\Sigma^{-1}]$.
For groups, commutativity is an axiom of this kind: the canonical arrow from $G$ to its abelianization is required to be an isomorphism.

When the needed diagrams are in $D'$ or $D''$, the following are axioms of this kind: an arrow between constructions is a monomorphism (its diagonal is an isomorphism), is an epimorphism, or two parallel arrows between constructions are equal (equalizer or coequalizer an isomorphism).
“$X$ acts faithfully on $Y$” cannot be expressed by inverting arrows, even in a topos: it is not stable under base change.
“An object of a topos is locally constant with $n$ sheets” cannot be so expressed; the corresponding theories are not algebraic, not representable.

Rule 3 (adding arrows): if $T$ is algebraic and represented by $R$, and $H$ is a small set with source and target maps $\alpha_1,\alpha_2\colon H\to\mathrm{Ob}\,R$ (formal arrows between constructions), $T'(C)$ is the category of pairs $(\psi,\beta)$ with $\psi\in T(C)$ and, for each $h\in H$, an arrow $\beta(h)\colon\psi(\alpha_1h)\to\psi(\alpha_2h)$ in $C$; $T'(C)\to T(C)$ is faithful, no longer full.

Additive categories as an exactness property

The lecturer asks for examples of enveloping categories, additive or abelian; the room points to a universal additive category, but he stresses that his version also requires initial and final objects to coincide.

A semi-additive category has finite products and sums, the canonical arrow from the initial to the final object is an isomorphism (so zero morphisms exist), and the canonical arrow $X\sqcup Y\to X\times Y$ is an isomorphism.
In a semi-additive category every object carries a unique monoid structure and a unique comonoid structure, both commutative (Eckmann–Hilton), and the Hom-sets are commutative monoids.
A semi-additive category is additive iff every monoid object is a group, which is an exactness property: the map $(x,y)\mapsto(x,x+y)$ of $X\times X$ is an isomorphism.
No simple construction of an enveloping additive category is known when both direct and inverse limits occur; for finite inverse limits only, functors into abelian groups give one.
