If $F:E\to E'$ is $\pi$-accessible and sends $E_\pi$ into $E'_\pi$ ($\pi$-accessible objects), $F$ is the extension $\mathrm{Ind}_\pi$ of its restriction $E_\pi\to E'_\pi$.

For $F$ accessible and $\pi$ large enough, $F(E_\pi)\subset E'_{\pi^{\pi_0}}$ ($\pi_0$ fixed, SGA 4); since $(2^\lambda)^{\pi_0}=2^\lambda$ for $\lambda\ge\pi_0$ infinite, $F(E_\pi)\subset E'_\pi$ if $\pi=2^\lambda$.
An accessible functor between accessible categories respects the canonical filtration by $\pi$-accessible objects for arbitrarily large $\pi$.
For $i:C\hookrightarrow E$ small full and $E'$ with colimits, the restriction $i^*:\mathrm{Hom}(E,E')\to\mathrm{Hom}(C,E')$ has a fully faithful left adjoint $i_!$.
For $E$ accessible, $F:E\to E'$ is accessible if and only if it is in the essential image of $i_!$ for some small $C\subset E$.
For $C$ small with split idempotents, $\mathrm{Ind}_\pi(C)$ has arbitrary colimits if and only if $C$ has colimits of cardinality at most $\pi$.

For such a $C$, $\mathrm{Ind}_\pi(C)$ is the $\Delta_\pi$–$\Delta$ envelope of $C$: $\mathrm{Hom}_\Delta(\mathrm{Ind}_\pi C,F)\simeq\mathrm{Hom}_{\Delta_\pi}(C,F)$ for every $F$ with arbitrary colimits.
Representability and accessible categories
The categories $R$ representing algebraic theories are exactly the “co-accessible” categories: $S=T(\mathbf{Set})\simeq R^{\mathrm{op}}$ is accessible (and cocomplete).
On a cocomplete accessible category $E$, a functor $E^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Set}$ is representable if and only if it sends colimits to limits.
A functor $F:E\to\mathbf{Set}$ ($E$ cocomplete accessible) is representable if and only if it commutes with arbitrary limits and is accessible.
SGA 4: a functor $F:E\to\mathbf{Set}$ is pro-representable by a pro-object with small indexing if and only if it is left exact and accessible.
If $E$ has arbitrary limits, a pro-representable functor $E\to\mathbf{Set}$ is representable if and only if it commutes with these limits.
Between cocomplete accessible categories, $F$ has a right adjoint if and only if it commutes with colimits, and a left adjoint if and only if it commutes with limits and is accessible.
On $\mathbf{Grp}$, a functor with small values, pro-represented by a non-small system of simple groups, commutes with limits without being accessible.
items.name: SGA 4

items.text: Morphisms of algebraic theories

An example from SGA of a functor commuting with inverse limits yet not accessible, hence not representable: built from an inverse system of arbitrarily large simple groups, with small values on each group.
A morphism of algebraic theories $T\to T'$ is equivalent to a functor $S'\to S$ commuting with colimits; its right adjoint $S\to S'$ is $T(\mathbf{Set})\to T'(\mathbf{Set})$.
The functors $S\to S'$ arising from morphisms of algebraic theories are exactly those that commute with limits and are accessible.
If $F\to I$ is fibred over $I$ small, with accessible fibres and transition functors, the category of cartesian sections (2-limit) and that of all sections are accessible.
For $E$ accessible and $I$ small, $\mathrm{Hom}(I,E)$ is accessible, as is $\mathrm{Hom}(I[I^{-1}],E)$, the functors sending every arrow to an isomorphism.
The 2-colimit of a small system of cocomplete accessible categories, taken in cocomplete categories and cocontinuous functors, is accessible.
Is the 2-colimit in $\mathbf{Cat}$ of a small system of accessible categories accessible?
The coproduct in $\mathbf{Cat}$ of two nonempty categories with colimits has no initial object, nor a coproduct of an object of each.
For a morphism of algebraic theories, $T(\mathbf{Set})\to T'(\mathbf{Set})$ has a left adjoint (free structure); example: the enveloping group of a monoid.
If a fully faithful functor admits a left adjoint, this adjoint is a localization (passage to a category of fractions).

The full subtheories of $T_{R'}$ correspond to the localizations $R'\to R'[\Sigma'^{-1}]$ in $\Delta$, $\Sigma'$ stable under limits, and to the reflective full subcategories of $S'$ stable under limits.
For an algebraic subtheory, $\Sigma'$ is generated, by limit operations, by a small set of arrows.
Is a full subcategory $S$ of an accessible category $S'$, stable under limits and whose inclusion admits a left adjoint, accessible?
Constructing algebraic theories
Tape 3, side A
Limit-passage clause: the 2-limit, over $T^I$, of a filtered system of algebraic theories with base $I$ is algebraic with base $I$.
Representable theories form a full 2-subcategory of the $\Delta$-theories, 2-equivalent to $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}$ via $R\mapsto T_R$; it contains the algebraic theories.

$R$ is algebraic with (discrete) base $I$ if it is the end of a transfinite sequence in $\Delta$ starting from the envelope of $I$, each step inverting, equalizing or adding arrows, with 2-colimits at limit ordinals.
Faithfulness of $\mathrm{Hom}_\Delta(R,C)\to C^I$ for every $C$ does not suffice for $I\to R$ to be basic (known counterexample).
“Problem three” (open): is $I\to R$ basic if and only if every strictly full subcategory of $R$ stable under limits of type $D$ and containing the image of $I$ is equal to $R$?
This condition is equivalent to: the transfinite saturation of the image of $I$ under limits of type $D'$ and $D''$ reaches $R$.
If $D'$ and $D''$ are essentially small (and if problems one and two preserve smallness), the algebraic objects of $\Delta$ are exactly the small ones.
Conjectural statement: if $R$ is algebraic, one can enlarge $I$ so that no arrows remain to be added; $T_R$ is then a full subtheory of $C\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(I',C)$.
Representability of theories
Necessary condition for 2-representability: $T$ commutes with 2-limits, $T(\varprojlim C_i)\simeq\varprojlim T(C_i)$.
On a category with arbitrary limits, a functor to $\mathbf{Set}$ that commutes with these limits is pro-representable by a projective system, possibly non-small.
If $T$ is 2-representable, $T$ sends faithful (resp. fully faithful) $\Delta$-functors to faithful (resp. fully faithful) functors.
Exactness properties of theories

Exactness property given by $R\in\Delta_D$ and $\Sigma$: every $\Delta_D$-functor $R\to C$ inverts $\Sigma$; equivalent to: $\mathrm{Hom}_{\Delta_D}(R',C)\to\mathrm{Hom}_{\Delta_D}(R,C)$ is an equivalence, $R'$ the localization.
“Generalized exactness properties”: for a given $\Delta_D$-functor $R\to R'$, require that $\mathrm{Hom}(R',C)\to\mathrm{Hom}(R,C)$ be an equivalence, fully faithful or faithful.
The 2-subcategories of $\Delta_D$ so defined are stable under 2-limits in $\mathbf{Cat}$.
Requiring the arrow of $\{0\to1\}$ to be inverted defines groupoids.
items.name: $D=\varnothing$

items.text: Equalizing the two arrows of $\{0\rightrightarrows1\}$ defines preordered categories, equivalent to preordered sets, 2-equivalent to ordered sets.
The two conditions together define essentially discrete categories, 2-equivalent to $\mathbf{Set}$.
For $\Delta=\mathbf{Cat}$: the envelope of $I$ is $I$; problem two is solved by the category of fractions $I[\Sigma^{-1}]$ (Gabriel–Zisman).
For groupoids: the envelope of $I$ is its fundamental groupoid $I[I^{-1}]$, with the same connected components; problem two is trivial.
For preorders: the envelope of $I$ is $\mathrm{Ob}\,I$ with the preorder $x\ge y$ if there is an arrow $x\to y$.
Making relations $x_i\le y_i$ of a preorder invertible: take the preorder generated by the given preorder and the $y_i\le x_i$.
For discrete categories: the envelope of $I$ is $\pi_0(I)$, the set of connected components; problem two is trivial.
If $T=T_R$ and if $C$ has limits of type $\delta$ commuting with colimits of type $D''$, $T(C)$ has these limits, computed argumentwise.
Tape 3, side B
A morphism of representable theories $T\to T'$ gives $T(C)\to T'(C)$ commuting with these limits; likewise $T(C)\to T(C')$ if $C\to C'$ preserves them.
For every object $r$ of $R$, the evaluation functor $r_C:T(C)\to C$ commutes with limits of type $\delta$.
The category of torsors under a group $G\neq1$ has no products, no coproducts, and no initial or terminal object.
If $D''=\varnothing$ and if $C$ has limits of type $\delta$ (resp. arbitrary), $T(C)$ has them too.
For $\Delta'\subset\Delta$ (fewer limits required), restriction sends $\Delta$-theories to $\Delta'$-theories and algebraic theories to algebraic theories.
If problems one and two have a solution in $\Delta'$, the restriction of $T_R$ to $\Delta'$ is represented by the “$\Delta$–$\Delta'$ envelope” $R'$ of $R$.
$R'$ is obtained from the envelope of $R$ in $\Delta'$ by inverting the comparison arrows of the limits of type $D$ of $R$.
The restriction functor $\mathrm{Hom}(T_1,T_2)\to\mathrm{Hom}(T'_1,T'_2)$ is in general neither faithful, nor full, nor essentially surjective.
Envelopes and categories of fractions
For $J$ small, $J\to\widehat{J}$ is the envelope under colimits: for $D$ cocomplete, restriction of cocontinuous functors $\widehat{J}\to D$ to $J$ is an equivalence.
Every presheaf $F$ on $J$ is the colimit over $J/F$ of the objects of $J$ over $F$; the extension is $\widehat{\varphi}(F)=\varinjlim_{J/F}\varphi(X)$.
Problem one for $\Delta$ = categories with small limits: the envelope of a small $I$ is $\mathrm{Hom}(I,\mathbf{Set})^{\mathrm{op}}$, with the Yoneda embedding.
In $\Delta$, equalizing $f,g:X\rightrightarrows Y$ amounts to inverting the kernel $\mathrm{Ker}(f,g)\to X$.
Problem two: if $\Sigma'$ is the saturation of $\Sigma$, the category of fractions $C[\Sigma'^{-1}]$ taken in $\mathbf{Cat}$ is in $\Delta$, and $C\to C[\Sigma'^{-1}]$ is the solution.

The saturation $\Sigma'$ (arrows inverted by every $\Delta$-functor inverting $\Sigma$) contains the isomorphisms, is stable under composition and base change, and if two of $u$, $v$, $vu$ are in it, so is the third.
If $u:X\to Y$ is in $\Sigma'$, the diagonal $X\to X\times_Y X$ is in $\Sigma'$.
$\Sigma'$ admits a calculus of fractions: $\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)=\varinjlim\mathrm{Hom}_C(X',Y)$, over the filtered projective system of the $X'\to X$ in $\Sigma'$.
If $C$ has finite limits, so does $C[\Sigma'^{-1}]$, and the localization functor is left exact.
$\Sigma'$ is stable under arbitrary fibre products: if the $X_i\to Y$ are in $\Sigma'$, so is $\prod_Y X_i\to Y$.
$C[\Sigma'^{-1}]$ has arbitrary products, images of those of $C$; thus $C\to C[\Sigma'^{-1}]$ is a $\Delta$-functor.
Further remarks on algebraic theories
Session of 10 July 1973
Tape 1, side A
For $E$ in $\Delta$ and a non-small saturated class $\widetilde\Sigma$, the category of fractions $E[\widetilde\Sigma^{-1}]$ may have non-small $\mathrm{Hom}$s, and is then not in $\Delta$.
For an algebraic theory $R$ with base objects $I$, $I$ is not in general strictly cogenerating in $R$: a group structure is not determined by the maps $x\mapsto x^n$.
Strict generation is not transitive: $\mathbb{Z}$ is strictly generating in free groups, these are so in $\mathbf{Gr}$, but $\{\mathbb{Z}\}$ is not in $\mathbf{Gr}$ (likewise in $\mathbf{Ab}$).
An algebraic theory relative to limits is not always obtained in two steps (arrows, then axioms); a transfinite construction, indexed by a small ordinal, may be needed.

The lecturer retracts a theorem stated earlier: a small strictly cogenerating family is necessary for an algebraic theory but not sufficient, and he previews a counterexample involving the opposite of the category of sets.
If $R\in\Delta$ is algebraic, $R$ admits a small strictly cogenerating family; the converse is false.
$\mathbf{Set}^{\mathrm{op}}$ admits a strict generator (the two-element set) but is the category $T(\mathbf{Set})$ of no algebraic theory $T$.
$\mathbf{Set}^{\mathrm{op}}$ is equivalent to the category of complete atomic Boolean algebras, via $X\mapsto\mathcal{P}(X)$.
A listener objects that the opposite of sets is the category of complete atomic Boolean algebras; the lecturer replies that its axioms need a large family, so it is not algebraic here.
Completeness of a Boolean algebra concerns families indexed by an arbitrary set $I$: a non-small family of operations and axioms, excluded from the algebraic theories of the course.
Debate on whether joins over every index set count as a small set of axioms: the lecturer insists on smallness, others suggest bounding cardinalities, and he calls the choice partly one of taste.
Every complete Boolean algebra falls, for a suitable cardinal $\pi$, under the theory of $\pi$-complete Boolean algebras, which has only a small set of operations.

The lecturer admits long-standing unease with definitions quantifying over arbitrary sets, notes that no contradiction has been shown, and sets aside non-small infinitary operations as a different framework.
The objects of $\Delta$ representing algebraic theories are the $\Delta$-envelopes (adjoining small limits) of small categories of $\Delta_\pi$ (limits of cardinality ${\le}\,\pi$).
The categories $S=R^{\mathrm{op}}=T(\mathbf{Set})$ of set-theoretic realizations of these theories are accessible categories.
Accessible categories
A preordered set $I$ “dominates $\pi$” if it is filtered and every family of cardinality ${\le}\,\pi$ of elements of $I$ has an upper bound; for $\pi\ge 2$, the second condition implies the first.
$E$ satisfies $L_\pi$ if colimits indexed by every small $I$ dominating $\pi$ exist in $E$; $E$ satisfies $L$ if it satisfies $L_\pi$ for some small cardinal $\pi$.
$F\colon E\to E'$ is $\pi$-accessible if $E$ satisfies $L_\pi$ and $F$ commutes with colimits indexed by the $I$ dominating $\pi$; accessible if it is $\pi$-accessible for some small $\pi$.
An object $X$ of $E$ is $\pi$-accessible (resp. accessible) if the functor $\mathrm{Hom}(X,-)$ from $E$ to $\mathbf{Set}$ is $\pi$-accessible (resp. accessible).
$E$ is $\pi$-accessible if it has a small full strictly generating subcategory $C$ consisting of $\pi$-accessible objects (every object is a colimit of a diagram in $C$).
This definition is stronger than that of SGA 4, I, 9, which only required a small generating subcategory.
If $E$, $F$ satisfy $L_\pi$, the full subcategory $\mathrm{Hom}_\pi(E,F)$ of $\pi$-accessible functors is stable in $\mathrm{Hom}(E,F)$ under colimits computed argumentwise.
It is also stable under limits, computed argumentwise, indexed by a small category $J$ with at most $\pi$ arrows.
In $\mathbf{Set}$, colimits along an $I$ dominating $\pi$ commute with limits along a category with at most $\pi$ arrows.
Accessible functors form a full subcategory of $\mathrm{Hom}(E,F)$ stable under small colimits and limits computed argumentwise.
If $E$ satisfies $L_\pi$, the full subcategory $E_\pi$ of $\pi$-accessible objects is stable under colimits indexed by a category with at most $\pi$ arrows.
If $E$ satisfies $L$, the full subcategory of accessible objects of $E$ is stable under small colimits.
If $E$ is accessible, every object of $E$ is accessible.
Examples of accessible categories
Tape 1, side B
A small subcategory $C$ is generating by universal strict epimorphisms if every object is the target of a universally strictly epimorphic family from $C$; this is stronger than strictly generating.
In a topos, every epimorphic family is strictly epimorphic and universal.

If $E$ satisfies $L$, has fibre products, kernels $(u,v)\mapsto\mathrm{Ker}(u,v)$ forming an accessible functor, and such a $C$, then every object of $E$ is accessible and $E$ is accessible (SGA 4, I, 9.11).
Every topos is an accessible category.
A set $X$ of cardinality ${\ge}\,2$ is not an accessible object of $\mathbf{Set}^{\mathrm{op}}$; hence $\mathbf{Set}^{\mathrm{op}}$, which has small colimits and a generator, is not accessible.
The lecturer argues that the opposite of the category of sets is not co-accessible in the relevant sense, since large products break the commutation that is required.
For $\pi$ infinite, the subsets of cardinality ${\le}\,\pi$ of a set $I$ form an ordered set dominating $\pi$, and $\prod_{i\in I}Y_i$ is the limit of the corresponding partial products.

If $\mathrm{card}\,I>\pi$ and $\mathrm{card}\,Y_i\ge 2$, the indicator of a point of $\prod Y_i$ factors through no partial product; the opposite of a nondegenerate topos, or of $\mathbf{Ab}$, is not accessible.
If $E$ and $E^{\mathrm{op}}$ are accessible, is $E$ equivalent to the point category?
Ind-categories
For $C$ small, $\mathrm{Ind}(C)$ is the category of filtered inductive systems in $C$, identified via $\varinjlim$ with a full subcategory of $\widehat{C}$.
$\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ind}(C)}((X_i),(Y_j))=\varprojlim_i\varinjlim_j\mathrm{Hom}(X_i,Y_j)$ (SGA 4, I, 8).
$C\to\mathrm{Ind}(C)$ is universal: for $E$ with filtered colimits, restriction to $C$ of the functors $\mathrm{Ind}(C)\to E$ commuting with these colimits is an equivalence with $\mathrm{Hom}(C,E)$.

If $C$ has finite colimits, $\mathrm{Ind}(C)$ has small colimits and, for $E$ having them, $F\mapsto F|_C$ identifies the functors commuting with these colimits with the right exact functors $C\to E$.
$\mathrm{Ind}_\pi(C)$ is the full subcategory of $\mathrm{Ind}(C)$ of the systems indexed by an $I$ dominating $\pi$; for $C$ small, it is $\pi$-accessible.
An object of $\mathrm{Ind}_\pi(C)$ is $\pi$-accessible if and only if it is a direct summand of an object of $C$; a direct summand of a $\pi$-accessible object is again so.
$C$ is Karoubian if every idempotent has an image summand; $\mathrm{Ind}(C)$ and $\mathrm{Ind}_\pi(C)$ do not change if $C$ is replaced by its Karoubian envelope.
If $C$ is Karoubian and $E=\mathrm{Ind}_\pi(C)$, then $C\simeq E_\pi$ and $E\simeq\mathrm{Ind}_\pi(E_\pi)$.
Cardinal filtrations

For $\pi'\ge\pi$, $\mathrm{Fil}^{\pi'}=\mathrm{Ind}_{\pi,\pi'}(C)$ (systems indexed by an $I$ dominating $\pi$ with $\mathrm{card}\,I\le\pi'$) filters $\mathrm{Ind}_\pi(C)$ by essentially small subcategories, and $\mathrm{Fil}^{\pi}\simeq C$.
The objects of $\mathrm{Fil}^{\pi'}$ are $\pi'$-accessible; if $\pi'^{\pi}=\pi'$, every $\pi'$-accessible object of $\mathrm{Ind}_\pi(C)$ is a direct summand of an object of $\mathrm{Fil}^{\pi'}$.

“Cardinal filtration”: a family $(\mathrm{Fil}^{\pi'})_{\pi'\ge\pi}$ of essentially small subcategories, stable under $\varinjlim$ of index $I$ dominating $\pi$, $\mathrm{card}\,I\le\pi'$, every object of $\mathrm{Fil}^{\pi''}$ being a colimit of objects of $\mathrm{Fil}^{\pi'}$ with index dominating $\pi'$, of cardinality ${\le}\,\pi''$.
The $\mathrm{Ind}_{\pi,\pi'}(C)$ form a cardinal filtration of $\mathrm{Ind}_\pi(C)$ if one restricts to cardinals such that $\pi''^{\pi'}=\pi''$ (bound $\pi''^{\pi'}$ of SGA 4, I, 9).
If $E$ has small colimits, the following are equivalent: a) $E$ is $\pi$-accessible; b) $E\simeq\mathrm{Ind}_\pi(C)$, $C$ small; c) $E_\pi$ is essentially small and strictly generating.

If $C\subset E_\pi$ is small and full, the extension $\mathrm{Ind}_\pi(C)\to E$ is fully faithful; it is an equivalence if $C$ is strictly generating and stable under limits with at most $\pi$ arrows.
A colimit indexed by a small category $I$ is the limit, along the ordered set (dominating $\pi$) of subcategories of $I$ with at most $\pi$ arrows, of the partial limits.
If $E$ is $\pi$-accessible and has small colimits, $E\simeq\mathrm{Ind}_{\pi'}(E_{\pi'})$ for every $\pi'\ge\pi$.
A $\pi$-accessible functor does not necessarily send $\pi$-accessible objects to $\pi$-accessible objects (example: $E$ a point).
If $E$, $E'$ are $\pi_0$-accessible with small colimits, $F\colon E\to E'$ is accessible if and only if there exist $\pi\ge\pi_0$ and $f\colon E_\pi\to E'_\pi$ with $F\simeq\mathrm{Ind}_\pi(f)$.
Strictly generating functors
Session of 11 July 1973
Tape 1

For $i\colon C\to E$, $\varinjlim_{(Y,u)\in C/X}i(Y)\to X$ is an isomorphism for every $X$ if and only if $E\to\widehat{C}$, $X\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(i(-),X)$, is fully faithful: $i$ is then called strictly generating.
Then every $X$ is the target of a strictly epimorphic family $i(Y_\alpha)\to X$; the converse holds if $i$ is fully faithful and $E$ has fibre products and universal strictly epimorphic families.

If $E$ has small colimits and $C$ is small, $i$ extends to $i_!\colon\widehat{C}\to E$, left adjoint to $E\to\widehat{C}$; $i$ is strictly generating if and only if $i_!$ makes $E$ a category of fractions of $\widehat{C}$.
A category with small colimits has a small strictly generating subcategory if and only if it is equivalent to a reflective full subcategory of some $\widehat{C}$, $C$ small.
$\mathbf{Set}^{\mathrm{op}}$ (complete atomic Boolean algebras) and $\mathbf{Ab}^{\mathrm{op}}$ (compact abelian groups) have small colimits and a small strictly generating family.

Whether compact spaces admit a small strictly generating family: a listener proposes ultrafilter operations, but the lecturer argues the point cannot strictly generate, since the forgetful functor to sets is not fully faithful.
In the category of compact spaces, the one-point space is not strictly generating: the underlying-set functor is faithful but not fully faithful.
Theories defined by finite limits

The lecturer warns that a statement of the previous day was false: exactness conditions on objects and on functors must match, since existence conditions without uniqueness give no existence theorems for envelopes.

For $\Delta_D$ (limits of type $D'$ only), the envelope of $C$ is the subcategory of $\mathrm{Hom}(C,\mathbf{Set})^{\mathrm{op}}$ generated by $C$ under iterated limits of type $D'$; $C$ embeds fully in it.
If $R_0$ represents a theory for $\Delta_D$, the theory extended to $\Delta$ is represented by $R=T(\mathbf{Set})^{\mathrm{op}}$, the envelope of $R_0$ under small limits; $R_0\subset R$ is full.
A theory relative to $\Delta_D$ is equivalent to the pair $(S,\Sigma_0)$, $S=T(\mathbf{Set})$, $\Sigma_0=R_0^{\mathrm{op}}\subset S$, where $S$ is the envelope of $\Sigma_0$ under small colimits.
For $D'$ consisting of the finite diagrams, the algebraic theories are the small categories $R_0$ with finite limits; dually, $\Sigma_0$ is small with finite colimits.
Finitely presented objects
$X$ is finitely presented ($\aleph_0$-accessible) if $\mathrm{Hom}(X,-)$ commutes with filtered colimits; we write $S_{\mathrm{fp}}$ for the full subcategory of these objects.
For a theory defined by finite limits, $\Sigma_0\simeq S_{\mathrm{fp}}$ and $S\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\Sigma_0)$; $S$ and $\Sigma_0$ determine each other, and $R_0\simeq(S_{\mathrm{fp}})^{\mathrm{op}}$.

For $\Sigma_0\subset S$ full, $\mathrm{Ind}(\Sigma_0)\to S$ is fully faithful if and only if $\Sigma_0\subset S_{\mathrm{fp}}$; if $\Sigma_0$ is stable under finite colimits, it is an equivalence if and only if $\Sigma_0$ is strictly generating.
In categories of groups or modules, the finitely presented objects are the groups or modules finitely presented in the usual sense.
$S$ with small colimits is $T(\mathbf{Set})$ for a theory defined by finite limits if and only if $S_{\mathrm{fp}}$ is essentially small and strictly generating.

In $\mathbf{Gr}$, for $C$ full on the object $\mathbb{Z}$, $\widehat{C}$ consists of the sets acted on by the monoid $(\mathbb{Z},\times)$; $G\mapsto(G,x\mapsto x^n)$ is faithful but not full: $\mathbb{Z}$ is generating, but not strictly.
For $C\subset E$ full, $E\to\widehat{C}$ fully faithful, faithful, conservative, or conservative on monomorphisms: distinct notions of generation, which coincide in a topos.

Clarifying generating versus strictly generating, the lecturer lists several notions that coincide in a topos but differ in general; free groups of finite type serve as the natural strictly generating family for groups.
Finitely generated free groups form a small strictly generating subcategory of $\mathbf{Gr}$.
The morphisms $T\to T'$ of theories defined by finite limits correspond to the functors $S'\to S$ commuting with small colimits and preserving finitely presented objects.
Lawvere theories and finite products

For finite products, the envelope of an object $X$ is $(\mathbf{Set}_{\mathrm{f}})^{\mathrm{op}}$, with objects $X^n$; for products of cardinality ${\le}\,\pi$, the opposite of the sets of cardinality ${\le}\,\pi$.

A theory with one base object defined by finite products is a category with objects $\mathbb{N}$, $n$ being the $n$-th power of $1$, given by the $H_n=\mathrm{Hom}(X^n,X)$ and their substitution (Lazard’s “analyseurs”).
The realizations of such a (Lawvere) theory in a category $E$ with finite products are the functors to $E$ commuting with finite products.
For a set $I$ of base objects, one starts from the opposite of the category of finite sets over $I$ (objects $\prod_i X_i^{n_i}$, $n_i$ almost all zero).
For a theory defined by finite products, $\Sigma_0$ is stable under finite coproducts and strictly generating in $S$, but this does not characterize the pairs $(S,\Sigma_0)$.

$S$ with small limits is the category of models of a theory with finite products and base objects $I$ if and only if its equivalence relations are effective and $I$, consisting of finitely presented objects, detects effective epimorphisms ($\mathrm{Hom}(i,f)$ surjective).
Then $S\to\mathbf{Set}^I$, $X\mapsto(\mathrm{Hom}(i,X))_{i\in I}$, has a left adjoint and is monadic (“tripleable”).
Birkhoff's theorem
Tape 2, side A
Birkhoff’s theorem: a full subcategory of a category of structures defined by finite products, stable under products, subobjects and quotients, is defined by equations.

On Birkhoff's theorem, a subcategory closed under products, subobjects and quotients is defined by equations; torsion-free abelian groups inside abelian groups show that closure conditions alone do not capture all subcategories.
Such a subcategory is reflective: the adjoint associates to $X$ its largest quotient belonging to the subcategory.
Torsion-free abelian groups, stable under products and subgroups but not under quotients, are not definable by equations in $\mathbf{Ab}$.
To a Birkhoff subcategory $S'\subset S$ corresponds $R\to R'$ bijective on objects and surjective on arrows: $T'$ is deduced from $T$ by equalizing arrows.
Groups are the monoids in which a certain arrow is invertible; not stable under submonoids, they are not definable by equations in monoids.
Groups inside monoids cannot be cut out by equations alone, since the integers contain the natural numbers as a submonoid that is not a group, so the subclass is not closed under submonoids.
The reflective full subcategories $S'\subset S$ such that the composite $S'\to\mathbf{Set}^I$ is monadic form a larger class than that of Birkhoff subcategories.
Pseudo-topoi and classifying topoi
A “pseudo-topos” satisfies Giraud’s axioms a), b), c): small colimits and finite limits; universal disjoint coproducts; universal effective equivalence relations.
The functors considered commute with small colimits and finite limits: they are the inverse images $f^*$ of morphisms of topoi in the opposite direction.

A topos $\mathcal{E}$ classifies a theory $T$, with universal object $U\in T(\mathcal{E})$, if $f\mapsto f^*U$ is an equivalence $\mathrm{Top}(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{E})^{\mathrm{op}}\simeq T(\mathcal{F})$ for every $\mathcal{F}$ (2-arrows oriented by the direct images).
For $C$ small with finite limits, the envelope of $C$ among pseudo-topoi is $\widehat{C}$, with the Yoneda embedding.
Continuous functors and morphisms of sites
$f\colon C\to C'$ between sites is continuous if $F\mapsto F\circ f$ sends sheaves on $C'$ to sheaves on $C$; this depends only on $\varepsilon_{C'}\circ f\colon C\to\widetilde{C'}$.
By composition with $\varepsilon_C$, the functors $\widetilde{C}\to\widetilde{C'}$ commuting with small colimits are identified with the continuous functors $C\to\widetilde{C'}$.
If $C$, $C'$ have finite limits and $f$ commutes with them, $f$ is continuous if and only if it sends covering families to covering families.
For $X'\to X$ continuous, the inverse image of open sets is such a continuous functor from the site of open sets of $X$ to that of $X'$.
In general, $f$ is continuous if and only if, for every covering sieve $R$ of $X$, $\varepsilon_{C'}f(X)=\varinjlim_{Y\in C/R}\varepsilon_{C'}f(Y)$.
A sieve $R$ of $X$ is covering if and only if $\varepsilon(X)=\varinjlim_{Y\in C/R}\varepsilon(Y)$ in $\widetilde{C}$.
If $C$, $C'$ have finite limits and the topology of $C'$ is coarser than the canonical one, a continuous $f$ induces a morphism of topoi if and only if $f$ is left exact.
A morphism of sites is a continuous functor that induces a morphism of topoi; it is oriented in the direction of that morphism.

For a site $C$ with finite limits and a topos $\mathcal{E}$, $\mathrm{Top}(\mathcal{E},\widetilde{C})^{\mathrm{op}}$ is equivalent to the left exact functors $C\to\mathcal{E}$ sending covering families to epimorphic families.
$\widehat{C}$ is $\widetilde{C}$ for the coarsest topology (covering families: those having a member with a section).
If $C$ has finite limits, $\mathrm{Top}(\mathcal{E},\widehat{C})^{\mathrm{op}}$ is equivalent to the left exact functors $C\to\mathcal{E}$.
Classifying topoi of finite-limit theories
Session of 12 July 1973
Tape 1

If $C$ is a small category with finite limits, $\widehat{C}$ classifies the theory $T_C$: $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Top}}(\mathcal{E},\widehat{C})\simeq\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{lex}}(C,\mathcal{E})$ for every topos $\mathcal{E}$.
The classifying topos of groups is the category of covariant functors from finitely presented groups to $\mathbf{Set}$.
The classifying topos of commutative rings is that of functors from finitely presented rings to $\mathbf{Set}$, i.e. of presheaves on affine schemes of finite type over $\mathbb{Z}$.
The envelope $\widetilde{C}$ of $C$ under finite limits is the opposite of the category of finitely presented functors $C\to\mathbf{Set}$; $C\to\widetilde{C}$ is fully faithful.
If $\mathcal{E}$ has finite limits, $\mathrm{Hom}(C,\mathcal{E})\simeq\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{lex}}(\widetilde{C},\mathcal{E})$.
Enveloping topos of a small category $C$: the topos of presheaves on $\widetilde{C}$; the morphisms from a topos $\mathcal{E}$ to it are equivalent to $\mathrm{Hom}(C,\mathcal{E})$.
Subtopoi and localization
Localization: for a set $\Sigma$ of arrows of a topos $\mathcal{E}$, one seeks a universal $\Delta$-functor $\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{E}[\Sigma^{-1}]$ making the arrows of $\Sigma$ invertible.
The subtopoi of $\mathcal{E}$ correspond bijectively to the saturated sets of arrows of $\mathcal{E}$ (stable under limits and local in nature) (SGA 4, exercise).
A morphism of topoi $i\colon\mathcal{E}'\to\mathcal{E}$ is an embedding if $i_*$ is fully faithful, i.e. if $i^*$ is a localization functor.
The subtopoi of $\mathcal{E}$ are identified with the strictly full subcategories whose inclusion admits a left exact left adjoint.
For a small category $C$, the topologies $J$ on $C$ correspond bijectively, via $J\mapsto\mathrm{Sh}(C,J)$, to the subtopoi of $\widehat{C}$.
A continuous map $f\colon X\to Y$ induces an embedding of topoi iff the topology of $X$ is the inverse image of that of $Y$; subspaces of $Y$ give subtopoi, but not all of them.

A morphism $\mathcal{F}\to\mathcal{E}$ factors through a subtopos $\mathcal{E}'$ iff its direct image factors through $\mathcal{E}'$, iff its inverse image factors through the localization $\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{E}'$.

To a subtopos $\mathcal{E}'$ one associates the arrows made invertible by $i^*$; to $\Sigma$, the objects $X$ such that $\mathrm{Hom}(Z,X)\to\mathrm{Hom}(Y,X)$ is bijective for every $Y\to Z$ in $\Sigma$.
$\mathcal{E}[\Sigma^{-1}]$ exists and is a subtopos of $\mathcal{E}$; every subtopos is obtained in this way by inverting a family of arrows.
If $\mathcal{E}=\mathrm{Sh}(C,J)$, its subtopoi correspond to the topologies on $C$ finer than $J$; likewise for the subtheories of the theory represented by $\mathcal{E}$.
Generating subcategories of a topos
If a small full subcategory $C$ generates the topos $\mathcal{E}$, $\mathcal{E}$ is a subtopos of $\widehat{C}$: $\mathcal{E}\simeq\mathrm{Sh}(C,J)$ for the induced topology.

For $C$ full in $\mathcal{E}$: (a) $\mathcal{E}\to\widehat{C}$ fully faithful is equivalent to (b) every $X$ is a colimit of the $Y$ in $C/X$; (b) implies (c): every $X$ is the target of a strictly epimorphic family from $C$.

The lecturer corrects an SGA claim on strictly generating families: a family with sources in a subcategory need not make the subcategory strictly generating, as the free groups on one and two generators show.
Counterexample to (c) $\Rightarrow$ (b): in groups, with $C=\{\mathbb{Z}\}$, $\mathbb{Z}*\mathbb{Z}$ satisfies (c) but is not a colimit of $C/(\mathbb{Z}*\mathbb{Z})$.
Enlarging a strictly epimorphic family can make it lose this property (all the arrows $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}*\mathbb{Z}$ in groups).
If fibre products exist and distribute over coproducts, $(X_i\to X)$ is strictly epimorphic iff $\coprod X_i\to X$ is; this is false in general.
A correction on strictly epimorphic families: the equivalence with the epimorphism of their sum needs fibre products distributing over sums, and the repaired statement asks for universality as well.
Corrected statement: (c$'$) every $X$ is the target of a family from $C$ that is strictly and universally epimorphic; then (c$'$) implies (b).
If a strictly and universally epimorphic family factors through a family $(X_i\to Y)$, the latter is again strictly and universally epimorphic.
(b) is equivalent to (b$'$): for every $X$, the family of all arrows $Y\to X$, $Y$ in $C$, is strictly epimorphic.
Tape 2, side A
A family $(Y\to X)$ is strictly epimorphic iff for every $Z$, $\mathrm{Hom}(X,Z)$ is identified with the compatible families of elements of the $\mathrm{Hom}(Y,Z)$ (sheaf condition).
Algebraic theories and topoi
$R\in\Delta$ represents an algebraic theory iff $R$ is a topos; $B\colon I\to R$ is basic iff the finite products of the $B(i)$ generate $R$.
Every topos $R$ represents an algebraic theory: if $C\subset R$ is small, generating and stable under finite limits, $T_R$ is a full subtheory of $T_C=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{lex}}(C,-)$.
For such a $C$, the morphisms of topoi $\mathcal{E}\to R$ correspond to the left exact functors $C\to\mathcal{E}$ sending covering families to epimorphic families.
If $R'\to R$ induces for every topos $\mathcal{E}$ a fully faithful embedding $T_{R'}(\mathcal{E})\to T_R(\mathcal{E})$, $R'$ is a subtopos of $R$ (exercise of SGA 4).
A subtopos of $R=\mathrm{Sh}(C,\tau)$ is $\mathrm{Sh}(C,\tau')$ with $\tau'$ finer; its theory is deduced from $T_R$ by a small set of axioms.
Limits of topoi
Arbitrary (not necessarily filtered) 2-limits of topoi exist; in $\Delta$, they are 2-colimits.
Construction: $C_i\subset R_i$ compatible small generating subcategories, $C$ the 2-colimit of the $C_i$ in $\mathbf{Cat}$, then localization of the enveloping topos of $C$ at a small $\Sigma$.
The 2-colimit of a system of small categories is obtained by inverting the cartesian arrows of the associated (co)fibred category.
A 2-limit of accessible categories, with accessible transition functors, is accessible.
Algebraic theories built from finite products
Tape 2, side B

The category $J_0$ freely generated by finite products over a set $I$ is the opposite of the families of finite sets indexed by $I$, almost all empty; it is also the envelope under finite limits of the discrete $I$.
$R_0=\widehat{J_0}$ classifies families of objects indexed by $I$: $\mathrm{Hom}_\Delta(R_0,\mathcal{E})\simeq\mathcal{E}^I$.
Adding axioms: $R_{\alpha+1}=R_\alpha[\Sigma_\alpha^{-1}]$ has the same objects as $R_\alpha$, so $J_0$ still generates it.

Adding arrows given by a graph $D=(H\rightrightarrows S)$: $R_{\alpha+1}$ is the 2-pushout in $\Delta$ of $R_\alpha$ and $\rho(\widetilde{D})$ over $\rho(S)$ ($\rho$ the enveloping topos, $\widetilde{D}$ the free category).
In this construction, every object of $R_{\alpha+1}$ is covered by images of objects of $R_\alpha$; hence $J_0$ generates $R_{\alpha+1}$.
Limit step: for $\alpha$ a limit, $R_\alpha$ is the 2-colimit in $\Delta$ of the $R_\beta$, $\beta<\alpha$; $J_0$ still generates it.
Necessity: if $I\to R$ is basic for an algebraic theory, $R$ is a topos generated by the finite products of objects of $I$.
Sufficiency: if the finite products of the objects of $I$ generate the topos $R$, the theory is obtained without transfinite recursion: finite products, arrows between them, then axioms.
For $J$ small with finite products, the theory $\mathcal{E}\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}_\Pi(J,\mathcal{E})$ of functors preserving finite products is represented by a topos $\rho_{\Pi,\Delta}(J)$.
If the subcategory $J_2\subset R$ of finite products of objects of $I$ generates $R$, $R$ is a subtopos of $\rho_{\Pi,\Delta}(J_2)$; two successive localizations make it one.
Preservation of finite products is an axiom: the arrow of constructions $\varepsilon_{X\times Y}\to\varepsilon_X\times\varepsilon_Y$ must become an isomorphism.
If $R\in\Delta$ represents a theory, its category of constructions is $R$; equalizing two arrows amounts to inverting a kernel, hence a single type of axiom.
Tape 3, side A
In a topos, $u\colon X\to Y$ is an epimorphism iff $Y\sqcup_X Y\to Y$ is an isomorphism; “being covering” is thus written as an invertibility axiom.
Classifying topos of an object and its subtopoi
The classifying topos of an object without structure is the category of functors from finite sets to $\mathbf{Set}$ (presheaves on $J=\{X^n\}$).
If $B_T$ classifies the theory $T$, its category of points is equivalent to $T(\mathbf{Set})$.
For all topoi $\mathcal{E}$ and $B$, $\mathrm{Hom}_\Delta(B,\mathcal{E})$ admits filtered colimits, since in a topos they commute with finite limits.
The essential points of the classifying topos of objects correspond to finite sets.
The smallest subtopos containing a family of points of a topos is defined by the arrows whose stalks at these points are isomorphisms.
The subobjects of the terminal object of the classifying topos $B$ of objects are $\varnothing$, the image of $X\to e$, and $e$: $B$ has three open subtopoi.
The closed complement $\Phi_0$ of $B^*$ classifies initial objects; it is equivalent to the point topos, whose point is the empty set.
The open $B^*$ classifies the objects $x$ such that $x\to e$ is an epimorphism; its points are the nonempty sets.
The empty subtopos classifies the theory that has a model only in the empty topos.
The subtopos $\Phi_{01}$ classifies the subobjects of the terminal object ($x\to e$ a monomorphism); its points are the sets with at most one element.
$\Phi_1=\Phi_{01}\cap B^*$ classifies terminal objects; $\Phi_0$ and $\Phi_1$ are equivalent to the point topos but are two distinct points of $B$.
$\Phi_{01}\simeq\widehat{\Delta_1}$, where $\Delta_1=\{0\to 1\}$: the morphisms $\mathcal{E}\to\widehat{\Delta_1}$ correspond to the monomorphisms $x\hookrightarrow e$.
$\widehat{\Delta_1}$ is the topos of the Sierpiński space (spectrum of a discrete valuation ring); a morphism to it is equivalent to an open of the source topos.
Every $T_0$ topological space embeds in a product of copies of the Sierpiński space.
The subtopoi of a topos form a complete lattice (arbitrary intersections and suprema).
Flat functors and torsors
In the opposite of finitely presented groups, the universal group is $\mathbb{Z}$ with its cogroup structure; the classifying topos of groups is its topos of presheaves.
$\widehat{C}$ classifies the functors $C\to\mathcal{E}$ whose continuous extension to $\widehat{C}$ is left exact (flat functors); if $C$ has finite limits, these are the left exact functors.
For a group $G$ viewed as a category $C$ with one object, $\widehat{C}=B_G$; a functor $C\to\mathcal{E}$ is an object $X$ with a $G$-action, extended by $P\mapsto P\wedge^G X$.
Contracted product: $P\wedge^G X$ is the quotient of $P\times X$ by the diagonal action of $G$, $(pg,x)\sim(p,gx)$.
This extension is left exact iff $X$ is a torsor under the constant group $G_{\mathcal{E}}$: $B_G$ classifies $G$-torsors.
The classifying topos of a group
Tape 3, side B
For a group $G$ of a topos $S$, represent on topoi $X$ over $S$ the 2-functor of torsors under the inverse image of $G$.
The objects of $S$ equipped with a left action of $G$ form a topos $B_G$: the forgetful functor $B_G\to S$ is faithful and commutes with all limits.
$p^*\colon S\to B_G$ equips an object with the trivial action; a group morphism $G\to G'$ induces by restriction an essential morphism $B_G\to B_{G'}$.
Universal torsor: $G$ acting on itself by left translations (an object of $B_G$), with the right action of $\overline{G}=p^*G$ by right translations.
Universality: for $q\colon X\to S$, the $q^*G$-torsors on $X$ correspond to the morphisms $X\to B_G$ over $S$, via the contracted product.
Classifying topoi: further examples

A question on what structure the classifying topos of a monoid, rather than a group, would classify: the lecturer does not know, and instead explains torsors and locally free modules as the case of interest.
On a stack, the category of objects locally isomorphic to a section $s$, with their isomorphisms, is equivalent to that of torsors under $\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}(s)$.
Locally free $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules of rank $n$, with their isomorphisms, are equivalent to torsors under $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal{O}_X)$.
The topos $B_{\mathrm{GL}_n}$ over the classifying topos of rings classifies ringed topoi equipped with a locally free module of rank $n$ (with isomorphisms).
Local rings are classified by the subtopos defined by the Zariski topology on affine schemes of finite type over $\mathbb{Z}$.
Strictly local rings are classified by a smaller subtopos, defined by a finer topology (the étale topology).
Locally constant objects do not come from a representable theory: they are not stable under colimits (totally disconnected spaces).
Covering spaces of rank $n$ of the terminal object do not form an algebraic structure: in $\mathbf{Set}$, sets with $n$ elements are not stable under filtered colimits.
With only isomorphisms as morphisms, the objects locally isomorphic to the constant object $I_n$ with $n$ elements are equivalent to torsors under the constant group $\mathfrak{S}_n$.
The topos $B_{\mathfrak{S}_n}$ of $\mathfrak{S}_n$-sets classifies covering spaces of rank $n$ of the terminal object, with their isomorphisms.
Connected rings
Connectedness of the spectrum of a ring can be written in any topos (every idempotent is $0$ or $1$, and $0\neq1$) and defines a subtopos of the classifying topos of rings.
“Having exactly $n$ connected components” does not define a theory: the property is not stable under filtered colimits.
A ring locally with $n$ connected components is equivalent to a pair: $I$ locally constant of rank $n$, and a 0-connected ring $A_0$ over $I$, of which $A$ is the direct image.
The functor $(I,A_0)\mapsto A$ is fully faithful if the ring morphisms taken are those inducing isomorphisms on the $\pi_0$.
The classifying topos of rings locally with $n$ components is constructed over $B_{\mathfrak{S}_n}$, by classifying a 0-connected ring over the universal covering space $I_n$.
Tape 4, side A
The classifying topos of a ring over an object $I$ of a topos $B$ exists; if $I$ is a sum of $n$ copies of the terminal object, it is $R^n\times B$, $R$ the classifying topos of rings.
Left exact functors and topoi
If $\mathcal{E}$ is a topos and $C$ has finite limits, $C\to\mathcal{E}$ is left exact iff its extension $\widehat{C}\to\mathcal{E}$ commuting with colimits is.
Converse: if $\mathcal{E}$ has a small strictly generating subcategory $C$ stable under finite limits and this property holds, $\mathcal{E}$ is a topos.
The classifying topos of a theory defined by finite limits is connected and acyclic.
Elementary topos: a category with finite limits, cartesian closed, equipped with a subobject classifier.
Faithfulness of a $G$-action on $X$ is not stable under inverse image: it is not an algebraic structure in the sense of topoi.
Topoi without points
Can topological spaces be seen as structures inside a topos? A suggestion based on the power-set object is discussed; the lecturer is not convinced that it behaves well with inverse limits.
A theory represented by a nonempty topos may have no set-theoretic model: there exist topoi without points.
Structures classified by toposes need not have set-theoretic realizations: the lecturer explains that toposes without points exist, and a listener recalls an example built from a measure space.
Borel sets of $[0,1]$ modulo null measure, countable coverings up to null measure; the resulting topos has no point.
items.name: Deligne

items.text: The classifying topos of fields
Classifying topos of fields: affine schemes of finite type over $\mathbb{Z}$, covering families generated by $\{D(f)\to X,\ V(f)\to X\}$ and by $X_{\mathrm{red}}\to X$.
For $X$ quasi-compact and quasi-separated, the constructible topology (opens: unions of constructible subsets) makes $X$ compact, with the same points.

For $X=\mathrm{Spec}\,A$, the colimit of the rings of functions of the finite constructible partitions (reduced structures) has as spectrum $X$ with the constructible topology, with stalks the residue fields.
The classifying topos of fields is identified with presheaves on these compact schemes (constructible morphisms) turning finite sums into products; the universal field is the ring of functions.
Flatness
Absolutely flat rings: rings all of whose modules are flat; these are the reduced rings of Krull dimension zero.
Flatness of a module over a ring of a topos is stable under inverse image by a morphism of topoi (Deligne).
Criterion: $M$ is flat over $A$ if for every $U$ and every finitely generated ideal $J\subset A_U$, $M_U\otimes J\to M_U$ is a monomorphism.
This criterion is a countable family of axioms: for each $n$, on $U_n=A^n$, the ideal generated by the $n$ universal projections.
Tape 4, side B
When a notion such as flatness or connectedness has several candidate extensions to toposes, the lecturer says he discards any not stable under inverse image, and so far has met no serious ambiguity.
For a relative scheme of finite presentation over a ringed topos, two notions of flatness (Hakim): a flat morphism of ringed topoi, or locally arising from a flat morphism of schemes.
Hypertopoi
In $\mathbf{Set}$, an arbitrary product of epimorphisms is an epimorphism (analogue of total disconnectedness); this does not hold in every topos.
The morphism $\mathcal{E}\to\mathrm{pt}$ is essential iff the constant sheaf functor commutes with arbitrary products (analogue of local connectedness).
The topoi $\widehat{C}$ have these two properties; that they are the only ones is stated without proof. “Hypertopos”: these topoi, with essential morphisms; the notion is not defined more precisely.
A small Karoubian category $D$ is determined by $\widehat{D}$: it is the category of its essential points.
The category of points of $\widehat{C}$, $C$ with finite limits, is $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{lex}}(C,\mathbf{Set})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(C^{\mathrm{op}})$.
For hypertopoi, the only candidate classifying object of $T_C$ is the topos of presheaves on the category of points of $\widehat{C}$, not small in general (“pseudo-hypertopos”).
Universes
A letter reports that Deligne has proved the Weil conjectures. The proof is not yet known to the lecturer, who expects it to use étale cohomology and hence universes.
The universe axiom is equivalent to: every cardinal is bounded by a strongly inaccessible cardinal; the existence of such a cardinal is not provable in ZFC, if ZFC is consistent.

Asked whether the universe axiom could be shown consistent relative to ZFC, the lecturer recalls having been told by logicians, ten years earlier, that there was no hope. This does follow from Gödel's second incompleteness theorem, since the axiom implies the consistency of ZFC.

Samuel's idea of “galaxies”, sets smaller than universes in which the union axiom is weakened, is recalled as a way to avoid a new axiom. The description given is unclear, and it is not reproduced here as a definition.
The standard conjectures

In a discussion of foundations and the continuum hypothesis, a listener recalls an abelian group statement settled by that hypothesis, and the conversation turns to whether such questions have a definite answer.
The standard conjectures are formulated on algebraic cycles modulo numerical equivalence, with no particular cohomology; they include the equality of homological and numerical equivalence.
The standard conjectures would allow one to construct motives from algebraic cycles alone, independently of any cohomology.
Asked for an example of a site that is not small, the lecturer proposes all schemes with the étale or flat topology, since some schemes are too big to be covered by a set.
Subtopoi of a presheaf topos correspond to topologies on the category; as classifying topoi of structures, they correspond to adding axioms to a type of algebraic structure.
Quotient topoi are suggested for foliations, where the naive quotient space may be very bad; the lecturer says a good quotient topos always exists, and points to exercises in SGA 4.
Session of 29 May 1973
Tape 1, side A
Affine algebraic spaces as functors
For an arbitrary set $I$, let $P_I=k[T_i]_{i\in I}$; a polynomial $f\in P_I$ defines a map $\tilde f\colon k^I\to k$, which in general does not determine $f$.
For every $k$-algebra $k'$, $u\mapsto(u(T_i))_{i\in I}$ is a bijection from $\mathrm{Hom}_k(P_I,k')$ onto $k'^I$ (universal property of the polynomial algebra).
A point $x\in k^I$ is equivalent to a homomorphism $\varepsilon_x\colon P_I\to k$, and $f(x)=\varepsilon_x(f)$.
For fixed $x$, $f\mapsto f(x)$ is a homomorphism of $k$-algebras $P_I\to k$: $(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)$, $(fg)(x)=f(x)g(x)$, $(\lambda f)(x)=\lambda f(x)$.
The standard affine space $E^I$ is the functor from the category of $k$-algebras to sets, $k'\mapsto k'^I$, a homomorphism $u$ acting by $u^I$.
A system of equations $S=(f_j)_{j\in J}$ in $P_I$ defines a subfunctor $V_S\subset E^I$: $V_S(k')$ is the set of solutions in $k'^I$.
The solutions of $S$ in every $k$-algebra $k'$ are those of the ideal $J$ generated by $S$: $V_S=V_J$, where $V_J(k')=\{x\in k'^I : f(x)=0\ \forall f\in J\}$.
The map $J\mapsto V_J$ from ideals of $P_I$ to subfunctors of $E^I$ is injective; its values are the subfunctors defined by equations.
A functor from $k$-algebras to sets is isomorphic to some $V_S$ if and only if it is representable: $k'\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}_k(A,k')$ for a $k$-algebra $A$, denoted $V_A$.
The functor $V_A$ embeds as a subfunctor $V_S$ of $E^I$ if and only if $A$ is a quotient of $P_I$, that is, generated as a $k$-algebra by a family indexed by $I$.
The isomorphisms from $V_A$ onto some $V_S\subset E^I$ correspond to the families $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ of generators of the $k$-algebra $A$.
Tape 1, side B
For an ideal $J$ of $P_I$, $V_J(k')$ is identified, via $\mathrm{Hom}_k(P_I,k')\simeq k'^I$, with the set of homomorphisms $P_I\to k'$ vanishing on $J$, hence with $\mathrm{Hom}_k(P_I/J,k')$.
The functor $V_J$ is represented by the $k$-algebra $P_I/J$, the isomorphism being functorial in $k'$: $V_J\simeq V_{P_I/J}$.
The functors $V_J\subset E^I$ are the closed algebraic subspaces of $E^I$; a functor isomorphic to one of them is an affine algebraic space over $k$.
Every $k$-algebra $A$ is isomorphic to a quotient $P_I/J$: take a generating family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ of $A$ (for instance $I=A$) and $J$ the kernel of $T_i\mapsto a_i$.
The affine algebraic spaces over $k$ are exactly the representable functors; an embedding into $E^I$ amounts to a family of generators of the algebra indexed by $I$.
A morphism $V_J\to V_{J'}$ is a natural transformation, that is, a family of maps $V_J(k')\to V_{J'}(k')$ compatible with the homomorphisms of $k'$.
A family $(F_{i'})_{i'\in I'}$ of polynomials of $P_I$ defines a morphism $E^I\to E^{I'}$, since $E^{I'}=(E^1)^{I'}$ and each polynomial gives $k'^I\to k'$ functorially in $k'$.
For functors represented by $A$ and $A'$, the morphisms from $V_A$ to $V_{A'}$ correspond bijectively to the homomorphisms of $k$-algebras $A'\to A$.
Every morphism $V_J\to V_{J'}$ is induced by a polynomial map $E^I\to E^{I'}$ sending $V_J$ into $V_{J'}$; it corresponds to a homomorphism $P_{I'}\to P_I$ sending $J'$ into $J$.
The functor $E^I$ is represented by $P_I$; a morphism $V_A\to E^I$ amounts to a homomorphism $P_I\to A$, that is, to a family of elements of $A$ indexed by $I$.
The morphism $V_A\to E^I$ defined by $P_I\to A$ is a monomorphism if and only if $P_I\to A$ is an epimorphism of rings; surjectivity is sufficient but not necessary.
The inclusion $k[T]\to k[T,T^{-1}]$ is a non-surjective epimorphism of rings ($k\neq0$): a homomorphism from $k[T,T^{-1}]$ is determined by the image of $T$, which must be invertible.
$\mathrm{Hom}_k(k[T,T^{-1}],k')$ is in bijection with the set of invertible elements of $k'$.
The monomorphism $V_{k[T,T^{-1}]}\to E^1$ is an isomorphism onto no closed subspace $V_J$ of $E^1$: otherwise $k[T]\to k[T,T^{-1}]$ would be surjective.
Session of 30 May 1973
Tape 1, side A
The functor $E^I$ is the $I$-th cartesian power of $E^1$, which is represented by $k[t]$.
The elements of $k'^I$ are called points of $E^I$ with values in $k'$ (or $k'$-points); the $k'$-points of $V_S$ are those that satisfy the equations of $S$.
The functors $X$ isomorphic to some $V_S$ are exactly the representable functors; if $V_S$ is defined by $J$, it is represented by $P_I/J$.
For an ideal $J$ of $P_I$: $f\in J$ if and only if $f(x')=0$ for every $k$-algebra $k'$ and every point $x'\in V_J(k')$.
It suffices to take $k'=P_I/J$ and the point corresponding to the canonical surjection $P_I\to P_I/J$ to recover $J$ as the ideal of the $f$ vanishing on $V_J$.
The map $J\mapsto V_J$ is an order-reversing bijection in both directions from the set of ideals of $P_I$ onto the set of closed subspaces of $E^I$: $J\subset J'$ if and only if $V_{J'}\subset V_J$.

The morphisms between affine algebraic spaces $X=V_A$ and $X'=V_{A'}$ correspond to the homomorphisms of $k$-algebras $A'\to A$; the category of affine algebraic spaces is anti-equivalent to that of $k$-algebras.
Radicals and the Nullstellensatz
If one tests only on fields $k'$, then $V'_J=V'_{\widetilde J}$, where $\widetilde J=\{f : \exists n,\ f^n\in J\}$ is the radical of $J$; indeed $f(x)^n=0$ in a field implies $f(x)=0$.
The radical $\widetilde J$ is the preimage in $P_I$ of the nilradical of $P_I/J$; $P_I/\widetilde J$ is the ring $P_I/J$ modulo its nilradical, with no nonzero nilpotents.

Over fields, $V'_J\subset V'_{J'}$ if and only if $\widetilde J\supset\widetilde{J'}$; $J\mapsto V'_J$ is an order-reversing bijection between radical ideals of $P_I$ and subfunctors of $E'^I$ (restricted to fields) defined by equations.
The radical $\widetilde J$ is the set of $f\in P_I$ vanishing on $V_J(k')$ for every field $k'$ over $k$.
If $A$ is a ring and $f\in A$ satisfies $u(f)=0$ for every homomorphism $u$ from $A$ to a field, then $f$ is nilpotent.
Tape 1, side B
Every nonzero ring has a maximal ideal (Krull); it follows that the intersection of the kernels of the homomorphisms of a ring into fields is its nilradical.
The kernels of the homomorphisms from $A$ to fields are the prime ideals of $A$; the nilradical of $A$ is the intersection of its prime ideals.
Nullstellensatz: if $k$ is an algebraically closed field and $I$ is finite, the radical of $J\subset k[T_1,\dots,T_n]$ is the set of polynomials vanishing at the points of $k^n$ where $J$ vanishes.
Algebraic form: if $A$ is a finitely generated algebra over an algebraically closed field $k$ and $f\in A$ is killed by every $k$-homomorphism $A\to k$, then $f$ is nilpotent.
Statement (a): if $A$ is finitely generated over an algebraically closed field $k$ and $A$ is a field, then $A=k$.
Statement (b): if $A$ is a finitely generated algebra over a field $k$, its nilradical is the intersection of its maximal ideals.
If $A$ is finitely generated over an algebraically closed field $k$, $u\mapsto\ker u$ is a bijection from $\mathrm{Hom}_k(A,k)$ onto the set of maximal ideals of $A$.
The Nullstellensatz is equivalent to the conjunction of (a) and (b); (b) holds over every field, whereas (a) requires $k$ to be algebraically closed.
Statement (a$'$): over an arbitrary field $k$, a finitely generated $k$-algebra that is a field is a finite extension of $k$.
If $A$ is finitely generated over a field $k$ and $f\in A$ is killed by every $k$-homomorphism from $A$ to a finite extension of $k$, then $f$ is nilpotent.
