The disjoint topological sum of the $X_i$, equipped with the sheaf of rings inducing $\mathcal{O}_{X_i}$ on each $X_i$, is the sum of the $X_i$ in the categories of ringed spaces and of locally ringed spaces.
This sum is a scheme; it is therefore the sum of the $X_i$ in the category of schemes (and in that of schemes over $S$), the $X_i$ being disjoint open sets covering it.
A morphism $S'\to\coprod_iX_i$ amounts to a decomposition of $S'$ into disjoint open sets $S'_i$ and morphisms $S'_i\to X_i$; in general it factors through no $X_i$.
In the category of Zariski sheaves on schemes, the sheaf represented by $\coprod_iX_i$ is the sum of the sheaves represented by the $X_i$.
A family of monomorphisms $F_i\to F$ of sheaves makes $F$ the sum of the $F_i$ if $F_i\times_FF_j$ is initial for $i\neq j$ and the $F_i$ cover $F$ (jointly epimorphic).
For $i\neq j$, $X_i\times_XX_j$ is the empty scheme; the empty scheme represents the initial sheaf (a point over the empty scheme, the empty set elsewhere).
Restriction of Zariski sheaves on $k$-schemes to sheaves on affine $k$-schemes is an equivalence of categories (comparison lemma).
Tape 2, side A
Epimorphisms of Zariski sheaves
A family of subsheaves $(F_i)$ of $F$ has $F$ as its supremum if and only if the family of inclusions $F_i\to F$ is epimorphic in Zariski sheaves.
A morphism $G\to F$ of Zariski sheaves is an epimorphism if and only if every section of $F$ over $S'$ lifts to $G$ locally on $S'$ for the Zariski topology.
Subsheaves $F_i$ cover $F$ if and only if every section of $F$ over $S'$ belongs, locally on $S'$, to one of the $F_i$.
For a Zariski sheaf $F$, $U\mapsto F(U)$ is an ordinary sheaf on each $S'$; a morphism of Zariski sheaves is an epimorphism if and only if it is one on each $S'$.
For $X=\coprod X_i$, the subsheaves $\widetilde{X_i}$ cover $\widetilde X$: every morphism $S'\to X$ factors locally on $S'$ through some $X_i$ (preimages of the $X_i$).
If $U=\bigcup U_i$ is a union of open sets of a scheme $X$, then $\widetilde U$ is the supremum of the subsheaves $\widetilde{U_i}$ of $\widetilde X$.
A question why a morphism into a sum of schemes need not factor through one summand, even for sheaves: it factors only locally, and the embedding into sheaves is fully faithful.
The inclusion of sheaves into presheaves commutes with all projective limits (products, fibre products), but not in general with inductive limits.
For a sum $F=\coprod_{i\in I}F_i$ of Zariski sheaves, a section of $F$ over $S'$ is a decomposition of $S'$ into disjoint open sets $S'_i$ with a section of $F_i$ over each $S'_i$.
Every decomposition of $\widetilde{S'}$ as a sum of disjoint subsheaves $F_i$ is of the form $F_i=\widetilde{S'_i}$, where $S'=\coprod S'_i$ is a decomposition of $S'$ into open sets.
For the sheaf condition, one may restrict to coverings of $S'$ by affine open sets, then by open sets $D(f)$, which form a base of the topology.
For $f_i\in A'$, one has $\mathrm{Spec}\,A'=\bigcup_iD(f_i)$ if and only if the $f_i$ generate the unit ideal.
A functor $F$ from algebras to $\mathbf{Set}$ is a Zariski sheaf if, for $f_i\in A'$ generating the unit ideal, $F(A')\to\prod F(A'_{f_i})\rightrightarrows\prod F(A'_{f_if_j})$ is exact.
A functor on $S$-algebras that is a sheaf extends, uniquely up to unique isomorphism, to a Zariski sheaf on $S$-schemes.
Open immersions of sheaves

A morphism of sheaves $F\to G$ is an open immersion if, for every $S'\to G$ with $S'$ a scheme, $F\times_GS'\to S'$ is isomorphic to the inclusion of an open set $U'$ of $S'$ (in the sense of $\widetilde{U'}\subset\widetilde{S'}$).
A property of morphisms of schemes that is stable under base change extends to morphisms of sheaves: $F\to G$ has it if its base change by every scheme $S'\to G$ has it.

If $U'\subset S'$ is open and $S''\to S'$ a morphism, the preimage $U''$ of $U'$ satisfies $U''=S''\times_{S'}U'$, also among locally ringed spaces: open immersions of schemes are stable under base change.
Open immersions of sheaves are stable under base change.
The composite of two open immersions of sheaves is an open immersion.
Tape 2, side B
A representability criterion
A Zariski sheaf $F$ on $\mathrm{Sch}/S$ is representable by a scheme if and only if it has subsheaves $F_i$ with (a) $F_i\to F$ an open immersion, (b) $F=\sup F_i$, (c) $F_i$ representable.
items.name: representability criterion

items.text: In the criterion, (c) may be replaced by (c$'$): each $F_i$ is representable by an affine scheme, that is, for $S=\mathrm{Spec}\,k$, by a $k$-algebra.

For $S=\mathrm{Spec}\,k$, the $F_i$ cover $F$ if, for every $a\in F(k')$, there exist $f_\alpha\in k'$ generating the unit ideal and indices $i(\alpha)$ such that $a|_{k'_{f_\alpha}}\in F_{i(\alpha)}(k'_{f_\alpha})$.
An open set $U'$ of $\mathrm{Spec}\,k'$ is a union of open sets $D(g_\lambda)$ and $\widetilde{U'}$ is the supremum of the subfunctors represented by the localizations $k'_{g_\lambda}$.

The open set $\mathrm{Spec}\,k'\setminus V(J)$ represents the subfunctor $B\mapsto\{u\colon k'\to B\mid u(J)B=B\}$; if $J=(g_\lambda)$, the condition is that the $u(g_\lambda)$ generate the unit ideal of $B$.
For a scheme $X$ covered by affine open sets $X_i$, the $\widetilde{X_i}\to\widetilde X$ are open immersions that cover $\widetilde X$: the conditions of the criterion are necessary, with (c$'$).
If $F_j\to F$ is an open immersion, $F_i\cap F_j\to F_i$ is one too (base change of $F_j\to F$ by $F_i\to F$).
Gluing schemes

Schemes $X_i$ over $S$, open sets $X_{ij}\subset X_i$ and isomorphisms $\varphi_{ij}\colon X_{ij}\to X_{ji}$ satisfying the cocycle condition on $X_{ij}\cap X_{ik}$ glue to an $S$-scheme $X$ covered by the $X_i$.
If a scheme $X$ is covered by open sets $X_i$, $\widetilde X$ is the gluing of the $\widetilde{X_i}$ along the $\widetilde{X_{ij}}$; likewise for the supremum of subsheaves $F_i\subset F$.
Projective space
Over a field $k$, for $V$ of dimension $n$, the set of lines of $V$ is the quotient $(V\setminus\{0\})/k^{\times}$.
In a basis of $V$, the subsets $X_i=\{x_i\neq0\}$ cover this set of lines, and each is in bijection with $k^{n-1}$ (normalize $x_i=1$).
For $n=2$, the projective line is obtained by gluing two copies of $k$ along $k^{\times}$ by $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{-1}$ (coordinates $y/x$ and $x/y$).
Tape 3
For $V$ finite-dimensional over a field, the lines of $V$ correspond bijectively to the hyperplanes of the dual $V^{\vee}$, and the hyperplanes of $V$ to the $1$-dimensional quotients of $V$.
$\mathbf{P}(V)$ henceforth denotes the set of hyperplanes of $V$, that is, of $1$-dimensional quotients of $V$ (and not the set of lines).
Invertible modules and the functor $\mathbf{P}(V)$
If the $f_i$ generate the unit ideal and each $L_{f_i}$ is free of rank $1$, the module $L$ is not necessarily free: being free of rank $1$ is not local on $\mathrm{Spec}\,k'$.
An $A$-module $L$ is invertible if $\widetilde L$ is locally free of rank $1$, that is, if there exist $f_\alpha$ generating the unit ideal with $L_{f_\alpha}$ free of rank $1$ over $A_{f_\alpha}$.
$L$ is invertible if and only if there exists an $A$-module $M$ with $M\otimes_AL\simeq A$; $M$ is then unique up to unique isomorphism and isomorphic to $\mathrm{Hom}_A(L,A)$, denoted $L^{-1}$.
$L$ is invertible if and only if it is finitely generated projective and $L_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is free of rank $1$ for every prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$.
For $V$ free of rank $n$, the invertible quotients of $V_{k'}$ correspond to direct-summand submodules of rank $n-1$ at every prime; one must require them to be direct summands.
If $L$ is an invertible quotient of $V_{k'}$ and $k'\to k''$ a homomorphism, $L\otimes_{k'}k''$ is an invertible quotient of $V_{k''}$ (right exactness of $\otimes$, stability of invertible modules).
For a module $V$ over a ring $k$, $\mathbf{P}(V)$ is the functor $k'\mapsto\{\text{invertible quotients of }V\otimes_kk'\}$ on $k$-algebras.
For every $k$-module $V$, with no finiteness hypothesis, the functor $\mathbf{P}(V)$ is representable by a scheme, of finite type over $k$ if $V$ is finitely generated.
$\mathbf{P}(V)(S')$ is the set of invertible quotients of the inverse image of $\widetilde V$ on $S'$; it is a Zariski sheaf, since the condition is local.
If $(e_i)$ generates $V$, $\mathbf{P}_{e_i}(k')$ is the set of quotients $L$ of $V_{k'}$ such that the image of $e_i$ is a basis of $L$; it is a subsheaf of $\mathbf{P}(V)$.
For every $e\in V$, $\mathbf{P}_e\to\mathbf{P}(V)$ is an open immersion: the locus where a section of an invertible sheaf is a basis is open.
If the $e_i$ generate $V$, the $\mathbf{P}_{e_i}$ cover $\mathbf{P}(V)$: locally on $S'$, one of the $e_i$ is a basis of the invertible quotient.
$\mathbf{P}_{e_i}$ is represented by $\mathrm{Sym}(V)/(e_i-1)$: a point is a homomorphism $V_{k'}\to k'$ sending $e_i$ to $1$.
If $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is a basis of $V$, $\mathrm{Sym}(V)/(e_i-1)$ is the polynomial ring in the $T_j$, $j\neq i$: $\mathbf{P}_{e_i}$ is the affine space of dimension $|I|-1$.
Tape 3, from 7:00:11
Zariski sheaves, reformulated
A contravariant functor $F$ on $\mathrm{Sch}/S$ is a Zariski sheaf if, for every $S'$ and every open covering $(S'_i)$, $F(S')\to\prod F(S'_i)\rightrightarrows\prod F(S'_i\cap S'_j)$ is exact.
To $F$ one associates, for each $S'$, the presheaf $F_{S'}\colon U'\mapsto F(U')$ on the space $S'$; $F$ is a Zariski sheaf if and only if all the $F_{S'}$ are ordinary sheaves.
Every $S$-morphism $f\colon S''\to S'$ induces a morphism of presheaves $F_{S'}\to f_*F_{S''}$, given by $F(U')\to F(f^{-1}U')$, functorial in $f$.

A contravariant functor on $\mathrm{Sch}/S$ is equivalent to presheaves $F_{S'}$ functorial in $S'$ such that $F_{S'}|_{S''}\to F_{S''}$ is an isomorphism for every open immersion $S''\to S'$; $F(S')=F_{S'}(S')$.
Session of 19 June 1973
Tape 1
Limits and epimorphisms of Zariski sheaves
Projective limits of Zariski sheaves on $\mathrm{Sch}/S$ are computed argument by argument, and $(\varprojlim F_i)_{S'}=\varprojlim(F_i)_{S'}$.
For an inductive limit $\varinjlim F_i$ computed in Zariski sheaves, $(\varinjlim F_i)_{S'}=\varinjlim(F_i)_{S'}$, the limit being taken in sheaves on the space $S'$.
A morphism $F\to G$ of Zariski sheaves is an epimorphism if and only if $F_{S'}\to G_{S'}$ is one for every $S'$: every section of $G$ over $U'$ is locally the image of a section of $F$.
A morphism of $S$-schemes $X\to Y$ is an epimorphism of Zariski sheaves if and only if it admits local sections over $Y$: every point of $Y$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ and a section $V\to X$.
A family of $S$-schemes $X_i\to Y$ is epimorphic for Zariski sheaves if and only if every point of $Y$ has a neighbourhood over which one of the $X_i$ admits a section.
An open immersion of sheaves is a monomorphism.
Projective bundles
Representability of a sheaf is local on the base: if $S=\bigcup S_i$ (open sets) and the restriction $F_i$ of $F$ to schemes over $S_i$ is representable for all $i$, then $F$ is.
In this case $F_i=S_i\times_SF\to F$ is an open immersion; if $F=\sup F_i$ with open subfunctors $F_i$, then $F$ is representable if and only if each $F_i$ is.
An $\mathcal{O}_S$-module is quasi-coherent if it is locally the cokernel of a morphism of free modules; it then comes from a module on each affine open set of $S$.
For $\mathcal{M}$ quasi-coherent on $S$, $\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})\colon S'\mapsto\{\text{invertible quotients of }\mathcal{M}_{S'}\}$ is a Zariski sheaf on $\mathrm{Sch}/S$.
The sheaf $\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})$ is representable by an $S$-scheme, the projective bundle associated to $\mathcal{M}$; by localization on $S$, one reduces to the affine case.

If $\mathcal{M}$ is generated by global sections $e_i$, $P_i(S')$ is the set of quotients $L$ of $\mathcal{M}_{S'}$ for which the image of $e_i$ is a basis of $L$; $P_i\subset\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})$.
The morphism $P_i\to\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})$ is an open immersion.
The set of points of $S'$ where a section of an invertible sheaf is a basis is open.
The $P_i$ cover $\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})$: if the $e_i$ generate $\mathcal{M}$, locally on $S'$ one of them generates the invertible quotient, hence is a basis of it.
For a $k$-module $V$, the functor $k'\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}_{k'}(V_{k'},k')=\mathrm{Hom}_k(V,k')$ is represented by $\mathrm{Sym}_k(V)$.
$P_i(k')$ is the set of homomorphisms $V_{k'}\to k'$ sending $e_i$ to $1$; it is represented by $\mathrm{Sym}(V)/(e_i-1)$, so $P_i$ is representable ($S$ affine case).
Tape 2
The universal quotient and vector bundles

On $\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})$ there is a universal invertible quotient $\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{P}}\to\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}}(1)$, corresponding to the identity point of the represented functor.
One sets $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}}(n)=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}}(1)^{\otimes n}$ for $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, with $L^{\otimes(-m)}=(L^{\otimes m})^{-1}\simeq(L^{-1})^{\otimes m}$ for $m\geq0$.
Universal property: for every invertible quotient of $\mathcal{M}_{S'}$, there exists a unique morphism $S'\to\mathbf{P}$ whose inverse image of the universal quotient is this quotient.
The vector bundle $\mathbf{V}(\mathcal{M})$ is the functor $S'\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{S'}}(\mathcal{M}_{S'},\mathcal{O}_{S'})$.
The subfunctor $\mathbf{V}^{*}$ of epimorphisms $\mathcal{M}_{S'}\to\mathcal{O}_{S'}$ (nonzero on each fibre) is represented by the open complement of the zero section of $\mathbf{V}(\mathcal{M})$.
The map $u\mapsto\mathcal{M}_{S'}/\ker u$ defines a morphism $\mathbf{V}^{*}\to\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})$, whose image is the free quotients of rank $1$.
The morphism $\mathbf{V}^{*}\to\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})$ is an epimorphism of sheaves: an invertible quotient is locally free of rank $1$, hence locally of the form $\mathcal{M}_{S'}/\ker u$.
Projective space as a quotient by $\mathbb{G}_m$
The functor $\mathbb{G}_m\colon S'\mapsto\Gamma(S',\mathcal{O}_{S'})^{\times}$ is represented by the affine line minus the origin, with ring $k[t,t^{-1}]$ over $S=\mathrm{Spec}\,k$.

The group $\mathbb{G}_m$ acts on $\mathbf{V}^{*}$ by multiplication; this action is free ($\lambda u=u\Rightarrow\lambda=1$ for $u$ an epimorphism), whereas it is not free on $\mathbf{V}$ (the origin is fixed).
The epimorphisms $u$ and $\lambda u$, with $\lambda$ invertible, have the same kernel: $\mathbf{V}^{*}\to\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})$ is $\mathbb{G}_m$-invariant.
Two epimorphisms $u,v\colon\mathcal{M}_{S'}\to\mathcal{O}_{S'}$ define the same quotient if and only if $v=\lambda u$ with $\lambda\in\Gamma(S',\mathcal{O}_{S'})^{\times}$.
The vector bundle minus its zero section is a $\mathbb{G}_{m,\mathbf{P}}$-torsor over $\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})$, and $\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})=\mathbf{V}^{*}/\mathbb{G}_m$.
The group $\mathbb{G}_m=\mathrm{GL}_1$ is the functor $S'\mapsto\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{O}_{S'})$ of automorphisms of the module $\mathcal{O}_{S'}$.
$\mathbb{G}_m$-torsors over $S$ are equivalent to locally free sheaves of rank $1$ on $S$, via $L\mapsto\mathrm{Isom}_{\mathcal{O}_S}(\mathcal{O}_S,L)$.
A $\mathbb{G}_m$-torsor over $S$ is a sheaf $F$ equipped with a free action of $\mathbb{G}_m$ such that $F\to S$ is an epimorphism; it is locally isomorphic to $\mathbb{G}_m$.
If a sheaf of groups $G$ acts freely on a sheaf $F$, then $F$ is a torsor under $G_T$ over $T=F/G$.

The $\mathbb{G}_m$-torsor $\mathbf{V}^{*}\to\mathbf{P}$ is that of trivializations of the universal invertible quotient: a point above $S'\to\mathbf{P}$ is an isomorphism of this quotient with $\mathcal{O}_{S'}$.
Projective space $\mathbb{P}^n$ over a field $k$ is $\mathbf{P}(k^{n+1})$.
A morphism $X\to\mathbb{P}^n$ is equivalent to an invertible sheaf $L$ on $X$ and $n+1$ sections of $L$ that generate it at every point, that is, an invertible quotient of $\mathcal{O}_X^{\,n+1}$.
$\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})(S')$ is the set of isomorphism classes of pairs $(L,\mathcal{M}_{S'}\to L)$, with $L$ invertible and $\mathcal{M}_{S'}\to L$ an epimorphism.
Session of 20 June 1973
Tape 1
Fibres and base change for projective bundles
Base change commutes with the projective bundle: $\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})\times_SS'=\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M}_{S'})$, as functors on schemes over $S'$.
The fibre $X_s$ of a scheme $X$ over $S$ at a point $s$ is obtained by base change along $\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(s)\to S$; it is a scheme over the field $\kappa(s)$.
The underlying space of $X_s$ is the set-theoretic fibre of $X\to S$ over $s$, equipped with the topology induced by that of $X$.
The fibre of $\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})$ at $s$ is the projective space of the $\kappa(s)$-vector space $\mathcal{M}(s)=\mathcal{M}_s\otimes\kappa(s)=\mathcal{M}_s/\mathfrak{m}_s\mathcal{M}_s$.
Asked whether the fibre of a projective bundle embeds as a closed subscheme, he says only for closed points, while a morphism from a projective bundle to a separated scheme has closed image.
If $\mathcal{M}$ is finitely generated and $X$ separated over $S$, every $S$-morphism $\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})\to X$ has closed image.
If $\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{N}$ is an epimorphism of quasi-coherent modules, there is a morphism $\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{N})\to\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})$, which is a closed immersion.

For an arbitrary homomorphism $\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{N}$, there is an open set $U\subset\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{N})$ of invertible quotients $L$ such that $\mathcal{M}_{S'}\to L$ is surjective, and a morphism $U\to\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})$.
One has $\mathbf{P}(0)=\varnothing$ and $\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{O}_S)=S$; for $\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{O}_S^{2}$, $\mathbf{P}(\mathcal{M})$ is the standard projective line over $S$.
Relative spectrum and affine morphisms
A question on what happens for the zero module: the projective bundle is empty, since no nonempty scheme has an invertible quotient of zero; the first interesting case is the projective line.
Over $S=\mathrm{Spec}\,K$, a quasi-coherent algebra structure on $\widetilde A$ is equivalent to a $K$-algebra structure on the $K$-module $A$.

For a quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_S$-algebra $\mathcal{A}$, $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathcal{A})$ is the functor $S'\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_{S'}\text{-alg}}(\mathcal{A}_{S'},\mathcal{O}_{S'})$; over affine $S$, it is $\mathrm{Spec}\,A$.
The functor $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathcal{A})$ is a Zariski sheaf representable by an $S$-scheme; over an affine open set $U\subset S$, it is $\mathrm{Spec}\,\Gamma(U,\mathcal{A})$.
The functor $\mathcal{A}\mapsto\mathrm{Spec}(\mathcal{A})$, from the opposite category of quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_S$-algebras to $S$-schemes, is fully faithful.
An $S$-scheme $X$ is affine over $S$ if the preimage of every affine open set of $S$ is affine; the essential image of $\mathrm{Spec}$ consists of the schemes affine over $S$.
The spectrum commutes with base change: $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathcal{A})\times_SS'=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathcal{A}_{S'})$.

If $f\colon X\to S$ is affine, $f_*\mathcal{O}_X$ is a quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_S$-algebra; $X\mapsto f_*\mathcal{O}_X$ is quasi-inverse to $\mathrm{Spec}$: an anti-equivalence with the schemes affine over $S$.
For $\mathrm{Spec}\,A\to\mathrm{Spec}\,K$ and $M$ an $A$-module, the direct image of $\widetilde M$ is the sheaf $\widetilde M$ associated to $M$ viewed as a $K$-module.
Fibre products of schemes
Finite projective limits exist in the category of schemes and in each $\mathrm{Sch}/S$, that is, a final object and fibre products.
The final object of schemes is $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}$, that of $\mathrm{Sch}/S$ is $S$.
Tape 2
If $S=\bigcup S_i$ is an open covering and each $X_i\times_{S_i}Y_i$ is a scheme, then $X\times_SY$ is a scheme: the question is local on $S$.
If $X=\bigcup X_i$ and $Y=\bigcup Y_j$ are open coverings, $X\times_SY$ is a scheme if and only if the $X_i\times_SY_j$ are.
For open sets $U\subset X$ and $V\subset Y$, $U\times_SV\to X\times_SY$ is an open immersion, and the $X_i\times_SY_j$ cover $X\times_SY$.
The fibre product of two $S$-schemes exists; in the affine case, the product $\mathrm{Spec}\,A\times_{\mathrm{Spec}\,K}\mathrm{Spec}\,B$ is $\mathrm{Spec}(A\otimes_KB)$.
The morphism $X_s\to X$ is a monomorphism, and a homeomorphism onto its image equipped with the induced topology.
In $X\times_SY$, the product $X_i\times_SY_j$ is the intersection of the preimages of $X_i$ and $Y_j$ under the two projections.
If the $X_i=\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathcal{A}_i$ are affine over $S$ and form a diagram, their projective limit exists in schemes, is affine over $S$ and equals $\mathrm{Spec}(\varinjlim\mathcal{A}_i)$.
In commutative algebras, the sum of a family is the tensor product (possibly infinite, a filtered inductive limit of finite tensor products).
An inductive limit of quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_S$-modules is quasi-coherent.

If $X=\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathcal{A}$ is affine over $S$ and $Z$ is an $S$-scheme with structure morphism $g$, then $\mathrm{Hom}_S(Z,X)\simeq\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_S\text{-alg}}(\mathcal{A},g_*\mathcal{O}_Z)$.
For every locally ringed space $Z$, $\mathrm{Hom}(Z,\mathrm{Spec}\,A)=\mathrm{Hom}(A,\Gamma(Z,\mathcal{O}_Z))$; this is what makes the preceding constructions valid in locally ringed spaces.
Grassmannians, flags and automorphism groups
For $\mathcal{M}$ quasi-coherent, the functor of locally free quotients of given rank of $\mathcal{M}_{S'}$ is representable: it is the Grassmannian bundle associated to $\mathcal{M}$.
Likewise, the functor of flags of locally free quotients of $\mathcal{M}_{S'}$ of given ranks $n_1,n_2,\ldots$ is representable (flag bundle).
If $\mathcal{M}$ is locally free of rank $n$, the functor $S'\mapsto\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{M}_{S'})$ is representable by a group scheme locally isomorphic to $\mathrm{GL}_n$.
Localization at a point
The localization of $X$ at a point $x$ is the affine scheme $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{X,x})$.

For an affine open set $U=\mathrm{Spec}\,A\ni x$, with prime $\mathfrak{p}$, $\mathcal{O}_{X,x}=A_{\mathfrak{p}}$ gives $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{X,x})\to U\subset X$, independent of the choice of $U$.
The morphism $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{X,x})\to X$ is a monomorphism of schemes, hence injective on points.
It is a homeomorphism onto its image: the topology of $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{X,x})$ is induced by that of $X$.
The spectrum of a local ring has a unique closed point, a common specialization of all its other points (the prime ideals are contained in the maximal ideal).
A continuous map preserves the specialization relation between points.
Session of 25 June 1973
Tape 1

Localization: $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathcal{O}_{X,x}\to X$ is a monomorphism, with image the set of generizations of $x$ (points $x'$ such that $x\in\overline{\{x'\}}$), the intersection of the open neighbourhoods of $x$.
For $X$ affine, the prime ideals of $A_{\mathfrak p}$ correspond bijectively to the prime ideals $\mathfrak q\subset\mathfrak p$ of $A$.

The structure sheaf of the localization is induced by $\mathcal{O}_X$: at every generization $x'$ of $x$, the local rings of $X$ and of the localization are isomorphic, since $(A_{\mathfrak p})_{\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p}}=A_{\mathfrak q}$.
Local, noetherian and artinian schemes
A local scheme is an affine scheme whose ring is local.
A scheme is local if and only if it is quasi-compact and has a unique closed point.

The morphisms from a local scheme $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathcal{O}$ to $X$ correspond to pairs consisting of a point $x\in X$ (the image of the closed point) and a local homomorphism $\mathcal{O}_{X,x}\to\mathcal{O}$.

For a ring $A$ and a local ring $\mathcal{O}$, giving $A\to\mathcal{O}$ amounts to giving a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $A$ (the kernel of $A\to\mathcal{O}\to\kappa(\mathcal{O})$) and a local homomorphism $A_{\mathfrak p}\to\mathcal{O}$.
A morphism $Y\to X$ sending $y$ to $x$ induces $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathcal{O}_{Y,y}\to\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathcal{O}_{X,x}$: localization is functorial in the pair (scheme, point).
The morphisms $\mathrm{Spec}\,k\to X$, with $k$ a field, correspond to pairs of a point $x\in X$ and a field homomorphism $\kappa(x)\to k$.

For $x\in X$, $\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(x)$ is a closed subscheme of $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathcal{O}_{X,x}$, and every morphism $\mathrm{Spec}\,k\to X$ with image $x$ factors uniquely through $\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(x)$.
A scheme reduced to a point is the spectrum of a local ring whose maximal ideal is nil; it is not necessarily the spectrum of a field.
A noetherian local ring whose spectrum is a point has a nilpotent maximal ideal and is of finite length, that is, artinian; the converse holds.
$k[t]/(t^n)$ is local of length $n$ and $\mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}$ is local artinian; their spectra are points that are not spectra of fields.
An irreducible scheme is connected.
For $G$ an infinite set, the constant scheme $G_k$ is a disjoint union of infinitely many nonempty open sets, hence is not quasi-compact.

A scheme is noetherian if it is quasi-compact and covered by finitely many affine open sets $\mathrm{Spec}\,A_i$ with $A_i$ noetherian; then $\Gamma(U,\mathcal{O}_X)$ is noetherian for every affine open set $U$.
A scheme is locally noetherian if $\Gamma(U,\mathcal{O}_X)$ is noetherian for every affine open set $U$; every quasi-compact open set is then a noetherian scheme.

The localization of a noetherian ring is noetherian, as is the completion of a noetherian local ring with respect to the powers of an ideal; but $\widehat{A}\otimes_A\widehat{A}$ is not noetherian in general.
A scheme is artinian if it is affine with artinian ring (of finite length as a module).
An artinian scheme is noetherian and discrete, hence finite: it is a finite sum of spectra of artinian local rings, and its ring is the product of these rings.
A scheme is artinian if and only if it is noetherian with discrete underlying space.
Tape 2
Finiteness conditions on morphisms
Quasi-compact morphisms are stable under base change.
Quasi-compact morphisms are stable under composition.
If $g\circ f$ is quasi-compact and $g$ quasi-separated (quasi-compact diagonal), then $f$ is quasi-compact.

$f$ is locally of finite type if, for all affine open sets $\mathrm{Spec}\,A\subset S$ and $\mathrm{Spec}\,B\subset X$ above it, $B$ is a finitely generated $A$-algebra; of finite type if it is moreover quasi-compact.
$f$ is locally of finite presentation if, for such affine open sets, $B$ is finitely presented over $A$; this notion and the preceding one are local on $X$.
For $X=\mathrm{Spec}\,B$ and $S=\mathrm{Spec}\,A$, $X\to S$ is locally of finite type (resp. finite presentation) if and only if $B$ is finitely generated (resp. finitely presented) over $A$.
If $S$ is locally noetherian, “locally of finite type” and “locally of finite presentation” coincide.
Quasi-compact, finite type, locally finite type and locally finite presentation morphisms are stable under base change and under composition.
Open immersions, closed immersions and immersions
An open immersion is a morphism that is a homeomorphism onto an open set of $Y$, the structure sheaf of $X$ being induced by that of $Y$.
The subobjects of $Y$ defined by open immersions correspond to the open sets of $Y$; open immersions are stable under composition and base change.
$f\colon X\to Y$ is a closed immersion if, for a covering of $Y$ by affine open sets $Y_i=\mathrm{Spec}\,A_i$, $f^{-1}(Y_i)=\mathrm{Spec}\,B_i$ is affine and $A_i\to B_i$ is surjective.
Intrinsic characterization: $f$ is a closed immersion if and only if it is a homeomorphism onto a closed set of $Y$ and $\mathcal{O}_Y\to f_*\mathcal{O}_X$ is surjective.
A question whether the sheaf condition forces a morphism to be affine; the lecturer first agrees, then retracts, saying this holds only if it remains true after any base change.
A closed immersion is a monomorphism.
The closed subschemes of $Y$ correspond to the quasi-coherent ideals $J\subset\mathcal{O}_Y$, via $J\mapsto V(J)=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_Y/J)$.
Closed immersions are stable under base change: $V(J)\times_YY'=V(J\mathcal{O}_{Y'})$, since forming the spectrum of an algebra commutes with base change.
For $X=V(J)$, the quasi-coherent ideals of $\mathcal{O}_X$ correspond to the quasi-coherent ideals $K\supset J$ of $\mathcal{O}_Y$ via $K\mapsto K/J$, and $V(K/J)=V(K)$.
Closed immersions are stable under composition.

If $f$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, the direct image of a quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_X$-module is quasi-coherent; the kernel of $\mathcal{O}_Y\to f_*\mathcal{O}_X$ for a closed immersion is therefore quasi-coherent.
Tape 2, from 1:18:29
For $Y=\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ and $J$ an ideal of $A$, $V(J)=\mathrm{Spec}\,A/J$; the map $J\mapsto V(J)$ reverses order.
Open subschemes of $Y$ are ordered like the open sets; closed subschemes are ordered like the corresponding quasi-coherent ideals, with the order reversed.
The intersection (fibre product) of two closed subschemes $V(J_1)$ and $V(J_2)$ is $V(J_1+J_2)$, since $\mathcal{O}_Y/J_1\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_Y}\mathcal{O}_Y/J_2=\mathcal{O}_Y/(J_1+J_2)$.
An immersion is a morphism that factors as a closed immersion $X\to U$ followed by an open immersion $U\to Y$.
An immersion is a homeomorphism onto a locally closed subset $X$ of $Y$; the largest open set in which $X$ is closed is $Y\setminus(\overline{X}\setminus X)$.
Intrinsic characterization: $f$ is an immersion if and only if it is a homeomorphism onto a locally closed subset of $Y$ and $f^{-1}\mathcal{O}_Y\to\mathcal{O}_X$ is surjective.
Equivalently, every $y\in f(X)$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ such that $f^{-1}(V)\to V$ is a closed immersion; for $V$ affine, $f^{-1}(V)$ is affine and the ring map is surjective.
Immersions are stable under base change and under composition.
Every diagonal morphism $X\to X\times_SX$ is an immersion; equivalently, every section of an $S$-scheme is an immersion, as is the kernel of two morphisms $u,v\colon X\to Y$ of $S$-schemes.
Tape 3, side A
Discrete valuation rings; reduced, integral and normal schemes

A discrete valuation ring (for instance $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$, $k[t]_{(p)}$, $k[[t]]$) is a local integral domain with a single nonzero prime ideal; its spectrum has a generic point and a special point, lying in the closure of the former.
A discrete valuation ring is not artinian ($\mathfrak m\supsetneq\mathfrak m^2\supsetneq\cdots$): its spectrum is finite and noetherian without being artinian.

The infinitesimal neighbourhood of order $n$ of a point $x$, $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathcal{O}_{X,x}/\mathfrak m_x^n$, is an artinian local scheme if $X$ is locally noetherian; for $I$ finite, the constant scheme $I_k$ is artinian.
For $G$ a group scheme of finite type over a field $k$, the identity component $G^0$ is a subgroup and $G/G^0$ is artinian.
$X$ is reduced if $\mathcal{O}_X$ has no nonzero nilpotent section over any open set; equivalently, its local rings are reduced.
Being reduced is a local property, and $\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ is reduced if and only if $A$ is reduced.
A scheme is integral if it is reduced and irreducible.
If $X$ is covered by nonempty open sets $X_i$, $X$ is integral if and only if the $X_i$ are integral and pairwise meet.
An affine scheme $\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ is integral if and only if $A$ is an integral domain.
A scheme is normal if all its local rings are integrally closed integral domains.
A locally noetherian normal scheme is a disjoint sum of integral schemes.
An affine integral scheme $\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ is normal if and only if $A$ is integrally closed in its field of fractions.
For $X$ integral with generic point $\eta$, the residue field at $\eta$ is the field $K$ of rational functions of $X$.

A morphism $X'\to X$ of finite type between integral schemes, $X$ noetherian, is called birational if it induces an isomorphism of function fields; it is then an isomorphism over a nonempty open set of $X$.
Zariski's Main Theorem: if $X$ is normal noetherian integral, every separated birational morphism of finite type $X'\to X$ with finite fibres is an open immersion.
The blow-up of a point of the affine plane is a birational morphism, with exceptional fibre a projective line, which is not an open immersion.
The normalization of a curve with an ordinary double point is birational, with finite fibres, and is not an isomorphism (the local ring at the double point is not normal).
The normalization of a curve with a cusp is birational and bijective without being an isomorphism (the local ring is not normal).
The normalization morphism $X'\to X$ is birational with finite fibres, and is an isomorphism if and only if $X$ is normal.
Regular schemes
A scheme is regular if all its local rings are regular.
For a regular local ring over an algebraically closed field the completion is a power series ring; asked about perfect fields, he explains residue field extensions and generic points break this.
A noetherian local ring $A$ is regular if its maximal ideal is generated by an $A$-regular sequence $x_1,\dots,x_n$; $x_1$ is a nonzerodivisor in $A$, $x_2$ in $A/x_1A$, and so on.
For an $M$-regular sequence (defined likewise on a module $M$), the associated Koszul complex is acyclic.
A field is regular; if $A$ is regular, so is $A[t]$; hence $k[t_1,\dots,t_n]$ is regular, as are $\mathbb{G}_{m,k}$ and $\mathrm{GL}_{n,k}$ (open sets of affine space).
A noetherian local ring is regular if and only if its global dimension is finite; the localization of a regular local ring at a prime is therefore regular.
items.name: Serre

items.text: A ring is called regular if its localizations at all primes are; principal ideal rings and Dedekind rings are regular (for example $\mathbb{Z}$ and rings of integers of number fields), as are their polynomial rings.
A noetherian local ring is regular if and only if its completion $\widehat{A}$ is.
A complete local algebra $\mathcal{O}$ over a field $k$, with residue field $k$, is regular if and only if $\mathcal{O}\simeq k[[t_1,\dots,t_n]]$ as a $k$-algebra; if $A$ is regular, so is $A[[t]]$.
A question on monoid schemes of finite presentation: a monomorphic endomorphism is an isomorphism, so left cancellation would make a monoid scheme a group, with a parallel statement for modules.

An endomorphism of a scheme of finite presentation over $S$ that is a monomorphism is an isomorphism (left as an exercise); consequently, a monoid scheme of finite presentation over the base whose left translations are monomorphisms (left cancellation on all points) is a group object.
Tape 3, side B
Surjective endomorphisms and classes of morphisms
A surjective endomorphism of a finitely generated module over a commutative ring is bijective.

The audience supplies the determinant argument that a surjective endomorphism of a finitely generated module is bijective; the lecturer contrasts it with his own limit argument for algebras of finite presentation.
A surjective endomorphism of a finitely presented algebra over a ring is an isomorphism (noetherian case: the kernels of the iterates stabilize; general case: pass to the limit).
If “surjective” is replaced by “epimorphism” in this statement, it becomes subtler: the noetherian property of the rings $k_i$ and arguments with Artin rings are then needed.
Affine morphisms contain the isomorphisms and are stable under composition and under base change.
A class of morphisms containing the isomorphisms and stable under composition and base change is stable under fibre product: $f_1\times_Sf_2\in M$ if $f_1,f_2\in M$.
For such a class $M$: if $g\circ f\in M$ and the diagonal $\Delta_g\colon Y\to Y\times_ZY$ is in $M$, then $f\in M$.
Giving a morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ over $Z$ is equivalent to giving a section $\Gamma_f=(\mathrm{id},f)$ of $X\times_ZY\to X$; $f$ is the composite of $\Gamma_f$ and the second projection.
The graph $\Gamma_f$ is a monomorphism and is deduced from $\Delta_g\colon Y\to Y\times_ZY$ by the base change $f\times\mathrm{id}_Y$.

For $g\colon Y\to S$ and a class $M$ as above, the following are equivalent: $\Delta_g\in M$; every graph $\Gamma_f\colon X\to X\times_SY$ is in $M$; for all $u,v\colon X\to Y$, the kernel of $(u,v)$ in $X$ is in $M$.
These conditions are also equivalent to: every section of every base change $Y\times_SS'\to S'$ is in $M$.
The affine plane with doubled origin (two copies of the plane glued along the complement of the origin) has a non-affine diagonal.
Monomorphisms are stable under base change and composition; every diagonal morphism is a monomorphism; if $g\circ f$ is a monomorphism, so is $f$.
Surjective morphisms (in the set-theoretic sense) are stable under composition and base change.
Epimorphisms of schemes are stable under composition but not under base change.
$f\colon X\to S$ is quasi-compact if the preimage of every quasi-compact open set of $S$ is quasi-compact.
Quasi-compactness of a morphism is local on the base: if $S$ is covered by affine open sets $S_i$, $f$ is quasi-compact if and only if each $f^{-1}(S_i)$ is.
Session of 26 June 1973
Diagonals and separated morphisms

The diagonal of an affine scheme $\mathrm{Spec}\,B$ over $\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ is the closed immersion given by $B\otimes_AB\to B$, $x\otimes y\mapsto xy$; it follows that the diagonal of every $S$-scheme is an immersion.
If $g\circ f$ is an immersion, then $f$ is one.
An immersion is locally of finite type; the diagonal of every morphism is therefore locally of finite type.
An immersion is locally of finite presentation if and only if the quasi-coherent ideal $J$ defining it on an open set is of finite type.
If $f$ is locally of finite type, its diagonal is locally of finite presentation.
If $B$ is generated as an $A$-algebra by elements $b_i$, the kernel of $B\otimes_AB\to B$ is generated by the $b_i\otimes1-1\otimes b_i$.
$f\colon X\to S$ is separated if its diagonal, which is an immersion, is a closed immersion, that is, if $\Delta_f(X)$ is closed in $X\times_SX$.
Equivalent: after any base change, every section has closed image; the graph of every $S$-morphism $Y\to X$ is closed; the kernel of every pair $(u,v)\colon Y\to X$ is a closed subscheme of $Y$.
Extension of identities: if $X$ is separated over $S$, $Y$ reduced, and two $S$-morphisms $u,v\colon Y\to X$ coincide on a dense open set $U$ of $Y$, then $u=v$.
Same conclusion if $u\circ i=v\circ i$ for a morphism $i\colon U\to Y$ with dense image.
A surjective immersion is a closed immersion defined by a nil ideal; if $Y$ is reduced, it is an isomorphism.
Every monomorphism is separated (its diagonal is an isomorphism), in particular every immersion is separated.
If $g\circ f$ is separated, then $f$ is separated.
A scheme is separated if it is separated over $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}$; an affine scheme is separated, since $A\otimes A\to A$ is surjective.
If $S$ is separated, an $S$-scheme $X$ is separated if and only if it is separated over $S$.
If $S$ is separated, every morphism from an affine scheme $X$ to $S$ is affine; in particular $X\times_SY$ is affine for $X,Y$ affine over $S$.
In a separated scheme, the intersection of two affine open sets is affine; the converse is false.
The affine line with doubled origin is not separated, although its diagonal is affine: two morphisms from the line to it coincide away from the origin without being equal.
Tape 2, side A
The complement of the zero section of $\mathbb{A}^n_S$ is affine for $n=1$ and is not for $n\geq2$ ($S$ nonempty affine).
The plane with doubled origin contains two affine open sets whose intersection, the complement of the origin, is not affine.
Quasi-separated and coherent morphisms
$f$ is quasi-separated if its diagonal is quasi-compact.
Equivalent: after any base change, every section is quasi-compact; or the kernel of any pair $(u,v)\colon Y\to X$ of $S$-morphisms is quasi-compact over $Y$.
A separated morphism is quasi-separated; every monomorphism, hence every diagonal morphism, is quasi-separated; if $g\circ f$ is quasi-separated, $f$ is.
A scheme is quasi-separated if it is so over $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}$; it is then so over every scheme beneath it.
If $S$ is quasi-separated, an $S$-scheme is quasi-separated if and only if it is so over $S$.
A scheme is quasi-separated if and only if the intersection of two quasi-compact open sets is quasi-compact.
$S$ is quasi-separated if and only if every morphism $X\to S$ from a quasi-compact scheme is quasi-compact.
$S$ is quasi-separated if and only if $X\times_SY$ is quasi-compact for all $X,Y$ quasi-compact over $S$.
If $S$ is covered by affine open sets $S_i$, $S$ is quasi-separated if and only if the $S_i\cap S_j$ are quasi-compact.
The complement of the origin in $\mathrm{Spec}\,k[t_1,t_2,\dots]$ is not quasi-compact; two copies glued along this open set form a scheme that is not quasi-separated.
Asked what must be added to quasi-separatedness to get separatedness, the lecturer finds nothing beyond the definition itself, after an example of a non-quasi-compact intersection.

If $g\circ f$ is quasi-compact (resp. of finite type) and $g$ quasi-separated, then $f$ is quasi-compact (resp. of finite type); the diagonal of a morphism locally of finite type is quasi-compact if and only if it is of finite type.
A morphism is coherent if it is quasi-compact and quasi-separated; a scheme is coherent if it is so over $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}$.
Coherent morphisms are stable under base change and under composition.
If $g\circ f$ is coherent and $g$ quasi-separated, then $f$ is coherent.
Nothing can be concluded about $g$ from $g\circ f$ coherent alone (take $f$ from the empty scheme): $f$ must have a reasonably large image.
If $S$ is quasi-separated, an $S$-scheme is coherent if and only if it is coherent over $S$.
If $f\colon X\to S$ is coherent and $\mathcal{F}$ a quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_X$-module, $f_*\mathcal{F}$ is quasi-coherent.
Under the same conditions, the higher direct images $R^qf_*\mathcal{F}$ are quasi-coherent.
Tape 3, side A
Geometric reducedness and irreducibility

For a field $k$, the following are equivalent: $k$ is perfect; $A\otimes_kB$ is reduced for all reduced $k$-algebras $A,B$; $A\otimes_kk'$ is reduced for $A$ reduced and $k'/k$ an extension; $k'\otimes_kk'$ is reduced for every finite purely inseparable extension $k'/k$.
If $x\in k\setminus k^p$ and $k'=k[t]/(t^p-x)$, then $k'\otimes_kk'\simeq k'[t]/(t-\alpha)^p$, with $\alpha^p=x$, is not reduced.
If $k$ is perfect and $K,L$ are two extensions of $k$, then $K\otimes_kL$ is reduced.

For a $k$-algebra $A$ and a perfect extension $K_1$ of $k$, the following are equivalent ($A$ is then called geometrically reduced, or separable): $A\otimes_kB$ reduced for every reduced $B$; $A\otimes_kk'$ reduced for every extension $k'$; $A\otimes_kK_1$ reduced; $A\otimes_kk'$ reduced for every finite purely inseparable extension $k'$.

A $k$-scheme $X$ is geometrically reduced, or separable, if $X\times_kY$ is reduced for every reduced $k$-scheme $Y$, which is equivalent to the analogous conditions on extensions; one reduces to $X$ affine.
A scheme separable over $k$ is reduced; the converse holds for every $X$ if and only if $k$ is perfect.
For every extension $k'/k$, $X$ is separable over $k$ if and only if $X_{k'}$ is over $k'$.
A field $k$ is separably closed if every algebraic extension of $k$ is purely inseparable; in characteristic zero, every field is perfect and separably closed is equivalent to algebraically closed.

For a field $k$, the following are equivalent: $k$ is separably closed; for $A,B$ with irreducible spectra, $\mathrm{Spec}(A\otimes_kB)$ is irreducible; likewise for $B$ an extension; $k'\otimes_kk'$ is an integral domain for every finite Galois extension $k'$.
If $k$ is separably closed and $K,L$ are extensions of $k$, the spectrum of $K\otimes_kL$ is irreducible.

For a $k$-scheme $X$ and $K_1$ separably closed, the following are equivalent ($X$ is then called geometrically irreducible): $X\times_kY$ irreducible for every irreducible $Y$; $X_{k'}$ irreducible for every extension $k'$; $X_{K_1}$ irreducible; $X_{k'}$ irreducible for $k'/k$ finite Galois.
A geometrically irreducible scheme is irreducible; the converse holds for every $X$ if and only if $k$ is separably closed.
For every extension $k'/k$, $X$ is geometrically irreducible over $k$ if and only if $X_{k'}$ is over $k'$.
Tape 3, side B
Geometric integrality and connectedness
The product of two separable (resp. geometrically irreducible) $k$-schemes is separable (resp. geometrically irreducible).

For a field $k$, the following are equivalent: $k$ is algebraically closed; the tensor product of two integral $k$-algebras is integral; $A\otimes_kk'$ is integral for $A$ integral and $k'/k$ an extension; $k'\otimes_kk'$ is integral for every finite extension $k'/k$.

For a $k$-scheme $X$ and $K_1$ algebraically closed, the following are equivalent: $X\times_kY$ integral for every integral $Y$; $X_{k'}$ integral for every extension $k'$; $X_{K_1}$ integral; $X_{k'}$ integral for every finite extension $k'$.
$X$ is geometrically integral if it is separable and geometrically irreducible; it is then integral, and the converse holds for every $X$ if and only if $k$ is algebraically closed.
Geometric integrality is invariant under extension of the base field and stable under the product of two $k$-schemes.
If $k$ is separably closed, the product over $k$ of two connected schemes is connected.
If $k'/k$ is a purely inseparable extension, the projection $X_{k'}\to X$ is a homeomorphism for every $k$-scheme $X$.
For $Y$ nonempty, the projection $X\times_kY\to X$ is surjective and open, so the topology of $X$ is a quotient of that of $X\times_kY$.
If $k$ is separably closed and $X$ connected nonempty, then $X_{k'}$ is connected nonempty for every extension $k'/k$.

The fibre of $X\times_kY\to X$ at $x$ is $\mathrm{Spec}(\kappa(x)\otimes_k\mathcal{O}_Y)$; in particular that of $X_{k'}\to X$ at $x$ is $\mathrm{Spec}(\kappa(x)\otimes_kk')$; that of $X\times_kY\to Y$ at $y$ is $X_{\kappa(y)}$.

If the product of two connected schemes over $k$ is always connected, then $k$ is separably closed: for $k'/k$ finite Galois with group $\Gamma$, $\mathrm{Spec}(k'\otimes_kk')$ is a sum of $|\Gamma|$ points.

For a $k$-scheme $X$ and $K_1$ separably closed, the following are equivalent ($X$ is then called geometrically connected): $X\times_kY$ connected for every connected $Y$; $X_{k'}$ connected for every extension $k'$; $X_{K_1}$ connected; $X_{k'}$ connected for $k'/k$ finite Galois.
A geometrically connected scheme (satisfying these conditions) is connected; the converse holds for every $X$ if and only if $k$ is separably closed.
A filtered projective limit of connected schemes, affine over a quasi-compact scheme $X$, is connected.
Geometric connectedness is invariant under extension of the base field and stable under the product of two $k$-schemes.
Complements on subschemes and coherence
For subsheaves $F_i$ of a sheaf $F$, the supremum is the image of $\coprod_iF_i\to F$, the smallest subsheaf containing the $F_i$; its sections are those that belong locally to one of the $F_i$.

The scheme obtained by gluing infinitely many (indexed by $\mathbb{Z}$) copies of a curve $S$ along $S\setminus\{s_0\}$ is connected, locally of finite type over $S$, non-separated and non-quasi-compact.
A module $\mathcal{F}$ on a ringed space is coherent if it is of finite type and the kernel of every morphism $\mathcal{O}_U^n\to\mathcal{F}$ is of finite type.
Coherent modules are stable under finite sums, kernels, cokernels, images and extensions.
items.name: Serre

items.text: If $\mathcal{O}_X$ is coherent, the coherent modules are exactly those of finite presentation; for $X$ locally noetherian, $\mathcal{O}_X$ is coherent.
A surjective immersion is an open immersion if and only if it is an isomorphism; there exist surjective immersions with target $Y$ that are not isomorphisms if and only if $Y$ is not reduced.

For $Y$ closed in $X$, the ideal $J_Y$ of sections vanishing at every point of $Y$ is quasi-coherent; it is the largest ideal defining $Y$, and $V(J_Y)$ is the unique reduced closed subscheme with underlying space $Y$.
For a closed subscheme $V(J)$, the $V(J^{n+1})$ have the same underlying space; they are its infinitesimal neighbourhoods of order $n$.
An immersion whose underlying map is open is a closed immersion defined by a nil ideal on an open set of $Y$; it is not an open immersion in general.
Every locally noetherian scheme is quasi-separated.
A scheme is coherent if and only if it is a finite union of affine open sets $X_i$ whose intersections $X_i\cap X_j$ are quasi-compact.

The quasi-compactness hypothesis is necessary: for $X$ a disjoint sum of infinitely many copies of an affine scheme $S$, $f_*\mathcal{F}$ is the product of the $\mathcal{F}_i$, and an infinite product of quasi-coherent modules is not quasi-coherent in general.
Why quasi-compactness is needed for direct images of quasi-coherent sheaves: an infinite disjoint union gives infinite products of quasi-coherent sheaves, which fail to be quasi-coherent.
An open set is retrocompact if its intersection with every quasi-compact open set is quasi-compact, that is, if the inclusion is quasi-compact, hence coherent.
If $U\subset X$ is a retrocompact open set, every quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_U$-module $\mathcal{F}$ is the restriction to $U$ of a quasi-coherent module on $X$, for instance $i_*\mathcal{F}$.
Session of 2 July 1973
Tape 1, side A
Finite presentation and limits

If $A=\varinjlim A_i$ is a filtered limit of rings, a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme of finite presentation over $A$ comes by base change from a scheme of finite presentation over $A_i$, for $i$ large enough.
Projective and ample morphisms
$X\to Y$ is projective if there is a closed immersion of $X$ into $\mathbb{P}(E)$, with $E$ quasi-coherent of finite type over $Y$; quasi-projective if one only has an immersion.
items.name: naive

items.text: If $E$ is quasi-coherent of finite type, $\mathbb{P}(E)$ is of finite type over $Y$; $\mathbb{P}(E)$ is separated over $Y$.
The naive notion of projective morphism is stable under base change, since $\mathbb{P}(E)\times_YY'=\mathbb{P}(E_{Y'})$.

The naive notion of projective morphism is not local on the base: even for $Y$ quasi-compact, a morphism that is projective over each open set of a cover need not embed into some $\mathbb{P}(E)$ over $Y$ (counterexamples exist), the embeddings over the open sets not gluing.
Making the notion local on the base (locally projective morphisms) does not repair it: the composite of two locally projective morphisms need not be locally projective.
The $Y$-morphisms $X\to\mathbb{P}(E)$ correspond to the invertible quotients $L$ of the module $E_X$, the inverse image of $E$ on $X$.

An invertible sheaf $L$ on $X$ is very ample relative to $Y$ if there exist a quasi-coherent module $E$ on $Y$ and an epimorphism $f^*E\to L$ whose associated morphism $X\to\mathbb{P}(E)$ is an immersion.
If $X$ has a sheaf very ample relative to $Y$, then $X$ is separated over $Y$; if moreover $X$ is of finite type over $Y$ coherent, one may choose $E$ of finite type.

If $Y$ is coherent, $X\to Y$ admits an immersion into $\mathbb{P}(E)$ with $E$ quasi-coherent of finite type if and only if $X$ is of finite type over $Y$ and has an invertible sheaf very ample relative to $Y$.
The property of being very ample is stable under base change.
The tensor product of two very ample sheaves is very ample (Segre embedding $\mathbb{P}(E)\times\mathbb{P}(F)\to\mathbb{P}(E\otimes F)$); hence $L^{\otimes n}$ is very ample for $n>0$ if $L$ is.

If $Y$ is quasi-compact and $X$ of finite type over $Y$, $L$ is ample relative to $Y$ if and only if a power $L^{\otimes n}$ ($n>0$) is very ample; then $L^{\otimes n}$ is very ample for all $n\geq n_0$.
Ample sheaves are stable under base change and tensor product; for $n>0$, $L$ is ample if and only if $L^{\otimes n}$ is.
A question whether the inverse of an ample sheaf is ample leads to the Picard group, the cone of ample classes, and the conclusion that this happens only when the structure sheaf is ample.
In $\mathrm{Pic}(X)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$, the classes some positive multiple of which is ample form a convex cone.
For $Y$ quasi-compact, $\mathcal{O}_X$ is ample relative to $Y$ if and only if $X$ is quasi-affine over $Y$; if moreover $X$ is proper over $Y$, then $X\to Y$ is finite.
Tape 1, side B

If $Y$ is quasi-compact, $L$ ample and $M$ any invertible sheaf, then $L^{\otimes n}\otimes M$ is ample for $n$ large enough; the ample cone therefore spans $\mathrm{Pic}(X)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ as soon as it is nonempty.
Quasi-projective and proper morphisms
$f\colon X\to Y$ is quasi-projective if it is of finite type and there exists an invertible sheaf on $X$ ample relative to $Y$.
$f$ is projective if it is quasi-projective and proper; $f$ is proper if it is of finite type, separated and universally closed.
If $Y$ is coherent, $f$ is quasi-projective (resp. projective) if and only if there is an immersion (resp. closed immersion) of $X$ into $\mathbb{P}(E)$ with $E$ quasi-coherent of finite type.
Quasi-projective and projective morphisms are stable under base change.
Proper morphisms are stable under base change and under composition.
If $X$ is proper over $Y$ and $Z$ separated over $Y$, every $Y$-morphism $X\to Z$ is closed.

If $X$ is of finite type over $Y$ and $g\colon X\to Z$ a $Y$-immersion into a proper $Y$-scheme $Z$, then $X$ is proper over $Y$ if and only if $g$ is a closed immersion; closed immersions are proper.
Projective morphisms are proper; over an algebraically closed field, there exist proper schemes that are not projective.
Chow's lemma: every proper scheme over a field is dominated by a projective scheme by means of a birational morphism.
Proper does not imply projective, though Chow's lemma gives a birational reduction; projective implies proper is not trivial and uses reduction to Noetherian base and valuative criteria.
If $E$ is quasi-coherent of finite type, $\mathbb{P}(E)$ is proper over $Y$; one reduces to $\mathbb{P}^n_{\mathbb{Z}}$ over $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}$.
Valuative criteria

Valuative criterion of properness: for $Y$ locally noetherian and $f$ of finite type, $f$ is proper if and only if, for every discrete valuation ring $A$ with fraction field $K$ and every $\mathrm{Spec}\,A\to Y$, the sections of $X$ over $\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ correspond bijectively to those over $\mathrm{Spec}\,K$.
Injectivity of this map is equivalent to separatedness of $f$ (valuative criterion of separatedness).

For $A$ a discrete valuation ring with fraction field $K$ and $M$ a finitely generated $A$-module, the quotients of $M$ that are free of rank one correspond bijectively to the one-dimensional quotients of $M_K$, via $H\mapsto M\cap H_K$; hence $\mathbb{P}(M)$ satisfies the criterion.
Integral extensions

For an $A$-algebra $B$ and $x\in B$, the following are equivalent: $x$ satisfies a monic polynomial with coefficients in $A$ (integral over $A$); $A[x]$ is a finitely generated $A$-module; $x$ belongs to a subalgebra of $B$ finite over $A$.
An $A$-algebra $B$ is integral if and only if it is a union (inductive limit) of subalgebras finite over $A$.

Subalgebras and quotient algebras of an integral algebra are integral; the tensor product of two integral algebras is integral; the elements of $B$ integral over $A$ form a subalgebra, the integral closure of $A$ in $B$.
Transitivity: if $B$ is integral over $A$ and $C$ integral over $B$, then $C$ is integral over $A$.
Finite and integral morphisms

$f\colon X\to Y$ is finite (resp. integral) if it is affine, $X=\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathcal{B}$, with $\mathcal{B}$ a quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_Y$-algebra finitely generated as a module (resp. integral over $\mathcal{O}_Y$).
Finite morphisms and integral morphisms are stable under base change and under composition.
Tape 2, side A
A morphism is finite if and only if it is integral and of finite type; an algebra $B$ is finite over $A$ if and only if it is finitely generated and integral.
An integral morphism is separated (being affine) and universally closed; a finite morphism is therefore proper.
Every closed immersion is finite, since $A/J$ is finite over $A$.
Lying-over (Cohen–Seidenberg): if $A\subset B$ is integral, every prime ideal of $A$ is induced by a prime ideal of $B$; this is the key point for integral morphisms to be closed.
For $k'/k$ algebraic and $X$ a $k$-scheme, the projection $X_{k'}\to X$ is closed.

Ample sheaves
For $X$ coherent and $L$ invertible, the following are equivalent: the $X_f$, $f\in\Gamma(X,L^{\otimes n})$, $n>0$, form a base of the topology; those that are affine form a base.

For $X$ coherent, these conditions are also equivalent to: for every quasi-coherent $F$ of finite type, $F\otimes L^{\otimes n}$ is generated by its sections for $n$ large; the same condition for quasi-coherent ideals of finite type.

If $X$ is coherent over an affine $Y=\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ and $L^{\otimes n}$ is very ample relative to $Y$ for some $n>0$, these conditions are satisfied; the converse holds if $X$ is of finite type over $Y$.
On a coherent scheme, an invertible sheaf $L$ is ample if it satisfies the preceding equivalent conditions.
$L$ is ample relative to $Y$ if there is a covering of $Y$ by affine open sets $Y_i$ such that $L$ restricted to $f^{-1}(Y_i)$ is ample; it is then so over every affine open set of $Y$.
If there is an invertible sheaf ample relative to $Y$, then $X$ is separated over $Y$.

For $f$ coherent and $Y$ quasi-compact, $L$ is ample relative to $Y$ if and only if, for every quasi-coherent module of finite type $F$ on $X$, $f^*f_*(F\otimes L^{\otimes n})\to F\otimes L^{\otimes n}$ is surjective for $n$ large.
If a power $L^{\otimes n}$ ($n>0$) is very ample relative to $Y$, then $L$ is ample; the converse holds if $f$ is of finite type and $Y$ quasi-compact.

For $f\colon X\to Y$, $g\colon Y\to Z$, $Z$ quasi-compact, $L$ ample (resp. very ample) relative to $f$ and $M$ ample (resp. very ample) relative to $g$, the sheaf $L\otimes f^*M^{\otimes n}$ is ample (resp. very ample) relative to $g\circ f$ for $n\geq n_0$.

If $X\subset\mathbb{P}^n_Y$ and $Y\subset\mathbb{P}^m_Z$, $X$ embeds into $\mathbb{P}^n_Z\times_Z\mathbb{P}^m_Z$, then by Segre into $\mathbb{P}^{(n+1)(m+1)-1}_Z$, the induced sheaf being $L\otimes f^*M$.

For $E$ quasi-coherent and $I$ invertible, $\mathbb{P}(E)\simeq\mathbb{P}(E\otimes I)$, the fundamental sheaf of $\mathbb{P}(E\otimes I)$ being that of $\mathbb{P}(E)$ twisted by the inverse image of $I$.
The notions of quasi-projective morphism and projective morphism are not local on the base.

These conditions are also equivalent to the existence of an invertible sheaf $L$ such that $L$ and $L^{-1}$ are ample.

A morphism is quasi-affine if and only if it is coherent and, for every quasi-coherent module $F$ on $X$, $f^*f_*F\to F$ is surjective.

An immersion is quasi-affine if and only if it is quasi-compact; if $g\circ f$ is quasi-affine and $g$ quasi-separated, then $f$ is quasi-affine.
A separated morphism of finite type with finite fibres is quasi-affine.

If $Y$ is coherent, such a morphism factors as a quasi-compact open immersion followed by a finite morphism (modern form of Zariski's Main Theorem); of finite type with finite fibres is called quasi-finite.
Radicial morphisms

The following are equivalent: $f$ is universally injective (injective after any base change); each fibre has at most one point $x$ above $y$, with $\kappa(x)/\kappa(y)$ purely inseparable. One then says $f$ is radicial.
$f$ is radicial if and only if $X(K)\to Y(K)$ is injective for every field $K$, if and only if the diagonal $X\to X\times_YX$ is surjective.
Radicial morphisms are stable under base change and under composition; every monomorphism is radicial.
An integral, radicial and surjective morphism is a universal homeomorphism; conversely a universal homeomorphism is integral, radicial and surjective.
For $k'/k$ purely inseparable (for instance the perfect closure of $k$), $\mathrm{Spec}\,k'\to\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ is a universal homeomorphism, so $X_{k'}\to X$ is a homeomorphism.
The normalization of a curve with a cusp is integral, radicial and surjective, hence a universal homeomorphism.
A nodal curve minus one preimage of the double point in its normalization is a homeomorphism onto the curve but not a universal homeomorphism, as base change to the normalization shows.
The normalization of a curve with an ordinary double point, with one of the two points above the double point removed, is a homeomorphism that is not universal.
Open and generalizing morphisms
$f$ is open if the underlying map is, universally open if it remains so after any base change.
Open morphisms are stable under composition but not under base change; universally open morphisms are stable under both.
The normalization of a curve with an ordinary double point, with one of the two points above it removed, is bijective and a homeomorphism, hence open, but not universally open.
An open morphism is generalizing: if $f(x)=y$, every generization of $y$ lifts to a generization of $x$, that is, $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathcal{O}_{X,x}\to\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathcal{O}_{Y,y}$ is surjective.

For $\eta$ a maximal point of $X$, $\mathrm{Spec}\,\kappa(\eta)\to X$ is generalizing; it is not open in general (for example for the affine line over a field).
If $f$ is locally of finite presentation, $f$ is open if and only if it is generalizing, and universally open if and only if it is universally generalizing.
The image of a morphism of finite type between noetherian schemes is constructible, that is, a finite union of locally closed subsets.

If $f$ is locally of finite presentation, $f$ is open at $x$ (the image of every neighbourhood of $x$ is a neighbourhood of $f(x)$) if and only if it is generalizing at $x$.
Every scheme over a field $k$ is universally open over $k$.

A module $M$ over $A$ is flat if the functor $M\otimes_A-$ is exact, faithfully flat if moreover it is faithful, that is, if $M\otimes_AN=0$ implies $N=0$.
A flat module $M$ is faithfully flat if and only if $u$ is injective (resp. surjective, bijective) as soon as $M\otimes u$ is.
A module $M$ is faithfully flat if and only if it is flat and $M/\mathfrak mM\neq0$ for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $A$.
An $A$-algebra $B$ is faithfully flat if and only if it is flat and $\mathrm{Spec}\,B\to\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ is surjective.
If $A\to B$ is a local homomorphism of local rings, $B$ flat over $A$ is equivalent to $B$ faithfully flat; the map of spectra is then surjective.
Flatness of an algebra is stable under localization: if $B$ is flat over $A$, $B[T^{-1}]$ is flat over $A[S^{-1}]$; the local rings of $B$ are therefore flat over those of $A$.
If $B$ is flat over $A$, $\mathrm{Spec}\,B\to\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ is generalizing.
A module on a ringed space is flat if and only if its fibres are flat as modules over the fibres of the sheaf of rings.
A quasi-coherent module $\widetilde{M}$ on $\mathrm{Spec}\,A$ is flat if and only if the $A$-module $M$ is flat.
A module $M$ on $X$ is flat relative to $f\colon X\to Y$ if each fibre $M_x$ is flat over $\mathcal{O}_{Y,f(x)}$.

$f$ is flat if $\mathcal{O}_X$ is flat relative to $Y$; a notion local on $X$ and $Y$, equivalent to $\mathcal{O}_{X,x}$ flat over $\mathcal{O}_{Y,f(x)}$ for all $x$; for $X,Y$ affine, to $B$ flat over $A$.
A flat morphism is generalizing, hence universally generalizing; flat morphisms contain the isomorphisms and are stable under composition and base change.
$f$ is faithfully flat if it is flat and surjective; these morphisms are stable under composition and base change.
A morphism $f$ is faithfully flat if and only if the inverse image functor $f^*$, from modules on $Y$ to modules on $X$, is exact and faithful.
If $f$ is flat, the closure of the image of every irreducible component of $X$ is an irreducible component of $Y$.

For a separable extension $k'/k$ of degree $2$, there is a proper smooth scheme of dimension $3$ over $k'$, not projective, equipped with a non-effective descent datum.
If $g$ is faithfully flat quasi-compact and $L'$ is ample relative to $S'$ with compatible descent datum on $(X',L')$, the descent datum on $X'$ is effective.
If $X'$ is of finite type over $S'$, an ample sheaf $L'$ has a very ample power, so the proof reduces to the very ample case.
If $f'$ is coherent and $(X',L')$ carries a descent datum, then $E'=f'_*L'$ inherits a descent datum, because direct image commutes with flat base change.
A faithfully flat quasi-compact morphism is of descent of rank $2$ for pairs $(X',L')$, $L'$ very ample relative to the base; the descended $L$ is very ample.

If $S'\to S$ is finite locally free of nowhere zero rank, every quasi-projective $S'$-scheme equipped with a descent datum relative to $S$ is effective, and the descended scheme is quasi-projective over $S$.

For a locally free algebra $B$ over $\mathcal{O}_T$, the norm $N\colon B\to\mathcal{O}_T$ (determinant of multiplication) is multiplicative, whence a norm of invertible sheaves from $T'=\mathrm{Spec}\,B$ to $T$.
Ampleness of an invertible sheaf is preserved under inverse image and under passing to the norm.
If $X$ is a scheme over a field $k$ and $X\otimes_k k'$ is quasi-projective (resp. projective) for some extension $k'$, then $X$ is quasi-projective (resp. projective).
Finite extension principle: a property stable under base change and passing to the limit, true after some extension of $k$, is true after a finite extension of $k$.
Two $k$-schemes of finite presentation that are isomorphic over an extension of $k$ are isomorphic over a finite extension of $k$.
Descent and group actions
If $G$ acts on $S'$ with $S'\times G\simeq S'\times_S S'$, a descent datum on an $S'$-object $X'$ is equivalent to an action of $G$ on $X'$ compatible with the projection to $S'$.
For $G$ the constant group defined by a group $\Gamma$, a descent datum is equivalent to an action of $\Gamma$ on $X'$ compatible with that on $S'$.
If $S'\to S$ is of descent of rank $1$, $X\mapsto X'$ equipped with the action of $\Gamma$ is a fully faithful functor.

If $S'\to S$ is a torsor under a group scheme $G$, a descent datum on an $S'$-scheme $X'$ is equivalent to an action of $G$ on $X'$ compatible with that on $S'$.

One has $\Gamma_k(k)=\Gamma$, and a descent datum on $X'$ relative to $k'/k$ is equivalent to an action of $\Gamma_k$ on $X'$ compatible with that on $k'$.
An action of $\Gamma_k$ on $X'$ is determined by the induced action of the abstract group $\Gamma$, the morphism from the constant group $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma_k$ being schematically dominant.
For arbitrary Galois $k'/k$, $\mathrm{Hom}_k(X,Y)$ is the set of $k'$-morphisms $X'\to Y'$ commuting with the action of $\Gamma$.
Descent for families of morphisms

Descent of degree $0$ for $(S'_i\to S)$: a morphism $X\to Y$ over $S$ is determined by its inverse images on the $S'_i$; degree $1$: morphisms over the $S'_i$ compatible on the $S'_i\times_SS'_j$ come from a morphism over $S$.

Descent of degree $2$: objects $X'_i$ over the $S'_i$, equipped with isomorphisms over the $S'_i\times_SS'_j$ satisfying the cocycle condition on triples, come from an object over $S$ (effective descent).

For a family $(S'_i\to S)$ and $S'=\coprod S'_i$, one has $S'\times_SS'=\coprod S'_i\times_SS'_j$ and the $S'$-schemes are the families of $S'_i$-schemes; descent for the family therefore reduces to that of $S'\to S$.

A gluing datum on $X'/S'$ is equivalent to the data, for every $S$-scheme $T$ and every pair $u,v\colon T\to S'$, of an isomorphism $u^*X'\simeq v^*X'$ functorial in $T$; the cocycle condition means that these isomorphisms are transitive.
The objects of $S'$ equipped with a descent datum form the category of cartesian sections of the fibred category of relative schemes over the full subcategory of $S$-schemes that factor through $S'$.
For a family $(S'_i\to S)$, this category depends only on the sieve generated by the family.
For a faithfully flat quasi-compact base change $S'\to S$, being an isomorphism, an immersion or proper are properties of morphisms that descend.

Morphisms $X_i\to Y_i$ over an open covering $(S_i)$ of $S$, compatible on the intersections, glue to a unique morphism $X\to Y$; the same holds for a faithfully flat quasi-compact morphism $S'\to S$.
Faithfully flat quasi-compact descent is effective for quasi-coherent modules and affine relative schemes, but not for arbitrary relative schemes.
Grothendieck topologies: fpqc, fppf, étale

The morphism $\mathbb{G}_m\to\mathbb{G}_m$, $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^n$ ($n\geq2$) is faithfully flat quasi-compact, with equivalence relation defined by $\mu_n$, but has no section locally for the Zariski topology.
A faithfully flat quasi-compact morphism $T\to S$ has a section after the base change $T\to S$ itself, hence locally for the fpqc topology.

A family $(S'_i\to S)$ is covering for the fpqc topology if $S$ is a union of open sets $U$ for which there exist finitely many flat quasi-compact morphisms $U'_\alpha\to U$, with images covering $U$, each factoring through some $S'_i$.
If faithfully flat quasi-compact morphisms and open coverings are of descent of degree $0$, $1$ or $2$ for a category of objects, so are the fpqc covering families.
fpqc covering families are stable under composition and base change: the category of schemes is a site for this topology.
A presheaf $F$ on schemes is an fpqc sheaf if, for every covering family $(S_i\to S)$, $F(S)\to\prod F(S_i)\rightrightarrows\prod F(S_i\times_SS_j)$ is exact.
A presheaf is an fpqc sheaf if and only if it is a Zariski sheaf and the exactness condition holds for every faithfully flat quasi-compact $S'\to S$.
In sheaves on a site, epimorphisms are effective and stable under base change, sums are distributive and base change commutes with inductive limits.

If $H$ is a subsheaf of groups of $G$, the quotient sheaf $G/H$ by the relation of right translations exists and $G$ acts on it by left translations; if $H$ is normal, $G/H$ is a sheaf of groups.
For every scheme $X$, the functor $S\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(S,X)$ is a sheaf for the fpqc topology.

A faithfully flat quasi-compact morphism $S'\to S$ is a universal effective epimorphism: for every scheme $X$, $\mathrm{Hom}(S,X)\to\mathrm{Hom}(S',X)\rightrightarrows\mathrm{Hom}(S'',X)$ is exact, $S''=S'\times_SS'$.
The finest topology for which representable functors are sheaves has as covering families the universally strictly epimorphic families.

fppf topology: in the definition of the fpqc topology, replace quasi-compact by locally of finite presentation; a fundamental system of coverings is given by the families of flat morphisms locally of finite presentation whose images cover $S$.
Discrete topology: a family $(S_i\to S)$ is covering if one of the $S_i\to S$ admits a section.
Zariski topology: a family is covering if every point of $S$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ over which one of the $S_i\times_SU\to U$ admits a section.
Étale topology: a fundamental system of coverings is given by the families of étale morphisms whose images cover $S$.
Quotients and algebraic spaces
An algebraic space (Artin) is obtained by gluing schemes for the étale topology rather than the Zariski topology, that is, by quotienting by an equivalence relation whose projections are étale.
A representable functor $F$ is an fpqc sheaf and satisfies $F(A)=\varprojlim F(A/\mathfrak{m}^n)$ for every complete noetherian local ring $A$; these necessary conditions are not sufficient.
A compact reduced irreducible complex analytic space whose field of meromorphic functions has transcendence degree equal to its dimension is an algebraic space (Artin).

If $R\rightrightarrows X$ is an equivalence relation whose projections are faithfully flat quasi-compact, a scheme $Y$ is the quotient of $X$ by $R$ in the sense of fpqc sheaves if and only if $X\to Y$ is faithfully flat quasi-compact and $R=X\times_YX$.
For every equivalence relation $R$ on $X$, the quotient sheaf $X/R$ exists, whether or not it is representable by a scheme.

If the projections of the equivalence relation $R$ are finite locally free, $X/R$ is representable by a scheme $Y$, with $X\to Y$ finite locally free surjective and $R=X\times_YX$, if and only if $X$ is a union of affine open sets stable under $R$.
This condition is equivalent to each equivalence class of $R$, a finite set, being contained in an affine open set.
If $X$ is quasi-projective over an affine base, or carries an ample invertible sheaf, every finite subset of $X$ lies in an affine open set; the condition is then satisfied.
For a finite group $G$ acting freely on $X$, the quotient $X/G$ exists as a scheme if and only if every orbit is contained in an affine open set.
Over a field, for a flat equivalence relation $R$ on a scheme $X$ of finite type, there is a dense open set of $X$, stable under $R$, whose quotient by the induced relation exists as a scheme.
If $G$ is an algebraic group over a field and $H\subset G$ a subgroup, the relation defined by $H$ is flat and the quotient $G/H$ is a scheme, a homogeneous space under $G$ by translations.

A functor $F\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}'$ commuting with finite products and the final object takes a group object $X$ of $\mathcal{C}$ to a group object $F(X)$ of $\mathcal{C}'$.
More generally, a functor commuting with the finite projective limits used to write the axioms of an algebraic structure (ring, module, group action) carries that structure over.
The affine algebraic spaces over $k$ form the full subcategory of representable functors from $k$-algebras to $\mathbf{Ens}$; it is equivalent to the opposite of the category of $k$-algebras.
The space $X$ represented by the $k$-algebra $A$ satisfies $X(k')=\mathrm{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(A,k')$ for every $k$-algebra $k'$.

A group structure on an affine space $X$ is equivalent to a group structure on each $X(k')$, functorial in $k'$: a factorization of the functor $X$ through the forgetful functor from groups to $\mathbf{Ens}$.
An affine algebraic group over $k$ is a functor from $k$-algebras to groups whose underlying set-valued functor is representable.
The additive group $\mathbb{G}_a\colon k'\mapsto(k',+)$ and the multiplicative group $\mathbb{G}_m\colon k'\mapsto k'^{*}$ are commutative affine algebraic groups.
The linear group $\mathrm{GL}_n\colon k'\mapsto\mathrm{GL}_n(k')$ of invertible $n\times n$ matrices with entries in $k'$ is an affine algebraic group, in general non-commutative.

Basic examples: $\mathbb{G}_a$, $\mathbb{G}_m$, $\mathrm{GL}_n$ and their subgroups

The functor $\mathcal{O}\colon k'\mapsto k'$ is a $k$-algebra object; $\mathbb{G}_a$ is $\mathcal{O}$ with its addition, and $\mathbb{G}_m$ is the largest subgroup of the multiplicative monoid of $\mathcal{O}$.
$\mathbb{G}_a$, $\mathbb{G}_m$ and $\mathrm{GL}_n$ are represented by $k[t]$, $k[t,t^{-1}]$ and $k[t_{ij}][1/\Delta]$, where $\Delta=\det(t_{ij})$.
The orthogonal group of a quadratic form $Q$ in $n$ variables, $k'\mapsto\{g\in\mathrm{GL}_n(k') : Q\circ g=Q\}$, is an affine algebraic group: it is a stabilizer for the action of $\mathrm{GL}_n$.
The upper triangular subgroup $T_n$ of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ is represented by $k[t_{ij}\ (i\le j)][t_{11}^{-1},\ldots,t_{nn}^{-1}]$.
The strictly triangular subgroup (diagonal equal to $1$) of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ is represented by the polynomial algebra $k[t_{ij}\ (i<j)]$.
The group $\{(x,y) : xy=1\}$, with coordinatewise law, is represented by $k[x,y]/(xy-1)\simeq k[x,x^{-1}]$: it is isomorphic to $\mathbb{G}_m$.
The homomorphism $\mathbb{G}_m\to\mathrm{GL}_n$, $\lambda\mapsto\lambda I_n$, is a monomorphism; its image consists of the scalar matrices.
The homomorphism $\mathbb{G}_m\to\mathrm{GL}_n$, $\lambda\mapsto\mathrm{diag}(1,\ldots,\lambda,\ldots,1)$ ($\lambda$ in the $i$-th place), is not central.
Centers and central morphisms
The center of a group object $G$ is the kernel of the morphism $G\to\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}(G)$ sending $g$ to the inner automorphism defined by $g$; it is a subgroup functor of $G$.

$g\in G(Z)$ lies in the center if and only if its image in $G(Z')$ is central for every morphism $Z'\to Z$. Over a field, the center of an affine algebraic group is representable (statement admitted).
A morphism $Z\to G$ is called central if it factors through the center of $G$; the morphism $\mathbb{G}_m\to\mathrm{GL}_n$, $\lambda\mapsto\lambda I_n$, is central.
In characteristic $p>0$, the functor $\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}(\mathbb{G}_a)$ is not representable; it is a filtered inductive limit of schemes (an ind-scheme).

The map $\lambda\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}1&\lambda\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is a homomorphism $\mathbb{G}_a\to\mathrm{GL}_2$; composed with $\mathrm{GL}_2\to\mathrm{GL}_n$ (identity on the other $n-2$ basis vectors), it embeds $\mathbb{G}_a$ in $\mathrm{GL}_n$.
Over a field, every affine algebraic group of finite type is isomorphic to a closed subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ for a suitable $n$ (statement announced, not proved).
Module functors $W(M)$ and $V(M)$
For a $k$-module $M$, the functor $W(M)\colon k'\mapsto M\otimes_kk'$ is a module over the ring functor $\mathcal{O}$.
If $M\simeq k^n$, then $W(M)$ is isomorphic to the standard affine space of dimension $n$.

If $M$ is a direct factor of a finitely generated free module (finitely generated projective), $W(M)$ is representable: it is the kernel of $1-p\colon W(L)\to W(L)$, where $p$ is a projector of $L=k^m$ with image $M$.
Conversely, if $W(M)$ is representable, then $M$ is finitely generated projective (proved in the next session).
A representable functor from $k$-algebras to $\mathbf{Ens}$ takes injections of $k$-algebras to injections.
A representable functor from $k$-algebras to $\mathbf{Ens}$ commutes with arbitrary projective limits, hence with products: $F(\prod_ik_i)\simeq\prod_iF(k_i)$.

$M$ is flat if and only if $k'\mapsto M\otimes_kk'$ takes injections of $k$-algebras to injections (take the algebras $k\oplus N'\subset k\oplus N$ with ideal of square zero); hence $W(M)$ representable implies $M$ flat.

If $W(M)$ is representable, $M$ is finitely generated (the identity $M\otimes k^I\simeq M^I$ forces every family of elements of $M$ to fall into a finitely generated submodule). Over a noetherian ring, flat of finite type is equivalent to finitely generated projective.
If $W(M)$ is representable, $M$ is finitely presented: for $0\to R\to L\to M\to0$ with $L$ finitely generated free, $R$ satisfies the same property $R\otimes k^I\simeq R^I$ (five lemma).
For an arbitrary $k$-module $M$, $V(M)\colon k'\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}_k(M,k')$ is a module over the ring functor $\mathcal{O}$.
The functor $V(M)$ is always representable, by the symmetric algebra $S_k(M)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}S^n(M)$; for $M$ free of rank $n$, this is the polynomial algebra in $n$ indeterminates.
The space $V(M)=\mathrm{Spec}\,S_k(M)$ is of finite type over $k$ if and only if $M$ is finitely generated.
The functor $M\mapsto W(M)$ is covariant and $M\mapsto V(M)$ is contravariant, with values in modules over the ring functor $\mathcal{O}$.

The functors $W$ and $V$ are fully faithful: the maps $\mathrm{Hom}_k(M,N)\to{}$ $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}}(W(M),W(N))$ and $\mathrm{Hom}_k(M,N)\to{}$ $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}}(V(N),V(M))$ are bijective.
The pairing $M\otimes k'\times\mathrm{Hom}_k(M,k')\to k'$ defines an $\mathcal{O}$-bilinear pairing $V(M)\times W(M)\to\mathcal{O}$, functorial in $M$.

Biduality: for every module $M$, the pairing $V(M)\times W(M)\to\mathcal{O}$ identifies each of the functors $V(M)$, $W(M)$ with the dual $\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathcal{O}}(-,\mathcal{O})$ of the other.
If $M$ is finitely generated projective, $W(M)\simeq V(M^{\vee})$, hence $W(M)$ is represented by the symmetric algebra $S_k(M^{\vee})$ of the dual of $M$.
